body:
I'm not sure constantly creating and deleting `AudioStreamPlayer` is a good idea from an optimization standpoint. We could use the `AudioStreamPlayer.max_polyphony` property, the new `AudioStreamPolyphonic`, or some other approach on the `AudioServer` side. Here are two options I've used in my projects for adding sound effects:

<details>
<summary>AudioStreamPlayer.max_polyphony</summary>

```gdscript
extends Node

var _players: Dictionary[String, AudioStreamPlayer]

func play(path: String) -> void:
    var player: AudioStreamPlayer = _players.get(path)
    if not player:
        player = AudioStreamPlayer.new()
        player.bus = &"SFX"
        player.stream = load(path)
        player.max_polyphony = 4
        add_child(player)
        _players[path] = player
    player.play()
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>AudioStreamPolyphonic</summary>

```gdscript
extends Node

var _playback: AudioStreamPlaybackPolyphonic
var _streams: Dictionary[String, AudioStream]

func _ready() -> void:
    var player: AudioStreamPlayer = AudioStreamPlayer.new()
    player.bus = &"SFX"
    player.stream = AudioStreamPolyphonic.new()
    #player.stream.polyphony = 32
    add_child(player)

    player.play()
    _playback = player.get_stream_playback()

func play(path: String) -> void:
    var stream: AudioStream = _streams.get(path)
    if not stream:
        stream = load(path)
        _streams[path] = stream
    _playback.play_stream(stream)
```

</details>

body:
I would allow very precise adjustments directly, without needing to adjust **Default Float Step** in the Editor Settings:

```suggestion
	ADD_PROPERTY(PropertyInfo(Variant::FLOAT, "pixel_size", PROPERTY_HINT_RANGE, "0.0001,128,0.0000001,suffix:m"), "set_pixel_size", "get_pixel_size");
```

`0.0000001` roughly matches the 32-bit float precision limit for values between `0.0` and `1.0`, so it's pretty precise already.

In the long run, the editor setting may be deprecated in favor of a more flexible solution, as per https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/3524.

Note that your PR currently doesn't adjust the lower bound, so it doesn't allow you to enter values smaller than `0.0001` regardless of this change.

> * Serialize NaN as `null` instead of `"NaN"`.
> * Print a warning when encoding NaN similar to PR [Core: Enforce strict JSON for non-finite numbers, document native workaround #111608](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/111608) (not the same message, and not for Infinity)
> * Add a warning to the documentation similar to PR [Core: Enforce strict JSON for non-finite numbers, document native workaround #111608](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/111608) (not the same docs, but similar, thanks @Repiteo).

Ok, so with these changes, I think this is now satisfying the requirements (as I remember them) that were set out at the core team meeting:

1. We match the behavior of another big project. I don't know how "big" graphite-web is, but serializing `NaN` as `null` also matches the behavior of `JSON.stringify()` in web browsers (if I open Chrome's devtools and type `JSON.stringify({"a": NaN"})` into the console it outputs `'{"a":null}'`) which is certainly a big enough target :-)
2. We print a warning, so developers have a clue to follow if they get unexpected results from a web service or whatever application they are giving the JSON to

So, I approve! However, since this was reverted, it should probably get a few more approvals before going forward

As an (unrelated) tangent, it *is* possible to force a MSAA level in the NVIDIA Control Panel on a Godot OpenGL game, but only if you use **Enhance application setting** instead of **Override application setting**. body:
Great job so far!

I think you need to rethink the logic for how this works. Currently you are bouncing the texture back and forth between MSAA and non-MSAA several times per frame which should never happen. When MSAA is being used everything should render in MSAA. There is no reason to even allocate the non-MSAA texture when MSAA is being used. There certainly isn't a good reason to copy the MSAA texture into the non-MSAA texture and back (that will lose the MSAA sample information by the way and defeat the purpose of having an MSAA texture in the first place)

While reducing the effects of `ClassDB` on compile time performance is a great goal, I'm not sure about the approach taken here (and the previous PR). I think this becomes more clear when we think about the implications of merging this PR:

If we decide the eventual goal is to remove automatic inclusion of the binding methods from the headers, we'll have to accept that every single `.cpp` file for an `Object` subclass that binds methods (i.e. all of them?) will have to include the binder headers explicitly.
From a quick glance, that's 900 files. That's a lot of work, and a lot of added includes. And in the end, every single Object subclass `.cpp` file will still include `ClassDB` because it needs to register its bindings to it. There might be some compile units that no longer need to include `ClassDB`, but I have a feeling it wouldn't be enough to be worth it.

Unfortunately, that makes the `ClassDB` include problem a bit difficult. I don't have a good idea for a solution yet, but I'm not sure it will be as straightforward here as to try to reduce how many headers include it, because it will end up in most compile units anyway.

Thanks! Optimizing `sprintf` sounds like a worthy goal to me. However, I have some reservations:

We've had some lengthy discussions over `StringBuilder` a year or so ago, and my current understanding is that it might not be as useful for optimization purposes as previously believed, especially when compared to `StringBuffer`. However, I have not pursued this investigation yet.
I suspect the main bottleneck to be solved here is `String`'s CoW checks when adding new chars individually. Using `StringBuilder` circumvents that, but so would `StringBuffer`. I'd like to see a performance comparison between the two in this context before I'd feel comfortable giving this an approval.

Outside the approach taken in the PR, I'd like to ask you to separate the `StringBuilder` changes from the `String` changes. I've previously attempted to optimize `StringBuilder` in a similar way, but found that there was no difference to the current implementation. So whether the re-write is an improvement should be tested separately.

body:
Note that this is a **very** strong case for us outputting `±1e99999` for `±INF` values: the overwhelming majority of parsers, *including our own*, already resolve the values as such. This is because RFC 8259[^1], the de-facto implementation standard for JSON, does not specify a limit on the precision:
> This specification allows implementations to set limits on the range and precision of numbers accepted.

However, in saying that, it DOES recommend limiting it to representable range:
> Since software that implements IEEE 754 binary64 (double precision) numbers [IEEE754] is generally available and widely used, good interoperability can be achieved by implementations that expect no more precision or range than these provide, in the sense that implementations will approximate JSON numbers within the expected precision.

As such, even if we do output it, we shouldn't "support" it. Like, it could be our "best-effort" fallback, but we should absolutely recommend parsing to/from native for non-finite values.

[^1]: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8259.html#section-6

If the number of arguments is not 4, line "0" will be added. This doesn't look right to me.

For `Tr()` and `TrN()`, the line number should be determined by the call, not by the optional argument (since these method calls can contain multiple translatable strings at once, and we want to specify only one starting line, not a line range). At least that's the logic in GDScript ([source](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/36b92128b1bce1f98687add98c84fd70ae9b20ca/modules/gdscript/editor/gdscript_translation_parser_plugin.cpp#L344-L400)):

`tr()`, `atr()`:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/36b92128b1bce1f98687add98c84fd70ae9b20ca/modules/gdscript/editor/gdscript_translation_parser_plugin.cpp#L355

`tr_n()`, `atr_n()`:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/36b92128b1bce1f98687add98c84fd70ae9b20ca/modules/gdscript/editor/gdscript_translation_parser_plugin.cpp#L375

But other methods like `set_text()`:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/36b92128b1bce1f98687add98c84fd70ae9b20ca/modules/gdscript/editor/gdscript_translation_parser_plugin.cpp#L379

Also note the comment:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/36b92128b1bce1f98687add98c84fd70ae9b20ca/modules/gdscript/editor/gdscript_translation_parser_plugin.cpp#L350

body:
Tested using the GDQuest TPS demo. I ran it in both Mobile and Forward+ to check for obvious visual regressions and I profiled a dev build. Since the optimization here is the number of times GPU driver code is called, the optimization level shouldn't make a differnece. 

I observed a reproducible 5-10% improvement in the `end_frame()` function. Out of a 1 second profile, that is 70 ms -> 60-65ms. Which would correspond to a 1% overall improvement in CPU time. 

On an optimized build that percentage would be a little higher since the driver code isn't affected by optimizations. But overall the expected improvement would be about 0.1 mspf.

In any rate, its still an optimization worth doing and it might have more of an impact on devices where the drivers are quite slow (i.e. mobile devices)

body:
Looking at the [edit history for the page](https://controllers.fandom.com/wiki/Sony_DualSense?action=history), it appears that [Nielk1](https://github.com/Nielk1) (who also wrote [the gist for building the packets](https://gist.github.com/Nielk1/6d54cc2c00d2201ccb8c2720ad7538db)) is the author and presumed reverse-engineer(er?).

In the [gist comments](https://gist.github.com/Nielk1/6d54cc2c00d2201ccb8c2720ad7538db?permalink_comment_id=3887913#gistcomment-3887913), they state:
> This logic was determined based on primarily Trial and Error. It was determined by inspecting Metro Exodus's output that only a few functions were used by the official libpad implementation. These functions utilize bit-packing to function and took some time to work out. I do not have access to libpad, so these function signatures may not match those of the official library.
> ...
> The "part of libpad" factories were found by partial reverse engineering. Some functions related to generating these values were found but were not reversed directly, instead they were monitored to determine what inputs were given to them and what outputs ended up eventually being sent to the USB device. 
> ...
> The bulk of the work was done by examining that at a specific point, the stack and CPU registers had specific values, and then shortly later the DualSense received a specific USB report structure.
> ...
> To further clarify, I am 99% confident that only 3 of these effects (and reset) are part of Sony's official API. The other effects were determined by intelligently fuzzing the controller after learning to avoid the debug/calibration effects and that the first byte of the effect appears safely to be the effect type enum value.
> ...
> After leaning how to reset the effect, it was reset between every random fuzz write which eliminated all false positives. Thanks to the Apple API, which appears to be a crude and direct wrapper for the official API with float parameters, testing of direct input and output was made much easier.
> ...
> Any other effect is simply leftover data and as there is no official code for them to even try to experiment with, all were invented entirely by trial and error as noted.

I've extracted what seemed to me like the most important/summarizing statements about how they performed the reverse-engineering – it sounds like they used trial and error, along with comparing to publicly available information in [Apple's public Game Controller APIs](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/GameController/GCDualSenseAdaptiveTrigger), to arrive at their code. That being said, it may be wise for others to read through their comments more thoroughly and confirm.

Their factory code (in the gist) is MIT licensed, and the documentation on the Game Controller Collective Wiki appears to be CC BY-SA by default.

body:
I've actually already anticipated and investigated this.
The `get_rect()` function and modifications of the rendering server canvas items luckily only affect the canvas item culling and rendering, not the actual rects used for the control workflow. This is because control nodes have their own `get_rect()` and related functions which only use the transform based rect.
Hence why `debug_canvas_item_get_rect()` on the rendering server differs from `get_rect()` on control nodes.

And for some amount of reassurance: I have tested this with both the [Control Gallery Demo Project](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-demo-projects/tree/master/gui/control_gallery) and my own game project that I have been working on for roughly 2 years and have found no apparent issues in any GUI scene, be it the main menu or the gameplay menus, which make heavy use of containers and anchors with skewed styleboxes and styleboxes utilizing expand margins and drop shadows.

This also fixes more than just the `clip_children` issue, mainly:
- `CanvasGroup` not including the whole area of *any* control child that draws outside of its bounds.
- Controls that draw outside of the regular control rect getting culled when they shouldn't be. See this video using the master branch with a simple control script that draws a box using `draw_rect`:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/fcd35808-db6b-4d3a-87fc-b5e6a8dd5d0f

*All of these issues occur for custom `_draw()` implementations too and have done so since Godot 4.0*.

The idea is to make the method agnostic with regard to other Android build tools (e.g: [bazel](https://bazel.build/start/android-app), [buck](https://buck2.build/)) which also have a concept of build directory.

The Android build template is set up such as another build tool can build the project either by converting `build.gradle` into their own format, or by providing their own build config via an export plugin. 
This flexibility is extended to the build provider such that non-gradle build providers can be used as well.

When preparing https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/111557, I initially wanted to go for a SConstruct based approach as well.
However, I got caught up on 2 problems:

- I don't know an easy way to query the build system whether `libc++` is in use.
- Editing `SConstruct` also affects thirdparty libraries, some of which break.

It seems like you've run into both as well, and decided to tackle them instead.
Your approach should work everywhere, but ends up a bit more complicated than https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/111557, and has to make some 'educated guesses' about when libc++ is used.

My approach (changing `typedefs.h`) is stupid simple. But it doesn't help in all compile units (depending on include order), and comes with a small risk of unexpected missing includes in headers, depending on include order of the compile unit.

I'd be fine with choosing either. Maybe time for more people to weigh in?

All settings other than **Landscape** will use portrait mode for resolution presets: Instead, **Landscape**, **Reverse Landscape** and **Sensor Landscape** should use a landscape resolution. - Resolution presets have no effect if the **Stretch to Fit** scale mode is selected in game embedding. - To allow for a smoother UX, I suggest automatically swapping back to **Keep Aspect Ratio** when selecting a preset. Also, when choosing **Stretch to Fit**, the previously selected preset should be unchecked in the list. - When choosing a preset, it enforces a maximum resolution and aspect ratio. It does not allow the viewport to render at a higher resolution than what's shown on screen, even when using the `viewport` stretch mode. This can result in different visuals than what you'll see on the target device due to the pixel count being different. Some shaders have resolution-dependent behavior, and of course, using the `disabled` stretch mode will also result in resolution-dependent visuals.

body:
Hi, thanks for submitting a fix! 

Have you checked that this solves the problem in the intended way? 
Reasoning about the code, I would expect `CRASH_NOW_MSG` to try to print, causing a new `ScriptBacktrace` object to be instantiated, entering `ObjectDB::add_instance`... which runs into the same slot count problem, causing recursive loop and eventually, a stack overflow.

Generally, printing to the standard console won't ever be perfectly secure because even if we don't, custom loggers could always try to create new objects.

I can think of 3 solutions that might be better (not sure which would be best):
1) Crash _before_ we run out of slots. But that would reduce our total slot counts by 1, so I'm not sure this would be a well liked solution.
2) Crash without printing a message
3) Print using a lower-level API instead, guaranteeing that no `Object` will be created. The message won't reach the console, but at least it will reach the logs

body:
You can basically remove any call to resize that is guaranteed to be less than 13 since those cases will be the same performance or slightly slower with the added call to resize. 

This highlights why it is important to profile. If you checked these "optimizations" with a profiler you would have seen that the added code doesn't make a difference. 

Please read our optimization guidelines https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/engine/guidelines/optimization.html which explain a bit more the thought process you should engage in when deciding to optimize code. Importantly, you should only spend time optimizing code that actually impacts the run time performance of games. Its not really a good use of time to add code that saves a few microseconds in a method that is only called once during some debug method. In fact, its a net negative since it just makes the code more complex for no tangible benefit

Hi, thanks for opening a pull request!
Please note our guidelines for new features: [Best practices for engine contributions](https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/engine/guidelines/best_practices.html#the-problem-has-to-be-complex-or-frequent).
Specifically, the problem should be _complex or frequent_.

Since the problem is not complex (it can be worked around with a subtraction), we should wait for the proposal to be popular before considering to merge it. If it becomes popular, that would be an indication that this is a frequent problem for people.

body: I think the analysis of the problem is wrong. It's not that `Variant` is inherently missing, it's that variant is called `Nil` in the variant type enum names (I think `Variant::NIL` is supposed to be GDScripts `Variant` but if someone more knowledgeable could confirm this it would be great). In completion it appears under that name: which is obviously wrong. This PR adds `Variant` to the list without handling the wrong `Nil` option. A fix should happen in `_find_build_in_variants` which is responsible for adding variant types. Don't be confused by the special case for `Nil` in `_find_build_in_variants` which converts it to `null`. That's an erroneous codepath. This method should not be resposible for adding `null`. There is other code to handle this.

Modules are in a weird spot, because they seem to want to dynamically insert themselves into different encapsulation levels, but are locked into a singular encapsulation level already. With more and more parts of the codebase getting the ability to be toggled at buildtime (drivers in particular), I don't think the whole separation aspect of modules holds the same significance it  once did

I don't want to ignore them though. This PR is about identifying breakage in encapsulation as it's currently defined, and making it obvious where these discrepancies exist is important if we want to eventually move to a new system

We define the reflect objects in the Shader Container, so that data flows outwards from Shader Container. It allows us to evolve what we reflect that is passed to the driver-specific shader containers.

Further, the `ReflectShader` type is passed to the driver-specific implementations to inspect the reflected SPIR-V.

Previously we were traversing the reflected SPIR-V and constructing `RDD::ShaderReflection`, which is used by the drivers and `RenderingDriver`. We were also using ShaderReflection to construct the internal state of the RenderingShaderContainer and also constructing the ShaderReflection from the internal state. We wanted to add more metadata to ShaderReflection, so Metal could build stable bindings, but that would mean changing ShaderReflection.

author: clayjohn

body:
The primary gain is that Metal is no longer using SPIRV-Cross reflection. It only calls the compiler to generate the Metal Shader Language source.

SPIRV-Cross reflection is lazy, so because we're not calling it, we're not paying the CPU and memory costs of instantiating basically equivalent metadata. 

----

The intent of `ReflectUniform` and `ReflectSpecialisationConstant` is to wrap their underlying `SpvReflect` type so that containers such as Metal can use this reflected metadata directly. The key is the `ReflectSymbol<SpvReflectSpecializationConstant>`, which wraps the spirv-reflect `SpvReflectSpecializationConstant` type, providing direct access to that metadata. There is an equivalent `ReflectUniform`, which wraps the `SpvReflectDescriptorBinding` so Metal can directly access any additional SpvReflect metadata without having to traverse the SpvReflect module again.

My thoughts were we don't count anything under a `Viewport` (or derived class) Node, and make this the only rule. If a scene root is Viewport we simply don't create thumbnails for it, then fallback to old-style thumbnail creation. IMO This would make up for most cases and is deterministic, if we go for complex conditions users might get confused.

(Just my thoughts, but I still respect maintainers decision, your call)

BTW the issue you mentioned above is due to fall-back to old thumbnail creation too, checking on that. The scene should not re-create thumbnails at all if file hash didn't change.

So in your case a scene with 100 2D nodes and a subviewport node in it, it will still count as 2D scene as the viewport node is ignored.

The most plausible way might be implement some tagging system for scene files, to explicitly tell the engine it's a 2d/3d scene.

body:
To leave comments and trace of deprecation, you can call it a bad habit of mine. But this particularly has confused me a lot:

`RSG::rasterizer::can_create_resources_async()` is a virtual function overridden by `rasterizer_gles3.h` and it simply returns `false`. This line was modified by PR https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/90400 and left untouched since then. Before that PR, it was `TextureStorage::can_create_resources_async()` and simply returns `true`

As far as I can tell this boolean is mainly used to determine if we initialize textures on thread or push to command queue at RenderingServer.

I did not dive deeper so I went with flipping this back to `true` here, and make all operations in this PR that's not thread-safe to be called on idle time using `call_deferred()` (creating scene, interact with main tree), and polish it out by testing, keep everything on thread as much as possible, move calls that causes issue to idle time.

> Also what if threads are not available? (on Web editor I presume)

I didn't know this, let me think further

				Sets the extra cull margin for this light, allowing it to not get culled by the Forward+ clustering algorithm or the AABB-based algorithm in Mobile and Compatibility. Set along with [member Light3D.light_extra_cull_margin]. This allows lights on vertex-shaded materials or custom light shaders to not get culled early while their influence is still visible on screen. For best performance, this should be set to the lowest possible value that does not result in the light disappearing while its influence is still visible on screen.

body:
Using keywords to list all possible values in an enumerated property or setting gives away a big flaw in how searches are made in the engine.
That is to say, this should **not** be the purpose of keywords and, in an ideal world, these values should be present in the class's XML file directly, ready to be queried as needed.

Portray yourself as the common user looking this setting. They may not know the proper term for this, so they may think about something like `resolution`, `scale`, `ratio`, even `width` or `height` if we're stretching (_pun intended_). They may certainly not look for `keep_height` (underscore _included_ otherwise the keyword doesn't match)

```suggestion
		The heightmap is represented as a 2D grid of height values, which represent the offset of grid points on the Y axis. Internally, each grid square is divided into two triangles. The grid is centered on the origin of the [HeightMapShape3D] node. Grid points are spaced 1 unit apart on the X and Z axes. If you need to use different spacing, you can adjust the [member Node3D.scale] of the shape. However, keep in mind that non-uniform scales are not supported: you'll need to scale the Y axis by the same amount as the X and Z axes, which means the values in [member map_data] will need to be pre-scaled by the inverse of that scale.
```

I would suggest moving anything following "_If you need to use different spacing, you can adjust [...]" to a separate note below the description. This whole line currently goes from describing the heightmap shape to a whole different tangent.
Speaking of the tip itself, we do not recommend to to scale collision shapes, so I'm not sure if this advice is sound, myself.
author: Mickeon

body:
I'm going to be stubborn and change it to "height map" consistently because the class name is `HeightMapShape3D`, not `HeightmapShape3D`.

Citing the Jolt PR #99895:

> Godot Physics supports scaling the transform of collision shapes, shape queries, as well as static and kinematic bodies, meaning StaticBody3D, CharacterBody3D, AnimatableBody3D and frozen RigidBody3D. It does not however support scaling simulated/dynamic bodies, such as a non-frozen RigidBody3D, and will effectively discard any such scaling, instead treating it as (1, 1, 1).
> 
> Jolt does however support scaling everywhere, and I've tried my best to utilize that, which means that RigidBody3D will support scaling when using Jolt, despite the warning shown on the node currently.
> 
> Jolt also supports non-uniform scaling, so long as the inherent primitive shape is preserved. For example, you can scale a cylinder along its height axis but not along its other axes. You will however currently see warnings on the shape node when doing this, due to Godot Physics not supporting this.

I've updated the advice to account for this.

Maybe someone sees a way to improve this reformulation of the first sentence? I think the reformulation is necessary, because the original version is confusing in two ways:

1) it's written in the wrong order: the angle actually goes from the X axis to the line between the two points, _not_ from the line to the X-axis
2) `line connecting the two points` implies symmetry, and that the order between the two points is irrelevant. That's not the case though: `a.angle_to_point(b) != b.angle_to_point(a)` !

Flickering has to do with thin geometry face and low pixel count. Nvidia suggests using MSAA with TAA to help with this issue and indeed does work. I will post video in next comment to help visualize the problem and how the result changes. 

With latest push the calculations have been moved to outside the shader. I removed one hardcoded parameter in the passed 16 bit buffer, since I think it's not good idea to make the buffer larger. body:
This makes sense to me. Sounds like a good first step to reduce `Variant` implicit conversions!

The only concern I have is that a lot of these conversions/comparisons are making allocations. Mainly, I'm talking about all the string literal comparisons.
This PR doesn't change this - the comparisons are already unnecessarily making conversions. But it would be "setting it in stone", not to be optimized later. And we would have no better alternative for anyone who wants to avoid this.

I'm not sure if there is a good solution to that. 
In my own code, I might use something like `variant.get_type() == Variant::STRING && String(variant) == "literal"`, but this is probably too verbose/unexpected for our own codebase.

The only thing I can think of would be to have an `operator==(const char *)` (implemented with the above check). Then, we wouldn't have to cast `"literal"` to `(Variant)`.
On the plus side, this would really optimize the PR, and give it a bit of a performance boost too.
On the negative side, this would make a "special case" for `String` `Variant` handling, which we may not want to add.

I think all in all, I'd be in favour of making that addition. But I'd be interested to hear your thoughts.

body:
Thank you for looking into it! Your patch makes a lot of sense and IMO it's _almost_ perfect as is :D

I say almost because there are lots of small timing quirks to ensure, ideally.

Technically, what we're actually looking for is a _commit_, which applies the position hint, not a frame event per se. Frame events and commits are related as to request a frame callback you (or the renderer, or whatever) need to commit the surface but it could already have been requested by the time we receive it.

Also, the current logic basically assumes that surfaces are always committed from the _main thread_ every `DisplayServer::process_events` loop, either from the renderer or our own refresh logic for low consumption mode, which also gives some synchronization (mutex) concerns.

Probably the _ideal_ solution would be to have a callback of sorts at the start of the event loop to signal (somewhat late) to the Wayland thread that the previous main thread loop ended and only then reset the constraint. This is terribly not ideal, as technically there's a frame where the cursor is locked, but that's what the pointer constraints protocol entails FWIU.

I'll note this down somewhere and take a look whenever the time comes.

> No compatibility methods registered because it breaks C# builds.

What do you mean by this? That since there's a compile-time error, there's no risk of breaking at runtime?

If yes, that misses the point: this is primarily about GDExtension (as indicated by file path), although it covers C# as well. GDExtensions must remain _binary compatible_, i.e. an extension compiled against Godot 4.1 must still run without UB under Godot 4.5.

In this case that is true because `float` and `double` are represented the same in GDExtension's FFI (namely as `double`), but that means you should change the reasoning here.

body: I think I may have made my earlier descriptions confusing. The "alternate convention" is that the products of intertia themselves are computed as positive products (eg. $I_{xy} = \Sigma m_i x_i y_i$) and then negated when placed in the tensor; it has nothing to do with the order in which they're presented. The choice of order $(I_{yz}, I_{xz}, I_{xy})$ comes from Voigt notation (or specifically the second half of a tensor in Voigt notation). It's the least arbitrary order to chose, in my opinion.

body:
The XY, XZ, YZ order comes from the typical order used in Geometric Algebra, which is to specify each pair of dimensions in a dimensionally-increasing order. The YZ, XZ, XY order comes from symmetry with 3D rotations in most game engines, where we think of things as rotating "around" X, but it's actually in the YZ plane. So we fill the Vector's X, Y, and Z components with the YZ, XZ, and XY rotations, respectively.

IMO, it is more intuitive to be consistent with the 3D rotation order used in the rest of the engine, even if these are not rotations. Users of 3D can intuitively understand the concept of the X value containing the value that exists perpendicular to the X axis, even if technically that acts on everything but X. For my 4D module I often chose to put things in YZ, XZ, XY, XW, YW, ZW order in the exposed API, to build on the intuitions of 3D users.

TL;DR: I think the version in this PR is good.

We discussed this fix in the core meeting.
We agree that the approach you take (rejecting the object deletion in the editor only) is appropriate.

However, there are two changes I think are needed:

- Check for whether it's actually the editor via `Engine::get_singleton()->is_editor_hint()`. Otherwise, the runtime using the editor binary will also reject the deletion, causing a discrepancy in `DEBUG` vs `RELEASE`.
- Move this check to `node.cpp` in the `NOTIFICATION_PREDELETE` handler, right after the `is_main_thread` check. This will prevent the same kind of bug when using `.free()` and `memdelete`. You can reject deletion here using `cancel_free()` (and `return`).

body:
This is always defined when ambient occlusion is enabled, so there's no way to use ambient occlusion without also having micro shadows enabled in the core shader. This leaves performance on the table if you set Micro Shadows to `0.0`.

I suggest adding a boolean **Micro Shadows > Enabled** property in BaseMaterial3D (`true` by default), then a **Micro Shadows > Strength** property (`0.85` by default). This way, you can set the first property to `false` and have no performance cost compared to 4.5.

(We can't use the existing Micro Shadows property alone, as inspector updates when dragging a slider currently don't work well.)

That said, maybe this option is too niche to be toggled on a per-material basis, and should be disabled in the project settings instead (similar to specular occlusion: `rendering/reflections/specular_occlusion/enabled`).
author: Calinou

body:
Let me see if I understood you correctly:

- You want a new property, micro_shadows_enabled, to be added to ambient occlusion in StandardMaterial3D.
- This property should be set to true by default.
- You want to add a new setting in the project settings to globally disable microshadows.
- This global setting should be set to false by default.

Is this what you are suggesting?
author: LiveTrower

body:
Yes, that sounds good to me. However, I would make the project setting affirmative (i.e. `micro_shadows/enabled` that is `true` by default).

In the future, we should look into adding similar "kill switch" properties for demanding BaseMaterial3D features, so that you can toggle them globally: https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/2455

This is however nontrivial to implement in a way that doesn't require a restart to be effective (so you can use it in graphics settings menus). That said, we can leave this for later for a first implementation.

🏎️ We're taking advantage of the new `binding` field, which means we are using the same buffer binding slot for all vertex attributes. Rather than binding 8 buffers (with potentially different frequency and stride values) every draw call, we now only bind one buffer. 

A binding specifies how the buffer is read by the GPU, controlled by `frequency` and `stride`. Assuming the driver doesn't coalesce all 8 bindings, that reduces bookkeeping from 8 to 1 buffer.

If so, I think a different collection type would be needed that has pointer stability around resizes (like a std::deque). Although those types might have less CPU caching benefits.
author: brycehutchings

body: You're right about the potential pointer invalidation. However, we're trusting the call-and-back itself is immune to that, so the line below about handling realloc should be enough. It'd be good to prove the former point more formally, though.
author: RandomShaper

body:
Here's the sequence that I am concerned about:
1. Thread A pushes a command
2. Thread B starts flushing. It completes `lock.temp_unlock();`
3. Thread A or C pushes another command but the LocalVector can't hold it so it resizes. In the process the `realloc` call has to create a new block of memory and copy the old contents into it. The old memory block is now freed
4. Thread B continues running. It now does `cmd->call()` but `cmd` is pointing to memory in the old block that was freed (and potentially reused for something else)

I think we'd have to make a copy of the contents of the struct to a local variable before unlocking to avoid risk of the pointer pointing to a stale memory address. Maybe this extra copy is worth it, compared to the alternative solutions?
author: brycehutchings

body:
Such `if` would indeed prevent concurrent flushing of the queue. However, that wouldn't be enough for memory synchronization. In the case of multiple flusher threads, the lock in this function protects both the command queue data and the "subject" data. For instance, any of both physics servers can be flushed both from its dedicated pumping thread and the main thread. If commands targeting that server were left run without the lock held, the two threads would be out-of-sync memory wise.

That said, out of the scope of this PR there are two potential enhancements:
- 1) Modify the cases of non-unique-flusher so they always flush from the same thread. That would clear the path towards what you're suggesting.
- 2) On top of the previous point, it'd be worth analyzing if there's any remaining case of "unlock allowance." If not, such feature could be completely removed.

body:
I found a paper explaining the idea of squaring the delta angle from the Jacobian Transpose.

https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~15464-s13/lectures/lecture6/iksurvey.pdf section 5

So I'm inclined to agree that this change could help.

That said, I am concerned about the possibility of `head_to_effector` having length units (as opposed to a unitless ratio). From what I can tell, this variable is the difference between two values in `p_setting->chain`, which themselves are assigned directly from `get_bone_global_pose(...).origin`, which are in units of meters. However, `get_bone_axis` is normalizng the returned axis, producing a unitless value. Hence, the resulting angle used in `to_rot` appears to be in units of `1/length`

I'd like to make sure that the IK produces different solutions between two equivalent skeletons with different uniform scales (for example, both a 1 meter humanoid reaching a target 1 meter away, and a 100 meter humanoid reaching a target 100 meters away should produce the same angle). During testing, it is common to use default cube or human scale skeletons with roughly 1 meter length head-to-effector, so it might obscure bugs that happen at very large or very small scale.

I'm okay trying this PR to solve issues at human scale, but we might want to test very small and very large skeletons to make sure that the distance between head and effector is properly divided out.

author: timothyqiu

body:
> How much do translations have to match to... be considered "matched"?

Anything above zero, is match. Which means at least language code is equivalent (string might be different, since there are platform specific aliases).

10 is full match. Which means all components are equivalent (but again, strings can be different, since it accounts for default and aliases).

e.g, following two case all full match (10):

```gdscript
compare_locales("zh_Hans", "zh_CN")
compare_locales("iw", "he")
```

A typical use case for `compare_locales` is picking a translation with the highest non-zero score.

This PR removes some of these checks.

Without any checks, setting the padding here was being applied even in immersive mode on older devices, while it worked as expected on Android 11+ devices. To fix the issue on older versions, I had added the check to apply padding only when not in immersive mode. I missed that this change caused a slight window shrink when the keyboard appeared, so I’m now updating it to always skip padding in immersive mode across all devices.

The horizontal size flag for `preset_vb` was set to expand, which caused it to try filling the parent’s width. Tested locally (rebased on top of `master` https://github.com/godotengine/godot/commit/9273a6a9a04d12299f05aa34606a1c386a00deda), it works as expected. Code looks good to me.

I've also tested combinations like `width=2em` and `height=10%`, which is unusual, but works as you'd expect.

This is particularly useful for button prompts, which are often embedded in text but can be found at different sizes depending on which text they appear in. However, note that DPITexture oversampling is not aware of the different sizing, so the icon can appear a little blurry at high font sizes (or grainy at low font sizes if the icon's base scale is high and mipmaps are disabled). https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/7411 could help reduce blurriness when mipmaps are enabled.

I think it's fine to use `em` as a unit in the end. While BBCode forums often supported `%` for font sizes relative to `100%`, this created an ambiguity with image widths and deviated from web development standards.

I couldn't test this in tandem with https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/116791 due to merge conflicts in that PR. Hopefully, both PRs *should* be able to work together, but this should be tested if that PR is merged first (or vice versa for the other PR).

In my opinion, exposing the documentation as a `Dictionary` is fine, given that this functionality is rarely needed, is already exposed in the virtual method `ScriptLanguageExtension::_get_documentation()`, and for `DocData` structures, we strive to maintain compatibility when converting to/from `Dictionary`.

I think creating a "more robust" API is overkill in this case. Since we don't have structs in the type system, the only choice is between a dictionary (in the spirit of `get_property_list()` and some other methods) and a complex API consisting of multiple classes/methods. But the machine-readable access to documentation is rarely needed and isn't that important, even if we accidentally break compatibility at some point.

In my opinion, the only question is how to document the dictionary structure. A full description is somewhat cumbersome. Should we include it, or could we just add a link to the source code?

body:
First impression after reading the code: `virtual` is an unnecessary cost on this new implementation. It's prone to the callee code being thrown out of the branch predictor, and the code cache, since it's not known at compile time which branch will be called.[^1] This cost should be especially present if other code is called in between calling this code (which I believe isn't accounted for in your cold tests, since you just churn memory instead of code). The use of `virtual` also unnecessarily increases the size of `AHashMap` / `AHashSet` because of the pointer tables.

I'd advise to remove polymorphism from `RawAHashTable`, and design it as a composeable property instead. 
If that turns out impossible, or too difficult, you could use [CRTP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curiously_recurring_template_pattern) to replace the runtime polymorphism with compile time polymorphism.
Also, I should mention that trying to add `RawAHashTable` might be an [inappropriate assumption](https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/engine/guidelines/best_practices.html#to-each-problem-its-own-solution) in the first place. We should only try to abstract when it's actually useful to reduce complexity in the code. If making it composeable is impossible, or CRTP turns out too complicated, it might be preferable to simply duplicate the hash table code for `AHashSet`.

[^1]: It's technically possible for the compiler to optimize the virtual call out, since everything is in headers, but I wouldn't rely on it.
author: Ivorforce

body:
> First impression after reading the code: virtual is an unnecessary cost on this new implementation.

I would assume that GCC devirtualizes and inlines them, as in perf reports they are shown as inlined functions. Clang probably does the same as well, but MSVC is the scary one here. We all know how conservative it is when it is when it comes to optimization.

> I'd advise to remove polymorphism from RawAHashTable, and design it as a composeable property instead.

While I would also agree on preferring composition over inheritance; in our case, turning RawAHashTable an inner field would heavily increase our complexity. It would require us to reintroduce the `_lookup_idx_with_hash` back into AHash* types and add some extras into the RawAHashTable, such as an iterator. I may try it, but can't promise with the results.

> If that turns out impossible, or too difficult, you could use [CRTP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curiously_recurring_template_pattern) to replace the runtime polymorphism with compile time polymorphism.

This probably is the solution with the least amount of code changes. I will try my hand with it.

> Also, I should mention that trying to add RawAHashTable might be an [inappropriate assumption](https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/engine/guidelines/best_practices.html#to-each-problem-its-own-solution) in the first place. We should only try to abstract when it's actually useful to reduce complexity in the code. If making it composeable is impossible, or CRTP turns out too complicated, it might be preferable to simply duplicate the hash table code for AHashSet.

My goal was less of an abstraction and more of sharing of logic between AHash* containers, with the least amount of code duplication. Just duplicating the code and removing anything related to values are they easy way, but somewhat defeats my main goal.

If C++ had a reliable way to have zero-size types we wouldn't even need the RawAHashTable to achieve any of this, but here we are.
author: Brogolem35

body:
> If C++ had a reliable way to have zero-size types we wouldn't even need the RawAHashTable to achieve any of this, but here we are.

C++20 has `no_unique_address`, which might be a solution. It may be a while until we shift to C++20, but we are also in no hurry to consolidate the types code wise. Copy-pasting the code for now, and consolidating later in C++20 `no_unique_address` would be preferable in my eyes to introducing `RawAHashTable` and removing it again in C++20, because we can just implement `AHashSet` on top of `AHashMap`.
(assuming we _can_ implement `AHashSet` on top of `AHashMap`)

```suggestion
			The duration to wait before a request times out, in seconds (independent of [member Engine.time_scale]). If [member timeout] is set to [code]0.0[/code], the request will never time out.
			For simple requests, such as communication with a REST API, it is recommended to set [member timeout] to a value suitable for the server response time (commonly between [code]1.0[/code] and [code]10.0[/code]). This will help prevent unwanted timeouts caused by variation in response times while still allowing the application to detect when a request has timed out. For larger requests such as file downloads, it is recommended to set [member timeout] to [code]0.0[/code], disabling the timeout functionality. This will help prevent large transfers from failing due to exceeding the timeout value.
```

I think this should not be changed. The purpose of the brackets is to ensure that the lock is only held for the following line of code. 

Currently, that line of code is the last line of code in the block, so this change won't change current behaviour. But it does change the semantics of the function. 

With the suggested change, we change from "hold this lock during this one line of code" to "hold this lock for the rest of this block". 

The former makes it safe and easy to extend or refactor this block as needed. The latter creates a hidden trap for future maintainers

body:
Makes sense in principle to have `String` conversions that don't involve `Variant`.

I'm a bit torn on adding normal constructors to `String`. Currently, it's not possible to e.g. convert from `double` to `String` without calling `num_real` explicitly. 
On the one hand, being able to convert anything to `String` is convenient and expected. Like the `str` function in `Python`, you can just expect anything to describe itself conveniently.
On the other hand, it's not 100% unambiguous what a conversion from a primitive to `String` means (bool and `nullptr_t` especially). For example in Rust, this is solved not by conversion operators, but by implementing traits `Debug` and `Display`, which are a bit more explicit about what kind of `String` conversion is expected. 

So in the end, I'm not sure we want to add non-contextual `String` conversion by default. Maybe something for another core meeting?

body:
You basically summarised word-by-word what I was thinking when I "casually" made that suggestion. It was not truly "casual" because I have been thinking about it for quite a while, but...

There's also one more reason that's not mentioned among @Ivorforce's: I don't think the **History** dock deserves that much vertical space to be displayed. While the history can go pretty far back in time, most users will only really be interested in the top-most options in the list (the most recent **EditorUndoRedo** actions).

Anyway, that's why I approve from an usability standpoint.

However, let's be wary of a few considerations before getting this merged:
- This will ruin some users' workflow, which is absolutely inevitable for any change of this kind.
	- We should merge this sooner than later, evaluate the feedback, and see if it matches our reasoning and expectations.
	- It is fairly intuitive for the user to move the **History** dock back where it used to be after this PR, if absolutely desired.
- You can easily debate that, for several reasons, the History dock could be hidden by default, instead.
	- I must heavily note that doing this would serve little to no purpose for the time being, if not just to declutter the editor. There must be a good reason to do so (for example, space for a new dock in its place).
	- [Since its introduction](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/65012), the original author [does not have a particular fondness](https://chat.godotengine.org/channel/editor-design?msg=NAR3SyvM32Nn5ysvY) of the **History** dock (😭)
	- Let's remember that no one is arguing to _remove_ the **History** dock. This is not an option; the **History** dock has proven to be useful, albeit niche.

body:
I can confirm it is illegal to store a reference into a mutating `AHashMap`, for the reasons given in the OP. For more information, see [Core types](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/engine_details/architecture/core_types.html#containers). 

This is notably not the case for `HashMap`, which was previously used, which I think makes this a regression from #92554 (4.4). Interesting how it didn't come up yet!

Considering this, an alternative solution to what's proposed here would be exchanging `AHashMap` for `HashMap` again, although this would regress the performance benefits measured in #92554.
Overall, I'd probably go with the solution proposed here. But I'll leave this decision for the animation team to make.

body:
> Remember that a GDScript test has more overhead than just AHashMap lookups and is more prone to fluctuations.

Yes, this is the reason I usually test from C++ instead of from GDScript for core containers. I agree that GDScript performance tests are preferable in general, since they can show that the improvement has an actual impact on GDScript code. 
But, that's only if the improvement is large enough for it to affect GDScript measurably. With container optimizations, this isn't often the case, because the GDScript bottlenecks lie elsewhere. Since the fluctuation is much higher than the improvement in your benchmarks, that makes these tests inadequate for this kind of change.

> Note that in many cases, replacing HashMap with AHashMap may either cause mixed results or a slowdown, something I've seen many times and is now visible in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/112039. And on the latter, having this PR on top actually sped things up even placing that on top of this.

When I look at those results, I'm seeing measurement fluctuations more than 'mixed results'. You're trying to optimize something with an improvement threshold far below the cost of the bottleneck of what you're trying to measure. It's very easy to misinterpret results like this as improvements or regressions.

> So, is this PR being judged more by my previous PRs than by itself?

No, I judge the code and tests first and foremost. I've commented my reservations multiple times above too.
You clearly put a lot of effort into profiling and benchmarking, and I appreciate that. That's exactly what we need for optimization PRs.
But so far, you've ignored the high fluctuations of your measurements, which often led to you amending your PRs to include various changes that are unlikely to have a performance impact. I highly suspect you're overinterpreting the fluctuations of your measurements, so I'm pleading with you to take a step back and review your targets and your methodology. If you're interested, we could have a chat about how.

I don't see why CodeEdit should handle color hints. 
The parsing logic is language specific and doesn't make sense for all languages. CodeEdit is general purpose, having color hints or even just a color picker on it does not suit it.
Once inlay hints are exposed, users can add color pickers on their own, and they probably will want to customize it. The current implementation is very opinionated since it has an option button injected into the default ColorPicker, so users will have to keep that in mind.
It shouldn't be too much effort to implement it either once the inlay hints are exposed, so its not saving users much time.

body:
We have an exception in the type system that allows untyped arrays to reference typed ones. Accordingly, typed arrays can also accept untyped arrays, but source lines involving such operations are marked as unsafe (at runtime, the untyped array may or may not be of the correct type). For constants, the situation is different in that we know the values ​​statically, and this part of the type-checking logic fails in a constant context.

```gdscript
# Godot 4.5.1

const UNTYPED_ARRAY: Array = ["a"]
const A: Array[int] = UNTYPED_ARRAY # Marked as safe.
print(A) # Bug: Prints `["a"]`.

var untyped_array: Array = ["a"]
# Runtime error: Trying to assign an array of type "Array" to a variable of type "Array[int]".
var a: Array[int] = untyped_array # Marked as unsafe.
print(a)
```

body: The difference is that regular constant folding always works, in both dynamic and constant contexts. Meanwhile, `make_*_reduced_value()` methods are called exclusively in constant context (constant initializers, annotation arguments). Thus, we prohibit treating `<constant array> + <constant array>` as a constant expression in dynamic context (via regular constant folding) and allow it in constant context (via the fallback constant folding mechanism).

body:
Core changes look good. Packed arrays are indeed shared inside `Variant`.

However, I think the history of the function should be considered before merge:

- The function started in GODOT IS OPEN SOURCE without considering packed arrays as shared.
- Later, @vnen changed this via https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/62462/, to fix setter related bugs.
- Later still, @vnen reverted this change via https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/72398 because packed arrays "are copied on C++/script boundaries".

Indeed, packed arrays behave differently inside and outside `Variant`. For example, `Variant` based calls copy the arrays across the boundary, while the `ptrcall` does not cause a copy to be made.
I still think `is_type_shared` makes sense to be `true` for packed arrays in the context of `Variant`, but we should tread carefully to not overinterpret this information.
I checked `is_type_shared` and `is_shared`, and they seem to only be used inside GDScript / the GDScript vm. 

So please confirm you're confident the GDScript changes are fine, especially with regards to https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/72398 / https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/62857. If so, I agree we should merge this.

It's fine for now but having to maintain this list here is sure going to lead to inconsistencies eventually when relevant args are added/removed in `main`.

Not sure what's the best way to handle this, it probably should be in `Main`, but there's an issue with the way command line arguments caused by macOS specific quirks:

- `OS_MacOS` need to know if it's headless on init to pick correct main loop for the app.

I've come up with a way to remove the `operator Variant()`: There's only a handful of places where we need to generically convert to `Variant`, and they are all internal, so I've made an internal helper method for it

body:
Most of the changes look pretty trivial. In particular, the `RequiredParam` changes mostly verify themselves, due to the protections of the class :)

I'm a bit more reserved about the `RequiredResult` changes. There is no way of making absolutely certain that a function doesn't introduce a non-erroneous `nullptr` return path in the future. Having it marked as `RequiredResult` may be incompatible with projects that assume `nullptr` is an error.
I have no ideas to avoid this, but since `nullptr` _does_ mean some kind of error for many getter functions maybe we don't _need_ to address this either?

The only other caveat i have is that in its current state, `RequiredParam` is slightly slower than `const Ref &`, since it requires a copy of the `Ref` be made. This overhead is hopefully not relevant in any of the functions, but I can't say for sure.
(I have a plan to optimize this in the future, so the regression should hopefully be temporary anyway)

Adding this if-statement would remove a feature from the engine where it is possible to change the microphone input_device while it is running.  

Instead you would have to call `set_input_device_active(false)`, then change the device, before calling `set_input_device_active(true)`.

This is actually how it is implemented under the hood on some of the platforms, see here:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/master/drivers/pulseaudio/audio_driver_pulseaudio.cpp#L557

However, this hot-swapping feature is hacky because it handles the case where the new_input_device fails by shutting down the thread, while being unable to inform the game that it has failed.

If changing the input device was only possible when the input was switched off (easy to do with the new function), then the failure case can be properly handled when it is switched back on when `set_input_device_active(true)` is called.

I think this PR is as ready to merge as it will ever get. Great job!
I'm not in the audio team, so it would be nice to get confirmation on its mergability as well. I'm hoping to fit it into 4.6, since it's a pretty riskless, potentially high impact change.

Since this PR has quite some history, I want to lay out my reasons for endorsing this form of the feature.
Full disclosure, I have been part of a few audio meetings discussing this, and further had dedicated meetings with @goatchurchprime discussing this feature in detail. This PR is the outcome of these discussions.

**First off, why is this feature needed?**
To cut it short, the current way to accept microphone data is inherently flawed. It is done through `AudioEffectCapture`, after it has [experienced a lot of travel](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/105244#issuecomment-2830480213) through the audio systems.
The main problem with this is that audio input is accepted asynchronously to the audio server's clock. Even when they have the same theoretical sampling rate, they inevitably drift apart. This can lead to either too many samples being produced to consume, or too few. In our codebase, this leads to audio stutters and gaps (previously, it led to capture ending abruptly), making audio capturing like this problematic. A way to fix it in place might be to resample on the fly, but this is expensive and difficult, and more importantly, it is not needed.

The above example shows that handling input data on the audio system designed for playback is inherently error prone. On the bright side, most games do not need to play back the audio. They just need to capture it, and send it elsewhere, also known as voice over IP (or, use it as an input, ala One Hand Clapping). So a system is needed to capture the audio before it enters the server at an incorrect sampling rate.

The three previous PRs were various attempts at this.
[The first PR](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/100508) injected an alternative usage path into `AudioStreamPlaybackMicrophone`, which is the class that handles the microphone input for playback in Godot's audio playback system. I can see the reasoning, but in my opinion it makes the class ambiguous, and adds unnecessary complexity to it.

[The second PR](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/105244) was created after maintainer feedback which suggested the perspective to handle the microphone input more like other control inputs, like mouse, keyboard and controllers, and add it to the `Input` class. That PR ended up similar to this PR. It's not bad, but the kind of data microphones generate is very different to the data `Input` usually deals with For that reason, I believe `AudioServer` is a more suitable class to working with it appropriately.

[The third PR](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/108773) was created after feedback that the system proposed in `Input` could not deal with multiple microphones at once, and was therefore underdesigned. 
However, I believe this feedback was misguided. By our [contribution guidelines](https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/engine/guidelines/best_practices.html#to-solve-the-problem-it-has-to-exist-in-the-first-place), we should strive to only solve problems that people actually have. Using multiple microphones at once is not a feature that has been requested by users. Even dedicated audio software does not support capturing input from multiple audio inputs simultaneously a lot of the time, probably because it's so rarely needed in actual projects. @goatchurchprime's PR indulging the feedback, and adding a microphone server and feeds, ended up [way more complicated](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/113288) than this one, with multiple new classes exposed, and functionality skeletons added for functions that are unlikely to be needed by anyone anytime soon. An alternative implementation by @adamscott attempted to implement the feature wholesale, but ended up even more complicated. In contrast to this PR, which adds and exposes barely any features, and solves the microphone needs of most games perfectly, I think this clearly shows why we should add demand-driven infrastructure, rather than infrastructure designed for a potential future case that is unlikely to be needed by most Godot engine users. (on that note, the addition of `AudioStreamPlaybackMicrophone` idea was probably premature in the first place, since it's unlikely many games want to play back the player's voice to them from their own speaker).
Even if people run into limitations with the system added here, we can deprecate this system and add a better one that solves whatever problem users run into at that time. Since this is an extremely small solution, it's easy to sculpt or remove completely when it outlives its designed purpose.

**All in all, I believe this PR is the appropriate solution for the problem at hand.** 
The PR is low risk, especially with @goatchurchprime's rigorous testing with his [bespoke tool](https://github.com/goatchurchprime/godot-demo-projects/tree/gtch/mic_input/audio/mic_input).
It is also potentially high-impact, since for the first time in Godot's history, it will be possible to have stable voice-over-ip technology in Godot made games. A demand for this is evident by the popularity of @goatchurchprime's extension [two-voip](https://github.com/goatchurchprime/two-voip-godot-4), which even in the current state of the godot interface is attracting users.

Due to the reasons given above, I'd like to restate my initial comment that I think this should be merged into 4.6.

body:
The code looks good. the only risk is this api is designed for single-consumer since it has only one global offset variable, and modifies with the same start/stop state as AudioStreamMicrophone.

Some day, I would prefer a higher level object oriented API which would also be used by `AudioStreamMicrophone`, that holds the offset internally and and can increment/decrement a "active counter" that will control start / stop so you can have two consumers of the audio data without interference. For the object oriented idea, we'd need a Vector<AudioFrame> version of the `get_input_frames` function (which `AudioStreamPlaybackMicrophone::_mix_internal` would call). 

As for my review, the code should do what it says so I'll approve.

I consider this to be a low level API which ideally users wouldn't use directly. If there was more time I'd really prefer an object oriented api that will have exactly the same performance but avoids the single global offset variable stored in AudioServer which limits our ability to improve things in the future.

body: There's a few changes to make, but I'll give my approval anyway right now. This saga has been long time coming. First of all, I tip my hat to @goatchurchprime's tenacity and to @Ivorforce for taking this over. --- If it was just by me, I wouldn't merge this PR to be honest. While the code is well made, it exposes a buffer that wasn't made to be exposed. All of this from an API that was built intending audio input to be used as an audio device (instead of as data entry). We need a refactor. I [created a branch](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/compare/master...adamscott:godot:new-microphone-feeds-mk2) that implements a prototype of a `MicrophoneServer`. While still flawed, I was able to record from two distinct inputs at a time. While games may not need multiple entries, we must still understand that Godot is used more and more as a general purpose engine. I showed @goatchurchprime that Web apps like Jitsi use multiple inputs to display VU meters of the available input devices to facilitate selection: It's also more in line with the current Godot way of dealing with input devices. See [`CameraServer`](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_cameraserver.html) for more details. (even if I found multiple flaws of `CameraServer` while experimenting on my `MicrophoneServer`) But a refactor is costly and takes time. And people needing some features cannot wait. The arguments made by @Ivorforce are convincing. Even if I'm not fully convinced, I'm enough to give this PR a go.

This looks incorrect. A constant name (identifier) ​​can't contain a period. At the very least, this is a hack, not a desirable option.

The main problem with proper enumeration support is that the core doc system doesn't properly support scoped enumerations. Instead, all enumeration elements are put into a common constant list. Native enumeration elements cannot be repeated, but custom enumerations can have elements with the same name in multiple enumerations.

body:
I wonder if it is possible to avoid this entire segment somehow. There are two things happening here I'm not a fan of:
- Copying existing mipmaps on the main graphics queue, which could cause stutters when textures are streaming in.
- Resource tracker getting created just for the initial copying phase, which would unnecessarily track the texture in later frames and incur CPU cost.

If the texture is immutable, it might be possible to transfer the existing mipmaps using transfer workers, by utilizing `VK_SHARING_MODE_CONCURRENT` on Vulkan and `D3D12_RESOURCE_FLAG_ALLOW_SIMULTANEOUS_ACCESS` on D3D12. So this way the copies can overlap with the previous frame and you wouldn't need any trackers. I don't know the performance implications of using these flags on readonly textures though.
author: blueskythlikesclouds

body:
Yeah.  I've no idea on performance aspects.  From some quick googling it sounds like it can have a definite negative impact. 

I've wondered if copying an existing texture even worth it though.  When increasing a texture quality you still have to upload the highest mip version which is largest, so the savings to disk io are lessened.  For lowering in quality in theory it sounds nice to not hit disk io but i've seriously wondered if its worth it.  I suppose it depends very much what you are on, a fast NVME drive it probably doesn't matter but some slow sd card....maybe.

I'm perfectly fine if we want to remove this and just create new textures instead.  Its definitely simpler, and may very well perform better.  At least until a real need develops.

body: I found a bigger issue. TexStreamingIO is completely bottlenecked by the rendering thread, since it has to wait for `texture_2d_create_from_texture` to finish executing on the command queue, as it executes render graph commands. This causes only one texture to be created per frame. Look at this: If we want to keep the "copy from existing texture" behavior, this function needs to be split into 3: - Allocate RID - Create texture and copy the new mipmaps to it, _which should always happen in the TexStreamingIO thread_ - Copy existing mipmaps from the existing texture, which can be delegated to the command queue

body:
Makes sense to me.

The if condition itself should be almost free[^1].
In contrast, many paths will probably pass the `absolute` check, and start comparing path parts. Each indirection could incur cache misses, which are very expensive in comparison[^2].

The only caveat i have is that I don't know how many `NodePath` instances have a valid hash cache, so I don't know how often this check will actually help in practice.
But this will be hard to estimate, and like I mentioned, the potential regression vs potential benefit is fairly large, so I think this is fine.

[^1]: See the cost of comparisons and jumps, both of which are just a few cycles https://www.agner.org/optimize/optimizing_cpp.pdf
[^2]: See the cost of cache misses https://www.agner.org/optimize/optimizing_cpp.pdf

body:
If you're just using `std::move`, and then calling the destructor, that means any access of `command_mem` as `CommandBase *` is now invalid (because the destructor has already been called).

In this case, you might as well use relocation semantics (call `memcpy` and don't call the destructor). Which would put us back to where we started.

Can you explain why changing to move semantics here should help if `command_mem` is never accessed as `CommandBase *` after this anyway?
author: Ivorforce

body:
From what I understood, only "trivially copyable" types can be memcpy'd safely according to C++ standard. See https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/types/is_trivially_copyable.html:

> Objects of trivially-copyable types that are not potentially-overlapping subobjects are the only C++ objects that may be safely copied with [std::memcpy](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/string/byte/memcpy.html) [...]

Since command_queue_mt is handling non-trivially copyable types, I didn't think any solution that involves memcpy is technically correct. I can imagine a C++ object that would not work correctly with memcpy (imagine one that has a member field that points to another member field. after a memcpy, that pointer will still point to the old location and not the new location). So I wanted to make a fix that stayed away from "undefined behavior" territory. 

However, in researching things to reply here, I see that it looks like Godot uses `realloc` which I would not have considered safe with C++ types since it's essentially doing a memcpy under the hood. So I am wondering if Godot types are generally written in a way that allows for memcpy to work in practice?

All that to say, I think what you say is in line with how Godot is written and I can change this to memcpy and not destroy the original copy.
author: brycehutchings

body:
> From what I understood, only "trivially copyable" types can be memcpy'd safely according to C++ standard. See https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/types/is_trivially_copyable.html:

This isn't totally true. Another use-case for `memcpy` is [trivial relocation](https://open-std.org/JTC1/SC22/WG21/docs/papers/2020/p1144r5.html), a concept that has only recently been formalized.

For Godot, we have made the decision to assume all (non-heap) objects must be trivially relocatable to make use of `memcpy` for improved speed (see https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/100509).

body:
We currently don't do this much in the codebase.
The reason is likely because C++ does not offer a lot of support for using enums. In languages like Swift, using them is extremely convenient, but in C++, you may have to look up the enum and write it out, which makes is cumbersome and verbose. 

I do agree that `get_enum_map(true)` is perfectly obtuse as to its behavior. I did consider making it an enum, but in this case, the enum would have to be placed in `GDType` because of namespacing. The lookup would actually be `get_enum_map(GDType.LookupMode.SELF_ONLY)` (or `get_enum_map(GDType.SELF_ONLY)`), which is very verbose (and in the latter requires non `enum struct`).

body:
This is a bit complicated to explain. I can give a hand if you need one.

Basically, the purpose of a "frame" event is to accumulate all data _before_ emitting events. This is to allow for composite data to be described predictably (e.g. from `shape` and `orientation`, which describe the same ellipse), along other things we can't really control.

We should strive to implement this properly to be as compliant to the Wayland specifications as possible, to avoid nasty surprises down the road.

Because of this, I advise to take the same approach as `wl_pointer::frame` and compare the data before/after.

This comparison is the reason behind the "buffer" concept, which as you can see with the pointer has a "buffer" and "committed" value.

For reference, [the spec says](https://wayland.app/protocols/wayland#wl_touch:event:frame):
> Indicates the end of a set of events that logically belong together. A client is expected to accumulate the data in all events within the frame before proceeding.

Hope that was clear, feel free to ask if you need anything :D

Note: this is not how you iterate on a HashMap. This probably works because the index is _usually_ 0, 1, 2, 3... but [the spec](https://wayland.app/protocols/wayland#wl_touch:event:down) does not guarantee this:

> A new touch point has appeared on the surface. This touch point is assigned a unique ID. Future events from this touch point reference this ID. The ID ceases to be valid after a touch up event and **may** be reused in the future.

I actually asked in the Wayland chat to make sure, and that "may" (emphasis mine), along with other wording choices, make it perfectly valid for a compositor to use whatever number it thinks of.

To iterate properly on all elements of a HashMap, you can do this:
```suggestion
	for (KeyValue<int32_t, TouchPoint> &pair: bf.touchs) {
		TouchPoint &td = pair.value;
```

This code iterates through all entries in the map, and selects the value from them.

body:
Did you measure the performance of this, when invoked with the default argument?

There's a very good chance that `std::log(e)` is not optimized away -- especially since the number literal isn't specified precisely enough -- which would mean that _every_ `log(x)` call now incurs an additional logarithm + float division operation. This would make GDScript `log` slower across the board, even for functions that don't use `base` (i.e. all usages up to now).
author: Bromeon

body: Could you add some comments what the individual parts here are doing?
author: Bromeon

body:
Furthermore, there's also the risk of introducing numerical imprecision -- previous results of `log(x)` may no longer be the same after this change, especially if `log(e)` turns out not to be exactly 1.

Given how centrally `log` may be depended upon, I feel like this is a case where a separate function with a `base` parameter would be the better option. (Unless there's a way in GDScript to dispatch depending on presence of the argument).

body:
RE register_utility_function_compat
this is all a copy/paste from https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/112290
When you register the compatibility function, it's the same as the regular register_utility_function, but instead of adding the function to the utility_function_table, it adds it to a separate list of compatibility functions with the same name.
When the function is looked up for binding (variant_utility.cpp:2008), it first grabs the function from the original utility_function_table, then checks the function signature hash to see if the function signature is a match. If it's not a match, it looks through the registered compatibility functions and finds one that has the right function signature, and returns that one instead.

On all the platforms/compiler that we currently support, `int` is a 32-bit integer and so effectively the same as `int32_t`. So, I don't really think of this as changing anything, but just making the size explicit and not potentially up to interpretation

body:
As mentioned [elsewhere](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/113654#issuecomment-3627032492), I do think this is the preferrable approach to this problem. However, outside of the review comments I have a few (mostly cosmetic) concerns:

1. The name `flush_kinematic_transform()` bothers me a bit, since we now have three different terms to refer to this kind of thing, with this using "flush", `Node*D.force_update_transform()` using "force update" and `Node.reset_physics_interpolation()` using "reset". I can't help but feel like this should be called `force_update_kinematic_transform()` instead, but I'd be curious to hear more thoughts on this.
1. I feel like the new project setting deserves to be in its own "Compatibility" sub-category, i.e. `physics/*d/compatibility/kinematic_body_initial_teleport`, similar to `animation/compatibility/default_parent_skeleton_in_mesh_instance_3d`.
1. Very few will ever see the note for `BODY_MODE_KINEMATIC` in the `PhysicsServer*D` documentation, which seems like a shame. We should mention this new method and the general behavior of kinematic transform changes in the class descriptions of `CharacterBody3D` and `AnimatableBody3D`, and maybe even `RigidBody3D` as well. Although, I believe the (somewhat broken) `sync_to_physics` property in `AnimatableBody3D` might complicate this a bit.
1. The documentation for this should be clearer about *why* we don't immediately move the transform of kinematic bodies. Just mentioning that a teleport will happen when calling this new method assumes too much of the reader, in my opinion.
