If we're making stuff `thread_local` anyway, do we even need this new `flushing` variable?

`flush_read_ptr` will only ever be accessed/modified from a single thread at a time, and it's always reset to zero before the mutex is unlocked, so it's effectively already `thread_local` in a sense.

Making it actually `thread_local` would mean that we could move the `MutexLock` back to where it was before #112506 (after the reentrancy check) and the recursive flushing would work like it used to, without this extra stuff.

body:
Is this check needed at all? When I look at how `flush_read_ptr` interacts with the mutex, it looks like it is always set to 0 before the mutex is released. So any time we get past the mutex being acquired, isn't `flush_read_ptr` guaranteed to be 0? It seems like it should just flow down to the while loop and run that normally.

This check used to be before the mutex acquire, and there it made sense to avoid the deadlock issue (although it had race condition problems). By moving it to after the mutex, the deadlock issue was introduced, but now the condition should never happen. At least I think so?
author: brycehutchings

body: The lock guard does `temp_unlock()` while `flush_read_ptr` is non-zero, so it's not guaranteed to always be zero when we get past the mutex. See [this](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/113802#discussion_r2602872859) discussion.

body:
Unfortunately, we cannot simply reuse the old macro; at least, not without further adjustments. While this correctly binds, documentation is mangled because a class/namespace is now prefixed. For instance, even without changing an existing enum like `MouseMode` to a scoped equivalent, prefixing the class will still break that output:
```cpp
	BIND_ENUM_CONSTANT(MouseMode::MOUSE_MODE_VISIBLE);
	BIND_ENUM_CONSTANT(MouseMode::MOUSE_MODE_HIDDEN);
	BIND_ENUM_CONSTANT(MouseMode::MOUSE_MODE_CAPTURED);
	BIND_ENUM_CONSTANT(MouseMode::MOUSE_MODE_CONFINED);
	BIND_ENUM_CONSTANT(MouseMode::MOUSE_MODE_CONFINED_HIDDEN);
	BIND_ENUM_CONSTANT(MouseMode::MOUSE_MODE_MAX);
```
```diff
 	<constants>
-		<constant name="MOUSE_MODE_VISIBLE" value="0" enum="MouseMode">
-			Makes the mouse cursor visible if it is hidden.
+		<constant name="MouseMode::MOUSE_MODE_VISIBLE" value="0" enum="MouseMode">
 		</constant>
-		<constant name="MOUSE_MODE_HIDDEN" value="1" enum="MouseMode">
-			Makes the mouse cursor hidden if it is visible.
+		<constant name="MouseMode::MOUSE_MODE_HIDDEN" value="1" enum="MouseMode">
 		</constant>
-		<constant name="MOUSE_MODE_CAPTURED" value="2" enum="MouseMode">
-			Captures the mouse. The mouse will be hidden and its position locked at the center of the window manager's window.
-			[b]Note:[/b] If you want to process the mouse's movement in this mode, you need to use [member InputEventMouseMotion.relative].
+		<constant name="MouseMode::MOUSE_MODE_CAPTURED" value="2" enum="MouseMode">
 		</constant>
-		<constant name="MOUSE_MODE_CONFINED" value="3" enum="MouseMode">
-			Confines the mouse cursor to the game window, and make it visible.
+		<constant name="MouseMode::MOUSE_MODE_CONFINED" value="3" enum="MouseMode">
 		</constant>
-		<constant name="MOUSE_MODE_CONFINED_HIDDEN" value="4" enum="MouseMode">
-			Confines the mouse cursor to the game window, and make it hidden.
+		<constant name="MouseMode::MOUSE_MODE_CONFINED_HIDDEN" value="4" enum="MouseMode">
 		</constant>
-		<constant name="MOUSE_MODE_MAX" value="5" enum="MouseMode">
-			Max value of the [enum MouseMode].
+		<constant name="MouseMode::MOUSE_MODE_MAX" value="5" enum="MouseMode">
 		</constant>
```
---
We *do* already have macros for handling enum classes, but those are currently isolated to `core_constants.cpp`. Specifically: `BIND_CORE_ENUM_CLASS_CONSTANT` and its variants.
```cpp
#define BIND_CORE_ENUM_CLASS_CONSTANT(m_enum, m_prefix, m_member)                                                  \
	{                                                                                                              \
		StringName enum_name = __constant_get_enum_name(m_enum::m_member);                                         \
		_global_constants.push_back(_CoreConstant(enum_name, #m_prefix "_" #m_member, (int64_t)m_enum::m_member)); \
		_global_constants_map[#m_prefix "_" #m_member] = _global_constants.size() - 1;                             \
		_global_enums[enum_name].push_back((_global_constants.ptr())[_global_constants.size() - 1]);               \
	}
```

They do more than simply casting the value and trimming the prefix though. This is because scoped enums take advantage of the fact that their class scope is required, and thus their contents have much shorter names. So if `MouseMode` was truly a scoped enum, it'd necessitate the following change:
```cpp
	enum class MouseMode {
		VISIBLE,
		HIDDEN,
		CAPTURED,
		CONFINED,
		CONFINED_HIDDEN,
		MAX,
	};
```
Otherwise declared variables would be comically verbose. In the most extreme case, failing to do so would result in `MouseMode::MOUSE_MODE_CONFINED_HIDDEN`.

This is a totally acceptable change, though! That's because the nature of using a scoped enum means that a ton of code will need to be touched anyway to account for explicit conversions and mandatory prefixes. In that same pass, there's no reason *not* to adjust the value names as well.

If this was a core enum type, we'd pass it to the macro which handles all this noise automatically:
```cpp
	BIND_CORE_ENUM_CLASS_CONSTANT(MouseMode, MOUSE_MODE, VISIBLE);
	BIND_CORE_ENUM_CLASS_CONSTANT(MouseMode, MOUSE_MODE, HIDDEN);
	BIND_CORE_ENUM_CLASS_CONSTANT(MouseMode, MOUSE_MODE, CAPTURED);
	BIND_CORE_ENUM_CLASS_CONSTANT(MouseMode, MOUSE_MODE, CONFINED);
	BIND_CORE_ENUM_CLASS_CONSTANT(MouseMode, MOUSE_MODE, CONFINED_HIDDEN);
	BIND_CORE_ENUM_CLASS_CONSTANT(MouseMode, MOUSE_MODE, MAX);
```
Everything outside of core has no such luxury. As such, I'd rather not integrate this change, as it'd hide a footgun of our own design. We absolutely *should* be able to support enum class binds out-of-the-box, but it needs to be accompanied with proper support for documentation

body:
I'm not too sure about this, since the exposure still gets applied to 3D objects, it's just the canvas background that doesn't handle it. 

Edit:

I've been looking into a solution and came up with this: https://github.com/blueskythlikesclouds/godot/tree/compatibility-canvas-background-exposure-fix

When exposure is enabled, we can force the intermediary buffer, and copy it with the exposure as the multiplier (alongside the luminance multiplier).

Converting the exposure to sRGB is an approximation. It might be more accurate to do this in the copy shader instead:
```glsl
color = srgb_to_linear(color)
color *= exposure
color = linear_to_srgb(color)
color *= luminance_multiplier
```

This forces the intermediary buffer to exist even with glow off, but it might be better than the feature just not working at all.

body:
To my understanding, this message would be sent every time an agent reached a point where they (most likely) cannot get any closer.  
I reckon the message is sent in order to tell the dev: "Just so you know, your agent cannot get any closer than this. You really should test if your destination is reachable. And if it's not, don't keep asking your agent to go there. Then I won't spam you with more messages."  
If navigation optimization is done, these messages would occur rarely.  
The reason they cannot get closer might be because the max path search parameters restrict the agent too much. Or some navigation link is not compatible with the agent. Or the region got fractured into islands. Or start and end polygon are in different regions that are not connected at all.

This looks good to me.

My review summary:
When a clip is being mixed, its playback position is always recorded ([code](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/a8643700ce8affae9fed0d2688b9f7867f5b7d4e/modules/interactive_music/audio_stream_interactive.cpp#L926)). The constant already works properly if set in the Transition Editor. body:
I believe they are guaranteed to be present, as per [their entry in the official LSP spec page](https://microsoft.github.io/language-server-protocol/specifications/lsp/3.17/specification/#diagnosticRelatedInformation):
> `DiagnosticRelatedInformation` is defined as follows:
> ```ts
> /**
>  * Represents a related message and source code location for a diagnostic.
>  * This should be used to point to code locations that cause or are related to
>  * a diagnostics, e.g when duplicating a symbol in a scope.
>  */
> export interface DiagnosticRelatedInformation {
> 	/**
> 	 * The location of this related diagnostic information.
> 	 */
> 	location: Location;
> 
> 	/**
> 	 * The message of this related diagnostic information.
> 	 */
> 	message: string;
> }
> ```

The `location` and `message` attributes aren't marked as nullable/optional, whereas other attributes sometimes are. For example, `Command.attributes` a little ways down the page:
> ```ts
> interface Command {
>	/**
>	 * Title of the command, like `save`.
>	 */
>	title: string;
>	/**
>	 * The identifier of the actual command handler.
>	 */
>	command: string;
>	/**
>	 * Arguments that the command handler should be
>	 * invoked with.
>	 */
>	arguments?: LSPAny[]; // <-- It has the ?, indicating it is optional(?)
> }
> ```

Following this logic, I may need to go through and double-check that any of the other LSP structures I added respect particular values being optional.

body:
> Multi-document undo redo (https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/114168#issuecomment-3830464005)

Do any of the current Code Actions work on multiple documents at once? If none of the current actions need it could be done later.
I tested how VSCode handles multiple document undo redo, and they work as long as the files are at the same undo level as when the action was done (a warning shows if any documents were changed and couldn't do the undo/redo with the rest). We don't have anything for it yet, but it makes sense to me to have it work across multiple documents for code actions.
I have a plan of how the undo/redo can work with multiple documents:
1. When a multi-document edit happens, save the file names and their undo versions (`TextEdit::get_version()`) in a new undo stack on ScriptEditor
2. Intercept undo and redo action handling before the TextEdit gets it (either with existing `_text_edit_gui_input` or a new one in ScriptEditor). On undo/redo, if the TextEdit current undo version matches the undo version in the current item in the stack, then we are going to do a multi-document undo/redo. If it does not match, don't accept the event and let TextEdit get the undo/redo like normal.
3. For the multi-document undo/redo, accept the undo/redo event, do an undo/redo in the current TextEdit, and check all the other files saved in the current undo stack item. If they are open and if their current undo version matches then undo/redo in those TextEdits too. And then move the stack position to the previous/next item.
	1. If the undo version does not match, warn the user about all the files that failed.
4. When a document is closed, go through all items in the undo stack and mark that file if it has it so it can no longer be a part of the multi-document undo/redo. This is because the TextEdit undo/redo stack is not saved when its closed.

Similar to `UNTYPED_DECLARATION`, warnings that apply to the entire class highlight the entire class over LSP, such as `redundant_static_unload` and `missing_tool`. These should also probably be limited to just the class declaration line since highlighting the entire file isn't helpful. Also for a future PR.
The script editor has a custom limit to make sure the warnings aren't too long which is why it only shows on the LSP side (`ScriptTextEditor::_update_background_color`).

Class-level warnings caused code actions to not work at all over LSP, (like `missing_tool` and `redundant_static_unload`) it just says no code actions available. If those warnings are not present, then it works fine for other warnings.

body:
I tested this locally and confirmed that it fixes the crash on my Adreno 640. 

My initial investigation led me to believe that the issue was memory alignment related and somehow the driver was getting into a state it could not recover where it could not properly function, but did not crash. In particular, I suspected that memory alignment issues were resulting in the radiance value property impacting the `directional_light_count` property in the Scenedata struct resulting in `directional_light_count` getting a huge value and crashing the driver. 

Bastiaan's initial refactor did not fix the issue, but it did split out the prev frame data from the current frame data (which removed a source of UB). 

I tested out forcing alignment manually in the shader by using a mat3x4 and that worked. Therefore, I think we can conclude that the problem was a shader code generation issue. The driver must assume tighter packing than what the spec actually specifies when using a mat3 inside a struct in a shader. https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/97151 triggered this issue because it moved the scene data from a uniform block directly to a struct. Many old drivers prefer using a uniform block instead of a struct.

That's not the right way to do it. Either TileData should fully support story polygons with `size < 3` (and TileMapLayer and editors should check before using it), or it should throw an error.

body: Tested locally, it works as expected. Some changes are needed, but overall, I think it's going in a good direction. **Testing project:** [control_gallery.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28123418/control_gallery.zip) Some feedback: - In terms of UX, I think it's fine to have this defined in StyleBox. It can still be configured across a whole range of buttons using Theme resources. It roughly matches CSS behavior where you define `transition` in the styles you want to be transitioned *to* (e.g. setting `transition` on `button:hover` only affects `normal` -> `hover` transitions, not the other way around). - Note that like in CSS, you have to be careful about transitions that try to interpolate from nothing. This can lead to artifacts with very thin outlines, for example when interpolating from no border to a 4-pixel wide border with blending enabled: https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6dfa1c4c-f86c-43aa-8d66-fcda67cd0b3d One way to avoid this is to have the border enabled with the same width and Blend property in the normal and hover states, but keep it invisible by setting its color to `Color(0, 0, 0, 0)` (transparent black): https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/77f8e180-4d95-41a4-8100-0bc91ca4f615 This is probably unavoidable, but we should be careful to document this both in the class reference and manual as it'll likely come up often in support requests. - I get a crash when using an animation with the **Unset** *transition* type: On the other hand, the **Unset** *ease* type doesn't seem to cause a crash. - Out of curiosity, what is the Unset type for? I couldn't figure it out. I assume it's meant to reuse the ease/transition type from the main animation (for the exit animation) or vice versa. What happens if both the main animation and the exit animation use the Unset type? - If this is the intended use case of Unset, perhaps it should be renamed to Inherit and made available only on the exit animation (and made the default for the exit animation too). ___ @AdriaandeJongh I'm curious about your thoughts on this PR, especially considering how it would play together with https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/111455 for audio.

I looked at this with the animation team and we are happy with the UI in terms of the animation editor.

As for the GUI code, ResizableScrollBar has some missing code for vertical scroll and it's not properly exposed and documented as GDClass.
The main issue is that we have unreviewed gui code being added to the Godot runtime, even though it is not public and only used in the editor. I looked at the code and I think it is good, but the gui team would need to take a look at it.

I see two ways forward for this PR.

1. We keep this just as an animation editor-specific change. We keep what you have for animation track editor, since it looks really good for this purpose, and move resizable_scroll_bar.cpp to the editor directory (or editor/animation), since it is not exposed and only used in the editor. Later, someone else can expose it to the gui when the time comes.
2. Or, if you have more time, do a few finishing touches, implement the missing cases for vertical scrolling, add documentation, and put it on the agenda for a gui meeting so the gui team can give feedback, and expose it as an official Godot GUI class.

body:
Because this calculation includes `XRServer::get_singleton()->get_world_origin().affine_inverse()`, we need to run `update_transform()` any time the `XROrigin3D` is moved/rotated as well.

I did some testing, and all was fine if I started the app with the `XROrigin3D` moved away from the origin and rotated. However, if I moved/rotated the `XROrigin3D` at runtime (like, when teleporting or snap turning), the composition layers would end up in the wrong spot (which can look really weird with hole punching, because the "hole" will be in the right spot, but the composition layer will be in the wrong spot).

To solve this, I think we'll need either:

1. A way to get the current `XROrigin3D` and then watch for it to move/rotate, or
2. A signal that's emitted every time `XRServer::get_singleton()->get_world_orgin()` has a new value
author: dsnopek

body: I went with the second approach and added a signal that's emitted when the world origin changes. This mirrors what we already do for the reference frame.

body:
Because `bind()` and `unbind()` are like Russian nesting dolls. The parameters used in the signal definition are the outermost layer. 

So the initial implementation of #60143 involved appending the source object to the beginning of the receiving function's parameter list. The order in which the Russian nesting dolls are opened:

> [source] [signal parameters] [unbind] [bind arguments]

However, @reduz disagreed at the time. So the current order is...

> [signal parameters] [unbind] [source] [bind arguments]

Initially, it was also implemented in `Object`. However, if implemented in `Object`, it would be necessary to determine and undo the nested layer of `unbind()`, then `bind(source)` ~~(if considering user scripts, there are many levels of nesting, this doesn't seem sufficient to guarantee the position of the source)~~, and then wrap it back to `unbind()`. And it seems that `CONNECT_APPEND_SOURCE_OBJECT` is primarily used for connecting dialogs. That's why it is the way it is now.

The current order in this PR is...

> [signal parameters] [source] [unbind] [bind arguments]

This also seems to be the reason that prevented #60143 from being merged for a long time. 

Currently, the first order seems to be the easiest to implement.

body:
If `050000005e040000130b0000ffff3f00` is present in both internal SDL and SDL_GameControllerDB, then it might be a bug that it's in SDL_GameControllerDB and it should likely be removed.

It seems like it was added in SDL_GameControllerDB in 2020 with https://github.com/mdqinc/SDL_GameControllerDB/commit/d1f0e1e798b6aac86c424fa999c985be9db72a6d, and later to SDL itself in 2021 with https://github.com/libsdl-org/SDL/commit/afd100f02b7689e3b1cf441f7abf40f0313f328b.

They're not too keen on receiving PRs from Godot contributors (understandably, as for several years we had our own non-SDL implementation and misunderstood the scope of that repo, and sent custom mappings that Godot needed but SDL itself didn't need). But I'll open an issue about it as I believe it's not a Godot specific issue, just one we happened to discover.

*Edit:* Done: https://github.com/mdqinc/SDL_GameControllerDB/issues/913.

For Godot, we can override the invalid `gamecontrollerdb.txt` mapping with the latest SDL one in `godotcontrollerdb.txt`, until we switch to proper SDL on Android too, in which case the solution can be to instead remove the mapping from both `gamecontrollerdb.txt` and `godotcontrollerdb.txt`.

body:
From a GDExtension perspective, documented or not doesn't really matter. The getter/setter methods are currently _exposed_ (i.e. advertised in `extension_api.json`), plus the property [_is_ mentioned in docs](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_audioeffectspectrumanalyzer.html#properties). As such it's rightful for code to depend on them.

The problem with straight removing them is that any extension that potentially calls them will run into UB under newer Godot versions. Compatibility methods, even if implemented as no-ops, prevent this.
author: Bromeon

body:
What is it that I should be doing then? This sort of situation is not given as example in the contributing docs. For context, the variable was only used in a single place, that was removed to fix the problem. Should I add every getter/setter back, even though they don't do anything, or try to add compatibility methods, as demonstrated [here](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/engine_details/development/handling_compatibility_breakages.html)?

If I'm doing the latter, my approach would be:

1. Add compatibility methods to header, while keeping the original getter/setter removed from both header and .cpp
2. Create .compat.inc file, where the getter returns the original default value of `tap_back_pos`, the removed variable, and a void setter (as in the original) that doesn't do anything (empty)
3. Include new file to .cpp
4. Keep `tap_back_pos` removed from the class documentation
5. Change .expected comment to something like: "Removed property that worsed the problem of jittered values in Spectrum Analzyzer.\nCompatibility methods registered."

My questions for this approach are:

- Should the original getter/setter stay removed in .h and .cpp, or does the compat methods only work if they exist? If they have to exist, doesn't that create an unnecessary property in the inspector?
- In .compat.inc, should the getter return the original value, or 0.0? And if I can't create an empty setter, what should be added inside?
- Should the property be removed or kept in the docs?
author: Akosmo

body:
I'll try to answer one-by-one, hoping to clarify how exactly compatibility breakage can happen and what you can do about it :slightly_smiling_face: 

---

> For context, the variable was only used in a single place, that was removed to fix the problem.

That applies to the engine-internal C++ code, however once a method is exposed (via the "bind methods" mechanism in a class), it can be used from GDScript, C# and GDExtension. Once it becomes part of a stable release, we generally (conservatively) assume that someone, somewhere, may use such a method.

Removing from GDScript is less problematic, as it will be hit by a parse-time or runtime-error, but for often-used APIs (not here), it should still be done carefully, as it adds a lot of churn to users and makes writing plugins across versions very hard.

Removing from GDExtension however means that an older extension (compiled against 4.5) now fetches a function pointer that is no longer existing in a newer Godot version. Depending on whether the binding checks validity of that pointer or not (and Release builds may skip that), it's possible to introduce undefined behavior.

---

> Should I add every getter/setter back, even though they don't do anything, or try to add compatibility methods, as demonstrated [here](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/engine_details/development/handling_compatibility_breakages.html)?

> Should the original getter/setter stay removed in .h and .cpp, or does the compat methods only work if they exist? If they have to exist, doesn't that create an unnecessary property in the inspector?

Only compatibility methods need to be added (i.e. the part that's facing GDExtension). The C++ internal API can be refactored much more freely.

Properties are not directly accessible from GDExtension, instead they are exposed as a pair of setter/getter methods. So those setters/getters would need a compat method, that is then registered. Their original implementation can be removed.

So from the API perspective, these APIs are still removed:
- They're no longer accessible in GDScript.
- They don't appear in the docs.
- They aren't advertised in `extension_api.json` (the class specification for GDExtension).

However if an old extension fetches a method with a specific class name, method name and hash, it will still be found.

---

> In .compat.inc, should the getter return the original value, or 0.0? And if I can't create an empty setter, what should be added inside?

You should stay as close as possible to the previous behavior, with reasonable effort. If you are confident that the previous implementation was flawed and thus not really usable, or if maintaining that would need to store complex extra state, it may not be worth it. It depends a bit how niche an API is. Here it's probably OK to keep things simple.

---

> Should the property be removed or kept in the docs?

The property itself can be removed, as long as setter/getter are registered via compat methods.

The setter/getter don't need to be registered as _regular_ methods any longer.

body:
Restoring the window from the Docks menu is fine when the docks are closed from the window. 
When closing the window itself, I feel like restoring all docks to the main window is probably the most expected behavior. 
Users will already be used to closing the window to restore the dock, and restoring all is more useful than closing all too, since there is only one of each dock and you generally don't want to close most docks.
I guess if there are a lot of docks or ones designed to be temporary, then it may be better to close them, but we don't really have that info.
If the user detaches the filesystem dock or another important dock we should try to prevent the user from accidentally closing it. They can still close it directly from the context menu if they do want it closed.
That's my take on it at least, we may want to get more opinions.

body: Tested locally, it works as expected. I think this is a great usability improvement in terms of designing character controllers. Combine this with a simple friction edit to the CharacterBody3D template, some mouselook code, then you have a fully functional first-person character controller. **Testing project:** https://github.com/Calinou/godot-cmvalley/tree/gh-114447 :warning: Also download [cmvalley.zip](https://github.com/Calinou/game-maps-obj/releases/download/download/cmvalley.zip), extract it, and move `cmvalley.obj` to the `cmvalley/` folder before opening the project in the editor. The above project contains a lot of complex geometry, with no manual clipping or simplified geometry for collision. It's a good example of a difficult scenario, and this PR handles it quite well (although not perfectly). Some feedback: - When walking near to a wall that can't be stepped on (but eventually becomes steppable due to a lowering height), stair stepping will fail to activate if you don't get momentum first. This is more common at higher physics tick rates. https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/47da5cbd-3e22-43b9-acf4-67a94bee02fe For example, if you try to step on the left, it won't work (as expected, since it's too high). If you try to step on the right, it will only work if you've already garnered enough speed. Trying to hug the slope's side then step up on the right won't work as one would expect. - Getting camera height smoothing and physics interpolation to work correctly is nontrivial. At the very least, it should be documented in the class reference (as per my review suggestions). - Stair stepping does not apply when you're airborne, which makes jumping up stairs cumbersome (you will hit the edge of stairs as you jump). It also prevents you from using the step height to successfully perform jumps that were just barely missing the edge of a wall, which can be frustrating for the player. - There should be a way to control the step height while airborne (airstepping), defaulting to the same value as the grounded step height. Some games use the same value as when grounded, while others will use lower values when airborne. - If stepping is changed to be applied when airborne, then this can be implemented in game logic by changing the step height according to the player's current state, without having to introduce a new property. The default behavior would then be to use the step height for airstepping as when grounded, which I think is reasonable for most games. For future PRs: - I wonder how this algorithm would behave if we applied it to hitting walls (somewhat like *skimming*, if you've played CPMA). Combined with camera smoothing, this could reduce the need for level designers to aggressively clip levels by smoothing out collisions not just with floors, but also with walls.

body:
I read this multiple times and I have to be picky, sorry. I had to rewrite this review multiple times because, as I tried to unwrap what this even meant, I kept coming to different conclusions.

Like, let's slow down, take a step back, and think about it.
The problem is that **virtual methods from Object _may_ be called before a node is ready**, or even before it is inside the tree node. [The original issue is very specific](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/113283), but the cause is way more generic and justifiable.

I have no exact suggestions right now. I just know that, with the explanation I gave above, this new note is **way too specific** right now:
- There's `class_name`, which doesn't have anything to do with it.
- There's the "Create New Node" dialog, which doesn't tell the whole story.
	- What if a node is created in the editor programmatically?
	- If anything it makes it sound like a quirk deriving from the dialog itself.
- There's `@tool`, which implies that it can really only happen with code running in the editor. But in truth it's just a quirk of Node.

The note also tries to re-explain information that could be (or is already) **alluded** to this description. Maybe some things could be rewritten, such that the natural conclusion from reading them would be "Oh, of course `Object._get` is called here, but there's no parent yet, so it gives me this error!".

> Regarding the looping methods at both ends, it might be worth documenting that when a loop like 11234566 is needed, you can use frame_progress as I mentioned in https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/7643#issuecomment-4057898440. I was struggling a little bit with how to concisely document this. Disclaimer that I went back and forth with ChatGPT (meh), the best I came up with was:

> Note: To accomplish time-based ping pong, double the duration of the first and last frame. When starting an animation, set the [AnimatedSprite2D] or [AnimatedSprite3D] [code]frame_progress[/code] member to `0.5` in order to avoid doubling the first frame's playback time.

body: ## Pull request overview This PR fixes ghost dependency issues by clearing undo history when resources referenced in AnimationPlayer keyframes are deleted from the file system. The implementation connects to the `FileSystemDock::file_removed` signal and clears the undo history for affected animations to release stale resource references. **Key Changes:** - Added `_file_removed` handler to AnimationPlayerEditorPlugin that triggers when files are deleted - Clears undo history for the current animation and AnimationTrackEditor when resource files are removed - Detects resource file types via hardcoded file extension list ### Reviewed changes Copilot reviewed 2 out of 2 changed files in this pull request and generated 4 comments. | File | Description | | ---- | ----------- | | editor/animation/animation_player_editor_plugin.h | Declares the new `_file_removed` method handler | | editor/animation/animation_player_editor_plugin.cpp | Implements connection to `file_removed` signal and handler that clears undo history when resource files are deleted | --- 💡 Add Copilot custom instructions for smarter, more guided reviews. Learn how to get started.
author: copilot-pull-request-reviewer

body: This implementation clears undo history for ALL file removals, even if the removed file is not actually referenced in the current animation. This unnecessarily discards the undo history and impacts the user experience when unrelated resources are deleted. Consider checking if the deleted file is actually referenced in any animation before clearing the undo history. You could iterate through the animation's tracks and check if any values reference the deleted file path.
author: copilot-pull-request-reviewer
copilot-pull-request-reviewer
copilot-pull-request-reviewer

body: The hardcoded list of file extensions is fragile and incomplete. It will miss resource types like mesh files (glb, gltf, fbx, obj, dae), fonts (ttf, otf, woff, woff2), animations (anim), materials (mat), and any custom resource formats. Consider using `ResourceLoader::get_resource_type(p_file)` which properly checks if a file is a resource without needing to maintain an extension list. This would be more maintainable and catch all resource types comprehensively.
author: copilot-pull-request-reviewer

body:
I think this is the wrong way to fix it.

The ghosting issue with undo fundamentally doesn't depend on the AnimationPlayerEditor. If you remove the AnimationPlayer in your MRP, and directly swap the Sprite2D texture, and delete previous texture and performing undo, ghosting should still appear there.

Therefore, handling undoredo solely within the AnimationPlayerEditor is at least misguided. If you want to eliminate ghosting, a fundamental implementation change is likely required.

As pointed out in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/114637#issuecomment-3717364226, I think adding some cleanup to AnimationPlayerEditor when closing Godot is the right approach, but this PR is currently doing the wrong thing.

I do love the constant threat of nasal demons though. It really sounds like something I don't want and will therefore ensure I always use a Plane[6]
author: clayjohn

body:
It's something I've seen around (explained [here](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undefined_behavior)), and that I've been using as a funny but completely accurate way to refer to undefined behaviour.

> In the [C programming community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C_(programming_language)), undefined behavior may be humorously referred to as "nasal demons", after a [comp.std.c](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comp.*_hierarchy) post that explained undefined behavior as allowing the compiler to do anything it chooses, even "to make demons fly out of your nose".

As for the actual reason for the comment: that struct is passed to functions that always expect the pointers to point at least to `Plane[6]` and `Vector3[8]`, which is the data required to represent a frustum. If the pointers points to something less than that, there's no bound checking, so you get undefined behaviour (hence nasal demons).

I thought about using vector, but when doing it this way I get to use stack arrays, saving some memory allocations during light setup. So I guess ultimately it boils down to slightly better performance and prettier if somewhat riskier code.

Then again, `DirectionalCullPlanes` is 1104 bytes...

We try to avoid unrelated changes in PRs for many reasons, including making tracking history difficult to follow, and make reverting etc more difficult in some cases.

Looks great, thanks!

For future reference, the root of the problem is that specular occlusion without bent normals relies on the ambient color to darken specular areas. The assumption is twofold:
1. That either lightmaps, or SSAO, Baked AO, or diffuse GI are being used and
2. That overall brightness of diffuse is a good approximation for specular occlusion

Obviously there will be many causes where both assumptions are false. 

In any case, we decided that specular occlusion is _never_ a good idea for SSR since SSR has more information and is able to handle occlusion much better anyway. 

Specular occlusion still applies to other sources of specular lighting like IBL, ReflectionProbes and specular GI. It may only make sense to apply specular occlusion to ReflectionProbes and IBL in the future. We need to evaluate if specular occlusion actually enhances VoxelGI sharp reflections or SDFGI sharp reflections.

body:
Makes sense to me. Here's how things currently work:
- When `AudioStreamPlayer.play()` is called, the playback will be instantiated, and then started in the audio server, setting its state to `PLAYING`, thus allowing mixing to happen there.
- When the scene tree is paused, it'll only pause relevant playbacks that are already playing. If tree is unpaused, all relevant existing playbacks will also unpause.

This means that if `AudioStreamPlayer.play()` is called while the scene tree is paused, playback will still start because the function doesn't check if the node can process. This is changed with this PR.

Now what happens with this PR is:
- After playback is instantiated and started in the audio server, `AudioStreamPlayer.play()` checks if the node can process. If it can't, `NOTIFICATION_PAUSED` is sent to `AudioStreamPlayerInternal.notification()`, which then pauses all playbacks, including the new one, setting its state in the audio server to `PAUSED`, disallowing mixing there.

Tested. Issue is valid and this PR fixes it to me.

body:
I haven't reviewed or tested this PR in detail, just glanced at the code.

In my opinion, this approach is one of the acceptable options for solving linked issues, but probably not the most conservative one. My main concern is that it changes behavior in a way that could be considered a breaking change. So we should add the label and mention this change in the migration guide, on the release page, etc.

At the same time, this approach has the advantage of minimal simplicity. Alternative solutions would likely lead to unnecessary complexity and configurability.

Also, as far as I understand, this actually doesn't violate the JSON specification. We can represent `Number` as either `int` or `float`. And the same number can have multiple representations (like `1` and `1.0`). But we're not required to use the shortest notation when encoding, and we're not prohibited from exploiting the notation differences to choose the target type when decoding (even if it can be unreliable). For example, PHP also relies on the fractional part to choose the target type:

```php
<?php

var_dump(json_encode(1)); // string(1) "1"
var_dump(json_encode(1.0)); // string(1) "1"
var_dump(json_encode(1.0, JSON_PRESERVE_ZERO_FRACTION)); // string(3) "1.0"
var_dump(json_encode(1.1)); // string(3) "1.1"

var_dump(json_decode("1")); // int(1)
var_dump(json_decode("1.0")); // float(1)
var_dump(json_decode("1.1")); // float(1.1)
```

body: Don't we use an RGBA16 buffer for FSR1? This looks like it will apply debanding before doing FSR1 upscaling
author: clayjohn

body:
In the case of:

- Forward+
- HDR 2D: disabled
- SMAA: disabled
- FSR1: enabled

Tonemap destination buffer will be RGBA16 (with nonlinear sRGB encoding) and FSR1 destination buffer will be RGBA8.

So to answer your question in short: yes, RGBA16 for FSR1. And yes, debanding before FSR1 upscaling.

FSR1 and MetalFX (Spatial) have not been modified to apply debanding, so it needs to be applied earlier than optimal. That is, debanding needs to be applied by tonemap, even though it would be better for debanding to be applied after FSR1 or MetalFX.

I decided it was simplest to not modify FSR1 to include a debanding step, like I did for SMAA, because FSR1 follows the same code paths as MetalFX and MetalFX cannot be modified to support debanding without another pass and intermediate buffer.

There is another potential issue that SMAA, FSR1, and MetalFX may be provided either linear or nonlinear sRGB-encoded values (based on `use_hdr`), even though they may be designed to work with only one or the other. But that's outside the scope of the debanding work that I was doing...

This calculation no longer makes sense. `vertex` is the position relative to the camera in camera space. So it can be viewed as a direction from the camera. Taking the dot product between the light direction and the vertex gives you a distance along the light direction. 

This new code doesn't really have the same geometric interpretation. The dot product between the camera direction in world space, and the vertex position in world space offset by the camera position isn't really a meaningful value

body:
"Compress Profile Compressed" sounds a bit odd. I would go for these instead:

- Automatic (`COMPRESS_PROFILE_BALANCED = 0`, move to enum 0 as it's automatic behavior and should be first as it's also the default)
- Quality (`COMPRESS_PROFILE_QUALITY = 1`, formerly `COMPRESS_PROFILE_MAX_QUALITY`)
- Balanced (`COMPRESS_PROFILE_BALANCED = 2`, formerly `COMPRESS_PROFILE_COMPRESSED`)
- Performance (`COMPRESS_PROFILE_PERFORMANCE = 3`, formerly `COMPRESS_PROFILE_MAX_COMPRESSION`)

In general, it's better for enum values not to contain `_MAX` as it makes autocompletion a bit more annoying to work with (due to the presence of `COMPRESS_PROFILE_MAX` in results).
author: Calinou

body:
I don't think these new names actually communicate the behaviour or intended purpose well. 

Balanced -> automatic is a good change, but compressed -> balanced is not a good change. Balanced implies it is a good tradeoff that makes the most sense in most cases and is safe to use by default. ASTC 6x6 is not a good format for most cases. Most people should stick with 4x4. 6x6 is only good when you are willing to lose some quality. If anything it should be 6x6 -> compressed 8x8 -> extreme compression

body:
You might want to do a bit more validate given what OpenXR itself seems to be using:
```

include/openxr/openxr.h
29:#define XR_CURRENT_API_VERSION XR_MAKE_VERSION(1, 1, 54)
32:#define XR_API_VERSION_1_0 XR_MAKE_VERSION(1, 0, XR_VERSION_PATCH(XR_CURRENT_API_VERSION))
1924:#define XR_API_VERSION_1_1 XR_MAKE_VERSION(1, 1, XR_VERSION_PATCH(XR_CURRENT_API_VERSION))
```

So the third int should go through `XR_VERSION_PATCH` (which doesn't seem to do anything relevant but I'm no Khronos dev :P), but most importantly I think the first two can only be `1.0` or `1.1`, at least until we upgrade to some OpenXR 1.2.x SDK.

And given how `XR_API_VERSION_1_0` and `XR_API_VERSION_1_1` are defined, you might want to document that users can choose to target OpenXR 1.0 even with the latest SDK by inputting `1.0.54` (which is not a tagged release, but seems to be the 1.1.54 release being able to still function as OpenXR 1.0 SDK with patch 54 changes.

Some XR runtimes gate old behavior behind version checks. This is non-standard OpenXR behavior.

The OpenXR repo does call itself an SDK: https://github.com/KhronosGroup/OpenXR-SDK
But yeah I'm fine with API too. And on second thought I think Bastiaan used `custom` because this is only used if set, while starting with `target` may sound like it needs to be filled.

In my mind "API" is the `major.minor` part, i.e. OpenXR 1.0 vs OpenXR 1.1.
And the "patch" version is the version of the headers and loader that implements (apparently) both API versions.

So... maybe `custom_version` isn't the worst option, if neither `api` nor `sdk` would be fully accurate additional specifiers.

Keeping it blank makes it easy to distinguish between "the developer didn't set it" (in which case we want both our default version and the OpenXR 1.0 fallback) and "the developer really specifically wants this version" (in which case we shouldn't try to fallback because we want this one).

body:
I think this logic in the PR already covers it:
```
if (result == XR_ERROR_API_VERSION_UNSUPPORTED && init_version == XR_API_VERSION_1_1) {
```

If we prepopulate and the version we retrieve from the field matches our default, then we apply the fallback if init fails, otherwise we don't as the current logic does.

Asides from the field name and description, I don't think pre-populate should change any of the current logic, so it's more of a matter of how this presented to the end user. I think another advantage is that we have a location that explicitly describe which version of OpenXR the engine is using.. I don't think we show that information currently.

body:
I can't remember exactly why but they started life in the OpenXR module. Either I was told to move them, or they were moved during a cleanup by someone else, I'm not sure. Might be worth a git blame.

Personally I think it makes more sense to have them in the module so they can also be compiled out if OpenXR is not included.

We also have to keep in mind that the behaviour we're trying to get here is not an OpenXR standard. We're doing this purely to deal with the behavior in Metas XR runtime. It's why I marked this as an advanced setting so people don't normally see it, and I'm personally partial to leaving it empty unless you have a reason to put something in there.

Btw, Akien, the patch number remaining in sync with OpenXR 1.0 and 1.1 is a standard, I was confused by this as well. It seems they do the same with Vulkan. They reset the patch number when the major version changes, so once OpenXR 2.0 releases, we're back at patch 0.

body:
I'm looking at this and I have some comments.

1st comment: good job everyone! Makes me happy to see motion blur progressing. it was a long and large team effort and it makes me happy to see everyone working together!

A couple of question
1. Why is it a camera effect and not a world environment effect? Was this dicussed somewhere? what's the rationale?
2. I see that `show in editor` for motion blur is a project setting. I wonder if it should be editor setting. Thoughts? If it's project setting it will be synced across collaborators on a project with git.

Critique:
1. I still feel like the properties about the tile (size and clamping) is not necessary to be exposed to the user. What are the different usecase for those? If they really need to be exposed, they should have more comprehensible names. I still don't understand what they're for.
2. What passivestar said about the property names. camera stuff should have `camera` prefix because right now it's extremely unclear of what is what without reading the tooltip
3. The default camera rotation blur imo should be much lower. I'm part of those people that get motion sick very easily and it's very disorienting as it is now.
4. I don't understand the usecase for fixed framerate. Sounds like something that was exposed "because why not" more than an actual usecase? If that's indeed the case, it should be removed until there's demand. I may 100% be wrong on this, so if there is a usecase please supply it.
5. I am a bit confused about reference framerate at 30, can somebody elaborate on why 30 and not 60?
6. Velocities threshold should be under a toggle instead of changing behaviour when they're both at 0 (unless i misunderstood how they work). It looks like a niche usecase to want to wiggle those manually.

Final thoughts:

I know we've discussed this at length but I still think there should be clearer options for what type of game needs what settings at what value. I understand that racing games, fps games, top down games etc will all have different needs, but as it is right now it's hard to understand the correlation between a property and the kind of game it suits at what value. The naming is a bit aseptic and I think we should sacrifice a bit of precision and technicality in the naming in favor of better clarity for someone that doesn't know in-depth how motion blur works.

body:
Tested locally (rebased on top of `master` https://github.com/godotengine/godot/commit/ef02314f2bd0305035ecbe907883401a393da7a7), it works as expected.

**Testing project:** https://github.com/Calinou/godot-reflection

## Preview

Recorded with Movie Maker mode at 60 FPS:

### No motion blur

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f2683c4a-0ae5-497b-9e29-4104f04f90c2

### With motion blur (intensity = 1.0)

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/64141f04-15b3-4b22-b1eb-aa746b89c387

### With motion blur (intensity = 10.0, time scale = 10.0)

*Very fast motion to see how well it holds up for timelapse-like recordings.*

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/7a7ab252-ea39-48fc-a2c2-0f03ff8f23de

Some feedback:

- In terms of quality, the effect looks pretty good out of the box. Behavior matches what I expect when the framerate varies; it doesn't get overwhelming at FPS < 30, and reduces itself at higher framerates to avoid the soap opera effect.

- Motion blur is independent of viewport resolution (as expected).

- However, motion blur is affected by `Engine.time_scale`, as `time_step` in RendererSceneRenderRD takes it into account. This also affects auto exposure.

  - This can cause motion blur to become too strong during slow motion, either during development with the Game tab tools, or during gameplay if not compensated for.

  - While it is possible for the user to cancel out the time scale manually by multiplying the motion blur intensity by `Engine.time_scale`, I wonder if these effects should ignore time scale by default. This would be more consistent with other temporal effects in the engine, such as TAA and SDFGI convergence.

    - If we decide to make this change, it should probably also affect auto exposure as well. This can be done in a separate PR, but we may want to land this in the same release that will feature motion blur to minimize visual changes on upgrade.

- There is no way to use this feature with [physical camera units](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/3d/physical_light_and_camera_units.html#setting-up-physical-camera-units), as this is only exposed in CameraAttributesPractical.

  - Physically accurate motion blur could be implemented based on the shutter speed defined in CameraAttributesPhysical, but this could be left for a future PR.

			Controls the quality of the motion blur. The motion blur uses noise to smoothen the transition between samples to prevent banding, but it can only do so much. Larger sample counts will mitigate the perceivable noise, at the cost of performance. The sample counts are as follows:

			- [b]Medium:[/b] = 8 samples
			- [b]High:[/b] = 16 samples

While it's nice to have the project setting apply at runtime[^1], I think we should have setter/getter methods in the Input singleton for this:

The essence of the issue mentioned in https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/12382 and https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/6709 is that manual assignment when bone estimation fails is cumbersome.

I'm skeptical about this PR's approach if it want to address the issue, because it's too narrow in scope and lacks reusability; Specifically, it is necessary to precisely specify the symbols for distinguishing left and right, and it cannot be applied to spine bones.

body:
Looks good to me. Issue exists, and the PR fixes it.
The issue: `AudioStreamPlaybackPlaylist` ignores `p_rate_scale`, and just calls `mix` on its sub-streams with a hard-coded pitch scale of `1.0`, essentially making the pitch scale property useless.
The fix: mixing and position updates now account for `p_rate_scale`.
**Disclaimer:** I can't comment much on the mixing step, that's something I'm not super familiar with. But it looks correct to me. The hard-coded values have been replaced, `offset` (records position) is modified by pitch scale, and `stream_todo` is now modified by pitch scale as well, which seems to ensure the playback moves to the next sub-stream at the right time.

Tested:
- Playback position
- Seeking
- Low and high pitch values
- Timing and transitions
- Looping

Did not test:
- [Global speed scale](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/109113) (maybe best handled in a separate PR, and may involve `AudioStreamInteractive` too)

Everything that I've tested seemed to have worked properly.

Closes: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/104527
IMO, supersedes half of https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/106550

As we discussed in the core meeting, I am all in favour of using explicit copy constructors to help us avoid accidentally copying an entire LocalVector. I think it makes a lot of sense for our commonly used containers. 

In this case it is extra useful since it helps highlight when LocalVectors are being passed around. As the name implies, they shouldn't really be passed around to wider contexts and are meant to stay local to the class they are declared in. So seeing them get copied and moved around makes it easier for us to notice when they really should be using a Vector or other container with COW

body:
As far as I understand the system, there are two parts to how a path maps to something that can be loaded from the pck.

Path changes that happen at import time. And path changes which happen at export time.

I suspect `path_remap` only takes care of the later, while `import_remap` takes care of the former. For a full transformation they need to be chained. This seems to be supported by my limited testing:

```
p_path:  res://TestScene.gdc
p_original_path:  res://TestScene.gd
ResourceLoader::import_remap(p_original_path):  res://TestScene.gd
ResourceLoader::path_remap(p_original_path):  res://TestScene.gdc
ResourceLoader::path_remap(ResourceLoader::import_remap(p_original_path)):  res://TestScene.gdc

p_path:  res://.godot/imported/import_test_target.test-f75ad55ac69400bc5d60d5af43574001.gd
p_original_path:  res://import_test_target.test
ResourceLoader::import_remap(p_original_path):  res://.godot/imported/import_test_target.test-f75ad55ac69400bc5d60d5af43574001.gd
ResourceLoader::path_remap(p_original_path):  res://import_test_target.test
ResourceLoader::path_remap(ResourceLoader::import_remap(p_original_path)):  res://.godot/imported/import_test_target.test-f75ad55ac69400bc5d60d5af43574001.gd
```
author: HolonProduction

body: Also worth noting, that the export plugin which does binary tokenization does not seem to account for import remaps. Which is why using `p_path` has the same behaviour as `import_remap(original_path)`. But in theory if there was a path that was import and export remapped they would not be equivalent from my understanding

body:
(the same for other textures)

These should be connected with `CONNECT_REFERENCE_COUNTED` flag to prevent disconnecting the callback in case the given texture is still assigned to a different "texture slot".

E.g. consider:
```gdscript
style_box.border_texture = texture1
style_box.shadow_texture = texture1

# This would disconnect `texture1.changed` even though it's still assigned to `border_texture`.
style_box.shadow_texture = texture2
```

And with `CONNECT_REFERENCE_COUNTED` the `is_connected` check is not needed (we always want to increment the connection ref count).
```suggestion
	if (border_texture.is_valid()) {
		border_texture->connect_changed(callable, CONNECT_REFERENCE_COUNTED);
```

> Are these the only values supported on Android (no Left/Right/Upside variants)?

Android only provides App orientation change callbacks for portrait and landscape. It does not distinguish between left/right landscape or upside-down portrait.

We can infer those cases using device rotation ( also called sensor-based orientation). However, these APIs do not respect user orientation preferences (auto-rotate is disabled in system settings) so would need to handle those cases as well.

I went with the current approach since knowing whether it's portrait or landscape should be enough?

body:
> The maximum number of simultaneous sounds this node can play.

"_At the same time_" was a fine and intuitive way to express the concept. "_Simultaneous_" means the same thing but introduces a more complex term for no benefit.
The class reference, especially for these very common classes, should be accessible to users with all sorts of backgrounds in the English language.

> Increasing this value allows multiple sounds to overlap (e.g., rapid gunfire or echoes), but at a higher CPU cost.

This line is redundant, as it repeats the same concept mentioned in the first line (that multiple sounds can be played at the same time).
The "_increased CPU cost_" is not particularly unusual. More things happening means more CPU power is consumed. So this information is also redundant.

> When the limit is reached, playing a new sound will instantly terminate the oldest active sound to stay within the limit.

This last added line gives the illusion of being more meaningful, but in practice it is saying the same thing as "_Playing additional sounds after this value is reached will cut off the oldest sounds._", which was present in the original description.

body:
I think we should use `peek(-1)` here rather than `last_token`, since we don't want allow whitespace between the minus sign and the numeric part (like `- 9223372036854775808`).

Also, I'm not sure this can be solved solely in the tokenizer if we want `-9223372036854775808` to be treated as `INT_MIN`, and `-9223372036854775808**2` to be a representation error. We could have `9223372036854775808` itself be treated as `INT_MIN` everywhere (since `INT_MIN` is the only integer other than `0` for which `-x == x` is true). But that would probably be confusing.

body: Played around with this and think this is a great feature in general. A few notes: - I was unable to raise the sticky count above 6. Why not? IMO it should be able to go to a large number just because it will enable this UX improvement on various specific workflows. Even in Rift Riff's settings screen I easily hit 6 layers of organization deep and it wasn't enough. I suggest having a maximum of 16. - Looking at the trees in my commercial-game-grade projects, I think the default maximum sticky items of 3 is too low making the sticky headers less useful than they can be. The point of that number is to avoid infinite sticky items and filling the entire panel with stickies making the panel unusable. -- It's not trivial to land on a better number without making assumptions about some sort of median height of Godot user's scene panel. -- ... but making assumptions based on my experience with the editor, `5` would be a better default. - I'm not sure yet whether this should be improved and how it even could be improved, but at the core of the sticky header is that it 'hides' all the in-between nodes that are not the shortest path to root. However, there is currently no visual indication of _when there are_ nodes in between the sticky ones or not. body:
Adding to ATS' findings, code-wise, on Linux/BSD, `FileAccessUnix::seek_end` does _no_ checks for this. It just passes the offset to `fseeko` with `SEEK_END`, which simply adds the offset to the end-of-file.

POSIX manual says:

> The new position, measured in bytes from the beginning of the file, shall be obtained by adding offset to the position specified by whence. The specified point is the beginning of the file for SEEK_SET, the current value of the file-position indicator for SEEK_CUR, or end-of- file for SEEK_END.

`core/io/file_access.h` says `///< seek from the end of file with negative offset` but apparently the negative offset is supposed to be provided by the user.

So this looks like intended behavior, probably as a result of mirroring system APIs.

body: Fun question to ponder: what happens when there is a selection not aligned to caret (with caret being fully inside/outside of selection) and user presses `[Shift] + [Left/Right arrow]`? How should selection behave in those cases?
author: maaxxaam

body:
I am unsure I can answer this well enough, and just tried to keep the changeset as simple as possible. Nevertheless, we may be over-indexing on the current implementation.

As a hypothetical user, I would expect selection expansion/contraction to behave statefully like in - say - MS word, regardless of how it was originally selected. To summarise in LTR scripts:


1. If you have just selected a substring (programatically or otherwise), the first shift-arrow always tries to expand:
    1. `SHIFT | LEFT` expands leftwards, by setting the caret to the end
    2. `SHIFT | RIGHT` expands rightwards, by setting the caret to the beginning
2. On subsequent presses, it behaves as in the updated implementation, and the new test cases.

Implicit in this is some kind of state though. 🤔 

Perhaps it should just "trust" the caret if it's at `begin` or `end`, and start at step 1. otherwise? If not we'd need to maintain a boolean state variable, indicating a contiguous chain of `SHIFT | ARROW_KEY` preceding this one.
author: wheatear-dev

body: That's an interesting complication, especially given how afaik selection in `LineEdit` atm has a constraint of `beginning <= end` (at least, it seems that `LineEdit.select(1,0)`, for example, fails to select anything), and in your example selection's beginning and end may have arbitrary relative positions.
author: maaxxaam

body:
In that case, it might be an interesting idea to try and not use a state, but rather pick beginning or end of selection based on which one of them is closer to the caret, picking the one mapped to action (left = beginning, right = end) in case of a tie:

1. If caret is on the edge of selection, this scheme should act just like the proposed change does now.
2. If caret is outside/inside of selection, we manage to pick one of the points to go with.

We'd need a tiebreaker due to the following edge case:

`12|34^56|789`, where `|` are selection bounds and `^` is caret position.

In this case we'd still want to "expand" in the caret's direction, so that would leave us with:

`123^|456|789` on `Shift | Left`

`12|345|^6789` on `Shift | Right`

It would not act exactly as you describe, though, in situatuons like:

`12|345^6|789`, where `Shift | Left` would end up with

`12|34|^56789`

Which might be mitigated by measuring distance from the column where caret would end up after the action, but I'm not sure whether it would unneccessarily complicate the logic or not

body:
I'm personally leaning towards impeding the ability to set both selection range and caret from a script.

They both have their uses in isolation, but I struggle to see value in being able to set both, as it leads to bugs like the one you found, or leads to confusing behaviour otherwise.

What about (from a script):

- set caret, or set selection, alone. Fine!
- set caret, then set selection. Selection "wins", and nullifies caret.
- set selection, then set caret. Caret wins, and nullifies selection

This means that in the specific case in your issue, there will be a selection but no caret. So we can just expand on first shift+arrow.

body:
I guess we don't have much of a choice. It sucks to have to do the extra memcpy for every instance. The idea was that using UMA would save us both from having to do a GPU->GPU copy (by omitting the staging buffer) and the CPU->CPU copy by not having an intermediate buffer. This effectively brings back the CPU->CPU copy in a slightly less efficient way since we now copy element by element instead of doing one big memcpy for the entire region of the buffer that will be used. 

That being said, trying to create two codepaths, one for UMA that avoids the copy and one for non-UMA that copies the entire buffer range at once feels way too complicated to justify. 

I think this solution is likely our best option even if performance won't be ideal, it should be fine.

The test that's failing is a stack overflow test; it uses a dictionary that contains an array that nest that same dictionary, so when the logic attempts to convert the data structure, it keeps looping over the nested elements until the stack is exhausted.

On older devices, the stack limit is much less than the previous depth limit (1024), so this update reduces that limit to a value that won't cause a stack overflow on older versions.

body:
A GDExtension can't be switched from non-reloadable to reloadable without restarting the Godot editor - if it's reloadable, there's bookkeeping that needs to start when it's first loaded.

So, at most, this should update the config, but it shouldn't actually mark the `GDExtension` object as reloadable _or_ attempt to reload it, unless it was already reloadable when the editor first started. Otherwise, bad things (including crashing) could happen

In fact, I just tested this with the [godot_openxr_vendors](https://github.com/GodotVR/godot_openxr_vendors) extension, and setting it to reloadable crashes the editor

They are usable, you have incorrect flags listed in that snippet (flags mismatch the comments). Fixed:
```gdscript
func _ready():
	var format := "%04o"

	var permissions_owner_only = (
			FileAccess.UNIX_READ_OWNER | FileAccess.UNIX_WRITE_OWNER
	) # 384 in decimal form (600 in octal form)
	print(format % permissions_owner_only)

	# Default UNIX permissions are 644 on files, 755 on folders.
	# On folders, the "execute" permission determines whether the user can list files in the folder.
	var permissions_default_file = (
			FileAccess.UNIX_READ_OWNER | FileAccess.UNIX_WRITE_OWNER |
			FileAccess.UNIX_READ_GROUP |
			FileAccess.UNIX_READ_OTHER
	) # 420 in decimal form (644 in octal form)
	print(format % permissions_default_file)

	var all_permissions_for_everyone = (
			FileAccess.UNIX_READ_OWNER | FileAccess.UNIX_WRITE_OWNER | FileAccess.UNIX_EXECUTE_OWNER |
			FileAccess.UNIX_READ_GROUP | FileAccess.UNIX_WRITE_GROUP | FileAccess.UNIX_EXECUTE_GROUP |
			FileAccess.UNIX_READ_OTHER | FileAccess.UNIX_WRITE_OTHER | FileAccess.UNIX_EXECUTE_OTHER
	) # 511 in decimal form (777 in octal form)
	print(format % all_permissions_for_everyone)

	var da = DirAccess.open("res://")
	da.copy("res://source.txt", "res://600.txt", permissions_owner_only)
	da.copy("res://source.txt", "res://644.txt", permissions_default_file)
	da.copy("res://source.txt", "res://777.txt", all_permissions_for_everyone)
```

body:
> Won't this mean that Variant is constructed twice now?

I would go even further and say this Variant is constructed three times !

- Once in `Variant ret`
- Once in `memnew_placement(r_return, Variant(ret));`
- An once within `callp` since this functions takes the ret parameter as a reference (i.e. `Variant &ret` ). So `ret`'s destructor is first called, then the actual return value is copied into it.

That's outside of the scope of this PR, but have we considered replacing the `Variant &ret` by a `Variant *r_uninitialized_ret` and then do the `memnew_placement(r_uninitialized_ret, ...)` within `callp` ?

In theory this would remove all the extra variant initialization (but in practice the compiler might already be smart enough when attempting to inline callp inside the caller, and figure out the intermediary variants can be omitted...)

body:
The fix is correct. It's concerning that with the design of `AHashMap`, that this sort of bug is so easy to trigger and produces a difficult to detect but dangerous use-after-free bug.

The problem is `nodes[p_new_name] = nodes[p_name]` is equivalent to
`operator=(operator[](nodes, p_new_name), operator[](const nodes, p_name))`

which means that both operator[] will be evaluated, in an arbitrary order before the operator= runs. One of the operator[] calls will invalidate the const reference returned by the other.

Since Node is a struct, it is safe to make a copy, and then store it, so this fix is correct.

body: Tested locally, it works as expected. I think this has a lot of potential, but we need to make sure we get the UX on properties right (while keeping the compatibility constraints in mind). I'd appreciate more reviews from @godotengine/usability, as well as anyone versed in level design. In the long term, we'll probably want some kind of higher-level editor for quick level design which uses CSG nodes as a backend, but exposes common actions through an overlay on the 3D editor viewport (e.g. create CSG nodes in a single click). In any case, we will need this feature to be available in CSG nodes so that future functionality can make use of it. **Testing project:** [test_pr_115926.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25753902/test_pr_115926.zip) Some feedback: - Top Material and Bottom Material should be in the Material section of the inspector. Right now, they are outside and therefore don't collapse if you collapse the Material section: | -|- - Capitalization should be added to EditorPropertyNameProcessor for `uvs` -> `UVs`, below `uv2`: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/c53c5a1f49fa1edf97e6b570297c90a57d30a558/editor/inspector/editor_property_name_processor.cpp#L310 - I think the Flip UVs property could do with more flexibility. Right now, textures like wooden planks may be misaligned, and you have to rotate the entire CSG node to fix this. This can be cumbersome if that CSG node has children, or an irregular shape where rotating it by 90° would lead to a different result than just rotating the UV. - I suggest having one enum property to rotate the UV by 90-degree increments, and another enum property to flip the U axis, the V axis, or both. As I understand it, this computation should be trivial (unlike rotating by non-90 degree increments). - I'd like to see similar UV mapping options in CSGPolygon3D, so that the roof in the above example can have its tiles property scaled (they are way too large right now). I use a CSGPolygon3D for the roof as it's an easy way to create prism shapes. - While in Depth mode, there could be separate Top and Bottom materials like in CSGBox3D.

The implementation overall looks good to me. But I'm not entirely sure if using the `<name> (<value>)` format is a good idea. Perhaps we should only have constant names (without values ​​in parentheses) if we don't think users should rely on "magic" numbers? This change definitely improves readability, but:

1. Constant values ​​are no longer valid expressions.
   * `GDScriptDocGen` already partially breaks this rule, displaying identifiers/calls in simple cases, hiding deeply nested or non-constant contents of arrays/dictionaries with `...`, or using `<unknown>` and `<Object>` placeholders.
2. This somewhat goes beyond the original meaning of the `value` attribute. It is now not just a reduced value the constant or variable/parameter default value, but a complex expression.
   * We cannot add clickable links for constants in the expression.
   * Third-party addons reading the XML documentation may break if they rely on the current `value` attribute semantics.

We also need to make sure that this works correctly for GDExtension documentation and that `make_rst.py` doesn't break.

body:
Shader previews are not real breakpoints, they just reuse the breakpoint gutter.
More importantly, we do not want shader previews to appear in the breakpoints for DebugAdapterProtocol or the `--breakpoints` or `--remote-debug` flags.
`get_breakpoints` needs to only be for actual script breakpoints.
`get_breakpoints` is not used for saving them either, that is separate, part of `get_edit_state`.

And for `edited_scene_changed`, it looks like it will cause `_update_modified_scripts_for_external_editor` to be called twice unnecessarily.

If the plan is to merge them in the future, we can just do it in the future. Having this base class IMO just makes things a little more complex and doesn't help that much.

When this button is used and the Go To Line popup finishes, the focus returns to this button but it should go to the text edit.

Linking these directly could cause confusion since Go To Line popup uses Line and Character, while the button uses Line and Column (tabs are 1 char but 4 cols). But it already can be confusing and I'm not sure how to fix it without larger changes like unifying them, which could be done later.

> I'd want to spawn the go to line popup just above the button – especially on a larger screen, it's a bit uncomfortable to click on a button in the right bottom and have a tiny window at the very top of the screen. Could also be a follow-up PR.

The Go To Line popup can't be interacted with the mouse (and can't be a SpinBox since it accepts columns too), so it doesn't really need to be next to the button IMO. It seems like having it close would encourage users to try using the mouse on it.
Also when opening by shortcut/menu I'd rather have it popup in a more prominent place like the top center than the bottom right, and for consistency the button should open it in the same place.
If we do add some mouse interaction to it (like custom up / down buttons), then it probably would be better to have it show next to the button, when it is opened by the button.

body:
The forward-progress check is intentional and acts purely as a safety guard against malformed chunks that could otherwise cause an infinite loop.

All structurally critical errors (truncated headers, invalid size fields, invalid channel count, out-of-bounds reads, etc.) already abort parsing via ERR_FAIL_*.
This specific check is not validating structure but ensuring that the loop always makes progress, even in edge cases like zero-sized or corrupted chunks.

Since parsing stops immediately after this condition and we may already have valid data loaded, escalating this to a hard error would be unnecessarily strict. A warning is sufficient here.

I prefer to keep this as a defensive safeguard to prevent potential infinite loops, especially considering future modifications to the chunk handling logic.
author: snosrati200

body:
Thank you for the feedback so far. To move this PR forward, I see two reasonable ways to handle the stalled parser when encountering malformed WAV chunks, and I’d like to hear which one the Godot maintainers prefer:

Option 1: Defensive Safeguard (Current Implementation)
This keeps a general forward-progress check at the end of the loop as a universal safety net against malformed or zero-sized chunks. It prevents infinite loops while allowing the parser to return already-loaded valid data (graceful degradation).

Option 2: Strict Validation (Hard Error)
We could instead perform an explicit chunksize == 0 check at the start of the loop and escalate this to a full ERR_FAIL return. This would strictly abort parsing on corrupted data and avoid partial returns, aligning with Godot’s usual error standards.

I am happy to implement either approach. If the maintainers prefer the stricter validation path (Option 2), please let me know and I will update the code accordingly with the necessary size checks and error handling.

Which option aligns better with Godot’s error-handling conventions?

body:
The issue is more complex than the min GPU, when baking shaders.

Unfortunately, when shaders are queried in the renderer, it asks the **host** platform for supported features, such as `RD::SUPPORTS_IMAGE_ATOMIC_32_BIT` (the primary culprit of the baking issues). On the host platform, this returns true. When baking the shader, the minimum GPU and Metal versions are passed to SPIRV-Cross, based on the MetalDeviceProfile. By default, the versions we pass do not support atomics, so it generates unsupported shader code, as SPIRV-Cross tries to emulate atomics. 

> [!IMPORTANT]
>
> If the user specified a target OS of iOS 17 (Metal 3.1) for iOS, the baked shaders should work. For earlier OS versions, Godot should fall back to compiling the code.

body:
The core problem here is that `material_set_shader` is not following a read-only constraint on shader and modifying it instead. Pushing the call to the command queue introduces a race between the mesh loading and the server thread where it'll fail to precompile pipelines in time if the command queue hasn't gotten to it yet.

The proper fix would be to fix `material_set_shader` instead. As it stands, the PR introduces a potential performance/stutter regression that will be very difficult to detect in the future as to why it happens.

The resource importer uses `beat_count` to determine the end point of an audio track. It's at that point where the audio will loop, or end if played on interactive streams. `beat_count` is set manually.
I used "The length of the audio track, in beats." because we're indeed getting the length of the track in beats, and it tells you the behavior changing that property causes - it changes the length of the track (not in all, but many cases).
"Number of beats" is correct too, but doesn't describe a behavior. IMO, it's easier to assume it just sets and returns the number of beats in a track, and that the property has no effect.

This looks good to me! I've also personally encountered problems that this would fix.

The only thing I'm unsure about is the name of the method as `push_gui_input()`. It makes sense to mirror the `Viewport` method, but on its own, it's a little weird. Perhaps `call_gui_input()` (like the original method but without the leading underscore) would be better? But that's really just bike shedding :-)
author: dsnopek

body:
There is a problem with exposing this method as is. It depends on `get_viewport()->is_input_handled()`, which is a state that changes depending on when this is called.

Calling `call_gui_input` would only work as expected if it is called after a `push_input` and before an event is accepted, but exposing it means it can be called from anywhere.
If you do call this after an event has been accepted *anywhere* in the current viewport, only the signal will be emitted, which will lead to differences in behavior with controls that use the virtual call or c++ `gui_input` instead.
This also prevents `call_gui_input` from working when called multiple times in a row.

And it can't easily be removed since a control will expect that accepting the event in the `gui_input` signal will stop it from going to the virtual method. So the accept event / `is_input_handled` has to know somehow if it is being set for the regular input propagation, or for this call. I don't know if that is possible reliably since they can be called at anytime.
author: kitbdev

body: I completely agree with the assessment of kitbdev and think that exposing this function is a bad idea. Calling `Control::_call_gui_input` not only executes the wanted functionality, but also has side-effects with other input handling aspects, its interaction with input_handled being one of them. If it wouldn't break compatibility, personally I would even go so far as to unexpose `Viewport::push_input`, because conceptually it suffers from the same problems. Basically we would need to separate the input system (covering all aspects of the internal system how input is handled) from the action system (the actions, that an input event causes). However, because `Viewport::set_input_handled` is exposed to GDScript, that function can be called in any action. We would need to find a way to move the call of set_input_handled (red) to the blue area in the above graphic. That would allow us to call the action without any interference with the input system. I believe, that there are also other hooks into the input system, which would also need to be addressed.
