body: As a serious issue, results become unstable when there are three or more holes. https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/4b49b92d-b03c-4c44-8407-278d8b7cb853 Based on testing, the result is stable with two holes. https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8f1fe8bc-aae9-4e0a-9580-eeadab058f6e [kusudama_test.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25640319/kusudama_test.zip) Therefore, if we implement this in 4.7, we should consider statically limiting the number of holes to two. If we statically limit holes to two, two structures come to mind. --- One is the same as the current implementation and just having two holes internally: ```cpp struct HoleSetting { Vector3 direction; real_t radius; } HoleSetting begin_hole; HoleSetting end_hole; ``` --- The other approach is to eliminate the Vector specification and instead treat it as a arc-shaped area spreading in the ±Z directions, with the offset delegated to JointLimitation: ```cpp real_t arc_angle; // 0 to 360deg. How to spread start and end to +Z and -Z. for example, 180deg means start hole dir is Vector3(0, 0, -1) and end hole dir is Vector3(0, 0, 1). real_t start_radius; // -Z real_t end_radius; // +Z ``` Offset is set by: The reason it expands in the Z direction is because HumanoidProfile defines X rotation as a Bend. In other words, specifying individual vectors makes sense when there are three or more holes. However, when there are only two holes, specifying individual vectors is redundant with the rotation offset parameter. This means the hole direction can be automatically generated from the arc parameter without necessarily specifying it individually. --- Personally, I think the latter approach makes the role of the offset clearer and allows for more intuitive range manipulation. If we don't plan to abandon implementing the three holes in the future (after 4.7), I think providing the two static hole approach as a class called JointLimitationArc is a somewhat good compromise. How do you think?

body:
Does this behave identically to before? I.e are there any edge-cases where this will return a different value from before (not including floating point precision differences of course).

The biggest considerations when merging PRs like this are:
1. What tangible benefit does this provide users? A 13% performance improvement is nice, but a 13% improvement on a function that is called only a handful of times doesn't really do anything. More directly, how often is this called in a frame and how many microseconds does this save in a typical frame?
2. The risk of bugs. Any change to the codebase risks introducing bugs. From looking at the code alone I can't tell how the behaviour differs, or even if it differs. But experience tells me that many safe-looking PRs can introduce bugs when edge-cases aren't properly considered. 

Basically, the performance benefit in actual games needs to justify the risk we take in merging this. Saving 25,000 microseconds is really nice, but nobody is calling this function 300 million times in a loop in their game. So what is the actual benefit for real games?

There is already a limit of 100000 per file, we probably shouldn't have 2 separate limits.

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/1aaea38e7f8dd9e2a94e2e339247fc976a84de75/editor/script/find_in_files.cpp#L236-L238

If we do add this, there should be a way to disable it too, like if it is set to -1.
Related https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/4717


Also it feels like does not work correctly, it will never show that it is finished searching and it looks like it is stuck. It should instead show a warning that there are too many matches instead, and that the limit can be increased or the search can be more specific.

But I don't think there needs to be a new result limit field in this PR, the search happens asynchronously so you can still use the editor already. It doesn't matter how long it takes since there is a clearly visible search progress bar and a cancel button. IMO this is already far better usability than the demo from https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/5544#issuecomment-1847419681 that just has a popup and no progress to completion or cancel.
If we are concerned about performance, we can improve it in multiple ways in a separate PR. Such as multithreading (see the `// This part can be moved to a thread if needed.`), or not using signals to update the ui immediately for every single find.

I'm not completely against a global result limit. But IMO it should be big enough that you generally don't need to care about it. And ideally it would only have to be a editor setting.

body:
My concern is that most users may not be aware of `NORMALIZE_32_RESCUE_THRESHOLD`. In other words, users cannot determine in advance whether a vector is normalizable, and they would only be able to perform a zero vector check after attempting normalization.

Although we could recommend performing a preliminary zero vector check using `is_zero_approx()`, this is equivalent to checking `length_sq` against `CMP_EPSILON2`, which implies that there is no need to be concerned about the case the length is smaller than `CMP_EPSILON2`.
author: TokageItLab

body:
This is why the existing functions are not ideally designed.

`normalize()` should return success or failure, and this is why all the new functions I wrote here `normalize_and_get_length()` and `safe_normalize()` return 0 in the case of failure.

With epsilons, you can't practically have the user check them _before_ calling the routine, it has to return success or failure. With the existing `normalize()` and `normalized()` you'd want to check with absolute zero (i.e. `== Vector3`), which is more expensive than just checking a single value `== 0`.

UPDATE: This should no longer be a concern as both the PRs only return success or failure now (the old functions no longer wrap the new), so you can simply call and check for failure. Ideally users should be caring about these epsilons at all, or have them exposed, they should just check for failure (if this is likely to happen).
author: lawnjelly

body:
I should first clarify that epsilons are chosen to pass `is_normalized()` in both non-precise and precise mode.
______________
Input vector (chosen to be just above a lowered threshold but small enough for float error to become visible):
gdscript
```
var v = Vector2(0.000030518, 0.000030518)   # ≈ (3.0518e-5, 3.0518e-5)
# original length ≈ 4.314e-5    → length² ≈ 1.861e-9
```

Now assume we lowered the safe threshold to something like 1e-8f (or even 5e-8f):

* lengthsq = 1.861e-9 > 1e-8 → fast path triggers
* Compute length = sqrt(1.861e-9) ≈ 4.314e-5 (already somewhat imprecise in float)
* Then v /= length → normalize in single precision

Typical outcome in real float32 arithmetic (reproduced in multiple environments):
After normalization:

Expected ideal: something very close to (0.7071, 0.7071)
Actual result (float32 rounding + sqrt imprecision): e.g. (0.70710677, 0.70710665)
length_squared() after normalization: ≈ 1.00000155 … 1.0000038 (or symmetrically below 1)

→ Deviation |length² - 1| ≈ 1.5e-6 … 4e-6 (sometimes up to ~8–9e-6 in worse directions)

Now compare to Godot's is_normalized():
Default UNIT_EPSILON = 0.001 → still passes easily
Precise checks (UNIT_EPSILON = 1e-5 or tighter custom) → fails the check
(deviation > 1e-5 in some directions / rounding alignments)

________________

Amusingly, I spotted that Grok made a mistake above. The length squared of the example is _outside_ the precise tolerance and so shouldn't fail. :laughing: 

I'm just trying to see whether the epsilons can be lowered a little as a result.
author: lawnjelly

It's claimed the epsilon is higher than it could be in the `SAFE` branch to ensure that the direction is preserved as well as possible, rather than only to pass the `is_normalized()` check. The rescue branch comfortably passes the `is_normalized()` check but better preserves the direction.

| epsilon | passes precise checks | direction quality |

|1e-7f | yes | excellent|
|1e-9f | yes | good|
|1e-10f | yes | bad|
|1e-13f | yes (until underflow) | garbage|

body:
At the end of the loop, `_add_to_batch` actually copies the bytes out of the 'new instance data' and into the stored buffer. 

``` c++
memcpy(&state.instance_data[state.instance_data_index], &state.intermediary_instance_data, sizeof(InstanceData));
```

So it saves us a little bit of time to just setup the buffer outside of the loop, and overwrite it + copy out each step, rather than set up a new buffer each step.

`MultiRect` was intended to be a fixed size type so it can be stored on the stack. There is a final allocation (even in 3.x) for copying to the command, but `Vector` is super heavyweight for bottleneck operations like appending etc.

`FixedVector` is the 4.x version that @Ivorforce made which is basically like `FixedArray` in 3.x (if I remember right).

`FixedVector` would work perfectly here as a slot in replacement I think.

body: Really look forward to this feature and took a bit of time to review today but will review more later: - `propagate_maximum_size` is a bit of a tricky boolean and I'm not sure we should introduce it with this PR. It propagates the max size to individual nodes which is a bit weird in the context of BoxContainers: … and it also propagates to grandchildren and beyond, even if those children are not in a container: I would argue that **the custom maximum size should primarily be set on the thing that has the potential to grow**, in the examples above: the Label and _not_ the PanelContainer. And with that approach we'd never need any propagation and thus removing one extra property and another layer of complexity – as well as remove something that may confuse new users (eg. "why aren't my labels growing?! ohh it's because 6 parents up something propagated all the way down here"). - I'd reorder first four properties inside the Layout section of Control to: custom min size, custom max size, (propagate max size here, if there's consensus on keeping it), and then clip contents. (and then layout direction, mode, etc) - Other than the above, I played around with Label and RichTextLabel and loved it! Precisely what I've been needing for the last two years. Will play with this a bit more later.

body:
I can't fully agree with that description.

The way a child's `combined_maximum_size` is computed (which is what determines the final size constraining) is by taking the lesser of their own `custom_maximum_size` and their parent's `combined_maximum_size` (if parent's `propagate = true`). So this:
> until a child node sets their own [member custom_maximum_size]

is only true if that child's `custom_maximum_size` is less than the ancestor's that is propagating.

A more accurate description would be:
* If `true`, this `Control`'s children will have their size limited by this `Control`'s `custom_maximum_size` and relevant theme properties.

I don't think the
> propagates to all child [Control] nodes [...] until that child node disables [member propagate_maximum_size].

is necessary. Recursion is already implied by the property's behavior. 

Maybe the property should be renamed to something that makes this more explicit, though I am struggling to find a suitable name.

body:
Maybe we can do the following:
* `custom_maximum_size`
```diff
The maximum size of the node's bounding rectangle. If set to a value greater than [code](0, 0)[/code], the node's bounding rectangle will never exceed this size. A value of [code](0, 0)[/code] means there is no maximum size.
+ [b]Note:[/b] The final effective maximum size is the one returned by [method get_combined_maximum_size]
[b]Note:[/b] Not all [Control] subtypes handle this gracefully, which may lead to unexpected behavior if the control's contents exceed this size.
[b]Note:[/b] This value has priority over [member custom_minimum_size]. For example, if you set [member custom_maximum_size] to [code](100, 100)[/code] and [member custom_minimum_size] to [code](200, 200)[/code], the resulting size will be [code](100, 100)[/code].
```

* `get_combined_maximum_size`
```diff
Returns the combined maximum size from [member custom_maximum_size] and [method get_maximum_size].
+ [b]Note:[/b] This also accounts for the parent's combined maximum size if the parent has [member propagate_maximum_size] set to [code]true[/code].
[b]Note:[/b] This method will always return a size greater than or equal to that returned by [method get_combined_minimum_size].
```

* `propagate_maximum_size`
```diff
+ If [code]true[/code], this Control's children will use the value returned by [method get_combined_maximum_size] in their own size calculations.
```

This way, the recursion is explicitly stated. It could still be refined, though. I am not the best at explaining things.

body:
This obviously isn't my area of expertise, but since [this comment](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/114690#discussion_r2669644485) was left unresolved in #114690, this seems worth bringing up again.

Last I heard there was quite the fundamental problem with having `GDScriptParser::get_dependencies` return GDScript dependencies like this, since `ResourceLoader` requires (?) that resource dependencies form an acyclical graph, whereas GDScript can have cyclical dependencies.

Is there something about the changes to `ResourceLoader` in this PR, or the way `dependencies` is populated, that addresses that concern? If not, then this change would presumably end up reopening issues like #91726 again, unless they've been mitigated in some other way since then.

Given what you said about this whole PR falling apart without this change it seems like this would be worth clearing up.
author: mihe

body: I'd suggest to just add an additional `get_cyclic_dependencies` method for the time being. We can add a default impl that just returns `get_dependencies` and GDScript can only implement the later. Systems from which we explicitly know that they were written with cyclic dependencies in mind can utilize the information without the risk of breaking existing stuff.
author: HolonProduction

body:
Let's leave concerns about support for cyclic references aside for a second.

I'm not convinced that tracking deps in the analyzer is a valid approach. Our other resource format loaders take special care not to actually load dependencies in `get_dependencies`. And previous regressions clearly show that current users are relying on this behaviour (If someone wants to play detective: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/commit/519fce94e97888d37efc11b44e6cc6cb01b51a3a).

Best we can do with that restraint is doing stuff in the parser. (I don't think anyone is keen on adding more behaviour flags to the analyzer?)

body:
Looking at this code, I'm not sure this is a great idea, performance wise.

The way it is implemented here involves a lot of runtime overhead: Creating new vectors, string checks, callbacks, etc.
Normally, I'd suggest that swizzling should be completely resolved at compile time, which would make it possible to compile swizzled access without much overhead in almost all cases (e.g. `vector.yx = [a, b]` can compile to `vector.y = a; vector.x = b`), avoiding all the parsing and allocations at runtime.

However, in GDScript we always have to deal with gradual typing, which means that swizzling would bleed into normal member access: If anything is accessing a member by anyone, we always have to check if it's a "swizzled access" because we weren't able to check this at compile time. Besides the additional overhead for _every single member access_ (including non-swizzled), an actual swizzle would incur the cost of runtime resolution, which would be very noticeable.

Overall I'm not convinced this is worth it.

I haven't followed discussions around replacing swizzles with "member-like access", e.g. `vector2.yx` is a "special member" on `Vector2` with a custom getter and custom setter taking and returning `Vector2`. This would alleviate most of my concerns. 
But I see you have rejected this possibility in the OP, so I'm guessing this was discussed and rejected before too.

body:
Skimmed through, didn't check/analyze the usage in the changed Controls. The currently used sorting is unstable, meaning the commands' ordering is not preserved even within the same `order+texture` spans. This is an issue for rendering commands relying on the command ordering like `CommandAnimationSlice`, `CommandClipIgnore`, `CommandTransform`. Either it should be changed to use stable sorting, or combining presorting with such commands should be made unsupported (docs + warnings/errors?).
Example of how it breaks using CommandTransform

```gdscript extends Node2D @export var use_presort := false @export var t_speed := 8.0 var row_count := 1 var rows_max := 128 var t := 0.0 func _process(delta: float) -> void: t += delta * t_speed if t >= 1.0: row_count = maxi(1, (row_count + 1) % rows_max) t = fmod(t, 1.0) queue_redraw() func _draw() -> void: var colors := PackedColorArray([ Color.RED, Color.GREEN, Color.BLUE, Color.VIOLET, ]) var s := get_viewport_rect().size var cell_size := s / Vector2(colors.size(), row_count) var ci := get_canvas_item() if use_presort: RenderingServer.canvas_item_set_presort_level(ci, 0) for y: int in row_count: for x: int in colors.size(): var color := colors[x] draw_set_transform(Vector2(x, y) * cell_size) draw_rect(Rect2(Vector2(), cell_size).grow(-1), color) if use_presort: RenderingServer.canvas_item_flush_presort(ci) ``` - `use_presort == false`: https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/3eba753e-8201-45d4-b295-99d5c05d0a87 - `use_presort == true`: https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6791be4b-e11f-46d8-8505-e96105177498

body:
One small remark here, and also for the same calculation in the render device version of this shader. We're doing an addition here which is counter intuitive because for un-projecting you would expect to subtract.

But we have to remember that originally we project our vertex by doing ` + z * projection[2][0]` and we are looking in the z- direction. So we end up with ` + -1.0 * projection[2][0]` which means we need to do ` - -1.0 * projection[2][0]` to un-project. Hence ` + projection[2][0]`...

Also very counter intuitive is the order in which we've stored our projection matrix entries into our vector, yes `projection.x` stores `projection[2][0]` while `projection.y` stores `projection[0][0]`.

Just interesting info to have for prosperity :)

body:
I'm almost surprised to say but I'm fine with the `class_db.h` explicit include.
It's a great approach: Just add it to all the implementation files of `Object` subclasses. Makes for a real simple PR, and one that unlocks us from removing the include from headers much easier.

I'm not 100% sure about the `.compat.inc`. Both positions come with potential downsides: If it's at the start it cannot use the `.cpp` file's static functions, if it's at the end, the `.cpp` files cannot use compat functions (though perhaps they shouldn't need to?). Overall I don't have a strong preference for this which is why I haven't made an official proposal to change this so far. Maybe it would be ideal to actually have it be a separate `.cpp` file altogether, and one that only affects the header by declaring like `_bind_compat_functions` or something like that. But I'm not sure it's worth the churn to change it at all right now? 

Anyway, enough rambling, i'd say it at least needs some separate discussion.

body:
This would also resolve #109213, which is essentially a duplicate of #113270, or the other way around I guess, but I did not realize this problem extended to things like child node transform propagation as well, which is much worse than just shape changes not being respected.

I mentioned a similar fix in #109213, but I must admit I'm hesitant to approve this, even if your change is arguably the correct and pragmatic thing to do here. The performance impact of this change can potentially be quite drastic, depending on the project.

Given how prevalent physics queries are in most games, and the fact that things like `Viewport::_process_picking` and `NOTIFICATION_INTERNAL_PHYSICS_PROCESS` runs right after `_physics_process` and `physics_frame`, you would pretty much be guaranteed to flush every single mutating `PhysicsServer*D` operation on the main thread now[^1], as opposed to the physics thread.

We would however still be running the actual simulation step on the physics thread at least, which I would imagine is the more costly part of the physics for most projects, so there would still be *some* benefit to running threaded I guess.

[^1]: Except for things like transform changes of kinematic bodies I guess, since those happen at the very end of the physics processing.

> StringName would work well. We can just replace TypeHash thash = 0; // Hash by Path + SubPath + TrackType. with something like StringName path_with_type // path+type.

I tested this along with `Pair<NodePath, TrackType>` with the current master (using thash). Again, using the same mrp:


|  | Master (uint32_t thash) | Master (uint64_t thash) | Pair | StringName |
|--------|------------|--------|--------|--------|
| FPS | 124.44 | 119.06 | 89.94 | 114.55 |

For StringName, I kept the `StringName path_with_type` in the track to make it stay in the memory and used its pointer as key (casted to `uint64_t`). In the PR description, I provided my initial benchmarks which included StringName as key (not the pointer), therefore I did not make another benchmark for it, assuming it would be worse anyways.

I didn't want to give up any performance, but at this point I don't think it can be avoided. The thread safety ruins everything. Now I'm leaning towards `StringName` as well.

As `uint64_t` version of master performs better, I think with some tweaks, the `StringName` pointer can give a similar performance as well. More importantly, it should eliminate thread safety concerns. Is this OK?

author: ugursoy

body:
> Here is the patch if you want to check it yourselves: [stringname.patch](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25788910/stringname.patch)

Looks good to me so far.

My only concern at this point is `AnimatedValuesBackup`. Right now it relies on `TypeHash`, but with this change `TypeHash` is effectively based on `StringName::data_unique_pointer()`, so it is only stable for as long as the backing `StringName` remains alive.

I think this could break in a case like this:
- `AnimationMixer::make_backup()` stores values keyed by `TypeHash`.
- Later, the relevant `Animation` resources are unloaded, along with their `Track`s and possibly the backing `StringName`s.
- If those animations are loaded again, `path_with_cache_type` may end up with a different `data_unique_pointer()`.
- At that point, `AnimationMixer::restore()` could be working with stale keys from `AnimatedValuesBackup` that no longer match the current mixer state.

Because of that, I think `AnimatedValuesBackup` should eventually use a stable identifier across unload/reload, such as `StringName` itself or `Pair<NodePath, TrackType>`, instead of `TypeHash`.

That said, I think this can be handled later once we have @TokageItLab's opinion on the current approach and when the PR is updated.

body:
[Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverse_domain_name_notation) says:

> Reverse-DNS strings are based on registered domain names ... Reverse-DNS names are a simple way of eliminating namespace collisions, since any registered domain name is globally unique to its owner ...

This article references [flatpak's definition](https://docs.flatpak.org/en/latest/conventions.html#application-ids):

> The format is in reverse-DNS style, meaning the first section should be a domain controlled by the project

However I agree that it is very ambiguous, and not all definitions of reverse-DNS mention this. The convention suggestion just felt a little pointless if I didn't include this, which is why I added it in.

body: Tested locally, it works as expected. Some feedback: - With this PR, it's no longer possible to install a `.tpz` file in the editor. I don't think this was used often in the 4.x days (as third-party builds that were available for multiple platforms became rarer), but it's worth noting. - When in offline mode, "Error getting the list of mirrors" still shows up when using a development build after a small delay: - Removing export templates should have a confirmation dialog, as there's no way to undo the operation. While official templates can be easily redownloaded, this is not the case if you are far away from an Internet connection, or if you installed third-party export templates. - The confirmation dialog could be skipped by holding Shift when clicking the delete icon. For future PRs: - There should be a way to remove all export templates for an associated version, so you can quickly clean up old data after upgrading to a new version. - In the long term, it might be worth deprecating the concept of a `.tpz` file and switch to a flat structure with ZIP files directly being downloaded (likely after moving the Windows/Linux templates to ZIPs). This could simplify the editor code significantly, and allow for CI platforms to download specific platforms easily. - Alternatively, we could add a command line argument to download specific platforms for CI usage, but this requires a Godot process to be spun up, which takes more time to start than `curl` or `wget`.

body: Tested locally, it works as expected. Code looks good to me. Note that it's up to the developer to correct the aspect ratio, as distortion is allowed in this mode. Example with the viewport on the left being 256×512, and the one on the right being 1024×512: [This is sometimes desired](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/11160), but it may increase the difficulty of using this feature in the most common use case scenario (pixel art games wishing to support widescreen with not too much hassle). It might be worth having another mode that sets a fixed resolution, but stretches it automatically according to the SubViewportContainer's aspect ratio to avoid distortion. You would set the size assuming the SubViewportContainer has a 1:1 aspect ratio, then it would automatically compensate behind the scenes. For example, setting the size to 100×100 would result in a 177×100 viewport on 16:9. I still think we should make the shrink factor a float in the long run, but doing so would break GDExtension compatibility. To do so in a way that preserves compatibility, a new property needs to be introduced (with a different name), then `shrink` can be deprecated (and set the new property automatically when assigned a value).

I think this is a great start overall 🙂 Some feedback: - The Ribbon node should be renamed to Ribbon3D for consistency with the rest of the inheritance tree: Personally, I would prefer if it was named Line3D to match Line2D naming, but I understand why a different name is used. - An editor icon should be added for Ribbon, e.g. something like this (which is a recolored Line2D icon): ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6ca4eb7f-080b-4345-b1cf-7e19c0d36f6c) - The editor constantly redraws when a Ribbon node is present in the scene tree (even if it's invisible). Remember to enable **Show Update Spinner** in the Editor Settings to diagnose this. - There's a "ghost" node configuration warning displayed after creating a Ribbon node. This warning goes away after reloading the scene, and clicking it does nothing (no dialog is spawned): - There should be a node configuration warning when the material mode is set to **Custom** and no material is specified. - The ribbon isn't visible in the editor until you save and reload the scene. This might be related to the above "ghost warning" issue. - Beams are not visible in the editor until you change their Length property. - Likewise, changing a beam's **Mesh Alignment** mode from Billboard to Local can cause issues until the length is adjusted to force the mesh to redraw. ___ For future PRs: - Overbright/HDR colors can't be used in the gradient curve (they will be clamped). Perhaps something like https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/97604 is needed for Ribbon in the long run. (I assume it relies on vertex colors for the coloring, which can't be overbright in 4.x, as opposed to a texture.) - Is it planned to add a Texture property? There are properties to set the tiling mode, multiplier and UV pinning, so one could logically expect to be able to use a texture on the default materials. - The default material could have a property to fade trails and beams that are nearly perpendicular to the camera, to avoid obvious rotation: https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6508dcda-83aa-4b52-b6aa-325a53c6e3f7 This is commonly done for beams that emulate volumetric light shafts, using a `dot()` product in the fragment shader. The TPS demo uses a custom shader for this currently. The value would be set as a threshold for the `dot()` product to start fading (`0.0` = no fade, `1.0` = start fading as soon as it's not perfectly perpendicular to the camera).

Our [shaders style guide](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/shaders/shaders_style_guide.html) doesn't recommend writing each render mode on its own line, so I would follow it:

```suggestion
			shader_type spatial;
			render_mode blend_mix, depth_draw_never, unshaded, skip_vertex_transform, cull_disabled;
```

We do the same in other built-in shaders like BaseMaterial3D.

PS: `blend_mix` is redundant here, as it's the default. It could be removed to make the shader more compact.

Items requiring a preview update originate from two sources:
1. File previews (`queue_resource_preview()`)
2. Resource instance previews (`queue_edited_resource_preview()`)

When the resource file is in use (i.e., no corresponding cached instance exists in the `ResourceCache`), file preview generation proceeds normally.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/82f2dda6-dd2b-4ead-84bf-f711669363cb

The call to `queue_resource_preview()` is made directly or indirectly in `FileSystemDock` or `EditorFileSystem` (`EditorResourcePreview::check_for_invalidation()`).

However, file changes should be detected in `EditorFileSystem`, so reload should complete there before `queue_resource_preview()`.

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/1eb0374e5f3efa05d8a9914f482b894b5b1f6b9c/editor/file_system/editor_file_system.cpp#L1064

As of now, it occurs quite late. Simply calling `EditorFileSystem::update_file()` will not trigger a reload.

body:
This is a minor compatibility hazard:

- Version 4.7 checks `if (variant_get_type_by_name(...) == VARIANT_MAX)`
- Version 4.8 adds a new variant type
- This changes the value of `VARIANT_MAX`
- The extension written under 4.7 but run under 4.8 will now have a silent runtime bug

This _can_ be OK if the caller just wants to check whether a variant of that type exists, but a user may assume "the variant type exists _and I know about it_".

Maybe documenting something like:

> Checking `type != VARIANT_MAX` may return true, even if none of the statically known variant types matches (namely, when the extension runs in a newer Godot version that has additional variant types).
author: Bromeon

body: Perhaps we should suggest checking for `type >= VARIANT_MAX`? If a new variant type was added, the GDExtension doesn't know about it, so it's invalid as far as its concerned anyway
author: dsnopek

body:
So if I understand correctly, the suggestion would then be to handle this on the godot-cpp in the sibling PR https://github.com/godotengine/godot-cpp/pull/1946?

There we could use the `result >= VARIANT_MAX` check and easily deal with when the engine returns a new variant type that godot-cpp does not yet know about.  Is that correct?

Here we would just amend the documentation to clarify this corner case.
author: Naros

body:
GDExtension isn't my area of ​​expertise, but in my opinion, `variant_get_type_by_name()` isn't a function that's required in the GDExtension interface for communicating with the engine. The list of `Variant` types is already present in `extension_api.json`, and binding generators can already recreate an equivalent of `Variant::get_type_by_name()` on the extension side.

Why don't we add more comprehensive and unified reflection for global symbols and `Variant` members in the form of `Variant` utility functions:

```gdscript
get_global_scope_enum_list() -> Array[Dictionary]
get_global_scope_constant_list() -> Array[Dictionary]
get_global_scope_function_list() -> Array[Dictionary]

get_variant_enum_list(type: Variant.Type) -> Array[Dictionary]
get_variant_constant_list(type: Variant.Type) -> Array[Dictionary]
get_variant_method_list(type: Variant.Type) -> Array[Dictionary]
get_variant_property_list(type: Variant.Type) -> Array[Dictionary]
```

Then both extensions and scripts could get the list of `Variant` types from the global `Variant.Type` enum (to populate the dictionary/hashmap `String -> Variant.Type`).
author: dalexeev

body:
> Why don't we add more comprehensive and unified reflection for global symbols and `Variant` members in the form of `Variant` utility functions

We should do this!

However, we already have `variant_get_type_name` in the GDExtension interface, and, in my opinion, it makes sense to have `variant_get_type_by_name` to go in the other direction as well.

Personally, I don't think we should block adding a missing method (which I suspect was just an oversight) on solving the bigger problem
author: dsnopek

body:
> So if I understand correctly, the suggestion would then be to handle this on the godot-cpp in the sibling PR [godotengine/godot-cpp#1946](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-cpp/pull/1946)?

The suggestion is just about updating the docs. I don't know that we can do anything in godot-cpp, we'd just need to pass on the same docs to users of godot-cpp
author: dsnopek

body:
> Personally, I don't think we should block adding a missing method (which I suspect was just an oversight) on solving the bigger problem

It does mean though that there's one more way to achieve the same thing. One could argue that `variant_get_type_name` is already redundant, no need to make it two :wink: and if we end up adding a general way to do these lookups in the future, there's yet another way :sweat_smile:

It's not a disaster, but it will increase redundancy in the available API and possibly require deprecations at some point.

---

> Perhaps we should suggest checking for `type >= VARIANT_MAX`? If a new variant type was added, the GDExtension doesn't know about it, so it's invalid as far as its concerned anyway

To circle back to the `VARIANT_MAX` issue, the subtle difference here is that the behavior depends on the runtime version of Godot, not the compiled GDExtension API (as one might suggest). I'm not sure if that discrepancy is clear from the docs alone.

And given the potential for bugs, I'm no longer sure if adding this method provides actual benefits over iterating the static list of variant types (which the extension _knows_ it can work with).

I'm also not personally that worried about this duplicating a future generic solution, given that this is such a tiny addition, and no one is even working on the generic solution.

That said, this PR has gotten way more push back than I would have expected, so we should probably discuss it at a GDExtension team meeting and try to get closer to consensus :-)

I've also tested vertex snapping in complex scenes like https://github.com/Calinou/godot-reflection and performance seemed OK. I do wonder if there's room for improvement on performance still, as dragging a mesh with vertex snapping is clearly less smooth the more complex the scene gets.

body: Tested locally, it works as expected. **Testing project:** [test_ssil.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26635077/test_ssil.zip) ### Before #### Normal https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/5ce289cc-bfcb-438c-8ff4-408d5c594807 #### Ultra https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c4b682b4-2f74-4629-96f2-ac26c42bc3c7 ### After #### Normal https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e3a5c970-a545-4653-9c20-d118484caea2 #### Ultra https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/fded556d-e576-4535-9513-6085ec0009bb Some feedback: - With this PR, the SSIL range becomes resolution-dependent (old SSIL did not have this issue). At higher resolutions, SSIL doesn't go as far: https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/fd976fdb-a19d-4229-9575-3e4ceaa15f03 This also affects toggling the **SSIL > Half Size** project setting. This makes adjustments more difficult, as the appearance effectively varies according to window size and the 3D resolution scale factor. If possible, look into adjusting the SSIL range automatically relative to a base viewport resolution (e.g. 1080 pixels tall). If you manually double the range when the viewport resolution is doubled on each axis, you get roughly the same SSIL appearance: Half resolution | Full resolution | Full resolution, doubled range -|-|- | | - The default quality leads to rather noisy visuals, especially when strong emissives are involved. To improve quality without affecting performance too much, I suggest reintroducing the noise, but only jitter it every frame when TAA or FSR2 is enabled. Keep the noise static otherwise, which should make it less noticeable. - We do something similar for shadow maps already: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/61834 - Look into using interleaved gradient noise: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/9495deaf7532313ff7154d8a06aa6fc100807532/servers/rendering/renderer_rd/shaders/environment/sky.glsl#L142-L147 TAA jitter can be performed by adding a offset every frame, with `taa_frame_count` being equal to `float(RSG::rasterizer->get_frame_number() % p_jitter_phase_count)`: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/9495deaf7532313ff7154d8a06aa6fc100807532/servers/rendering/renderer_rd/shaders/scene_forward_lights_inc.glsl#L305 - Backface rejection is now off by default, which likely explains why visuals can change so much in some scenes. It also means indirect lighting can be less temporally stable, especially when faces that are nearly parallel to the camera slowly become visible like the ceiling here: https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d263505a-88ef-4487-b668-e46a93cb2574

```suggestion
    StringName cycle_length = "cycle_length"; // If cycle_length != current_cycle_length, update inverted_cycle_length to avoid division every frame.
	StringName inverted_cycle_length = "inverted_cycle_length";
	const LocalVector<double> cached_lengths;
```

While the cached_lengths for child animations may not differ per instance, in the `SYNC_MODE_CYCLIC_MUTABLE` case, each instance must manage its `cached_delta_factors{}` using `set_parameter()`/`get_parameter()`.

This means that since `blend_position` is managed per instance, `cached_delta_factors` must be managed similarly. Storing an array here might not be ideal, so it's probably best to cache only the inverse of the animation length and handle the rest as a multiplication each frame.

This is worth discussing. `OS` is only used on Android and AppleEmbedded (iOS/visionOS) to call `OS::get_name` for an error message. So technically it's detected as unused if not on those platforms, so it should be conditional.

But that's the kind of things which could lead to developer annoyance if they're on one of those platforms, start using `OS` in non-conditional code, and it then fails CI. ```
0.7400000095367431640625000 // Entered in the editor.

body:
I may be a bit mistaken on this, but:
Having pixel values is also not ideal, imo. Hexagonal tiles are often anti-aliased and being able to put the the end of the flat side in in between two pixel can be more accurate. Pixel values are ints, meaning if they are used the flat side can end only on the beginning of a pixel. 
That being said, the value can be a float in the 0.0 to tile_size range.



Checked out how [https://thorbjorn.itch.io/tiled] implemented this feature, and they do have "Tile Side Length (Hex)" be an int value in pixels from 0 to tile_size. This is a bit less ergonomic when changing tile_size, but does allow for better precision for higher tile sized.  Just something for reference.

Can implement it this way if thats preferred. We need to make a decision on if a floating point or int px value to use. I think px values are fine for the most part, but for small tile sizes it might be a bit too coarse.

I don't think the inaccuracy is a big issue TBH, since there's no simple way to pixel-perfect align tiles in the float computations world under the hood, I think users should expect to have to add an additional pixel for precision.

My main issue with going with pixels is that we cannot provide a sensible default value, since it depends on the tile_size. So well, it means the hexagonal shape won't be usable out of the box. Also, it would need to be automatically clamped to the tile_size too, which is a bit annoying to track. 

Edit: also, it's kind of compat-breaking.

Or maybe... I have an idea! We could store the `flat_size_lenght` value internally as an integer offset from the `tile_size / 2` value.

So if `flat_size_lenght == tile_size / 2`, we store `0`, otherwise we store a negative value if it's smaller, and a positive value if it's longer. That way, the default value can stay 0 and, changing the tile_size should not impact the look of things with the default value.

author: groud

body:
Visualization of the issue with the current implementation (click to expand)

Here's an example tile (120x23 size; 88 flat side length; one pixel black border on transparent background): -><- To make the borders of the neighboring tiles overlap you can set `TileSet.tile_size` to 118x22 and keep `TileSetAtlasSource.texture_region_size` as 120x23. Inaccuracy after setting `flat_side_ratio` to `88.0 / 118` in the editor is visible even for the `(0, 0)` cell: The same with neighbor cells added, see the pixel overlaps: | -|- After setting the same ratio in code (add script + reload the scene): ```gdscript @tool extends TileMapLayer func _ready() -> void: tile_set.flat_side_ratio = 88.0 / 118 ``` you can see no misalignment/overlaps: || -|-|-

As seen the potential unintentional micro gaps/overlaps can be avoided (or rather the error can be minimized), we should aim for that. --- > Having pixel values is also not ideal, imo. Hexagonal tiles are often anti-aliased and being able to put the the end of the flat side in in between two pixel can be more accurate. Pixel values are ints, meaning if they are used the flat side can end only on the beginning of a pixel. That being said, the value can be a float in the 0.0 to tile_size range. > Can implement it this way if thats preferred. We need to make a decision on if a floating point or int px value to use. I think px values are fine for the most part, but for small tile sizes it might be a bit too coarse. To be clear, I meant pixel units, it doesn't have to be `int`. Just changing the unit to pixels already improves the precision a lot. Editor truncating something like `0.005` from the ratio is a potentially big issue (as visualized above), truncating `0.005` from the pixel value is likely to be negligble / just fine. But also note that for a whole-pixels/integer input there should be no error introduced at all even when the property is `float`. So I think using `float` only makes it more customizable, there's no penalty for the integer cases. Personally I'm in favor of a `float` property in pixels. So if you have slight/uneven antialiasing or whatever on the tile borders then you could try tweaking it to subpixel/non-integer values. I don't see why would we need to limit the user here. Again, even for `float` property type the integer values would be storable without any error (tile sizes are not that big to reach float's integer precision). I guess if we really want to discourage subpixel values then the editor slider could have `step = 1.0`; but then subpixel values would be assignable only from the code. I'm not a fan of that but it would be an acceptable compromise to me. Also note that we can't pick `int` now and change later to `float` only if there's a demand from the users, this would be compatiblity breaking. Hence I'm in favor of using `float` straight away. > Or maybe... I have an idea! We could store the `flat_size_lenght` value internally as an integer offset from the `tile_size / 2` value. > > So if `flat_size_lenght == tile_size / 2`, we store `0`, otherwise we store a negative value if it's smaller, and a positive value if it's longer. That way, the default value can stay 0 and, changing the tile_size should not impact the look of things with the default value. Makes sense to me! I'm still in favor of using float though. 🙃

Wait quick question, are we exposing `flat_side_length` to the user? If so then yeah i just keep the overlap float value on the backend, to preserve the shape when changing the size. One issue with `flat_side_length` is the editor default ui value cannot always make the regular hexagon. It has to be some constant length.

Unless there is a way to set default value in _validate_property, whoops cant check rn, sorry if im being silly. (I think its just xml, but will check in like 3hrs)

> Wait quick question, are we exposing flat_side_length to the user?

`flat_side_length` is exposed to the user yes, but it should be stored on disk as the offset in pixel (called `flat_side_modifier`).

>  If so then yeah i just keep the overlap float value on the backend, to preserve the shape when changing the size. 

No, the problem with that approach is that it's less precise compared to a value in pixel. This, indeed, can be a problem for pixel-art games.

> If we expose `flat_side_modifier`

No, only `flat_side_length` is exposed as a "proxy" property. `flat_side_modifier` is what's stored on disk.

>  Personally i think flat_side_length being exposed is better as its super easy to understand and doesnt need extra explaining to the users. Just want to get a confirmation that we are fine with default value in the editor being a bit weird(probably being 8px which is super short for larger tiles).

The default value of `flat_side_length` will depend on the default value of `flat_side_modifier` (zero) and `tile_size`. `flat_side_length` should be computed as `tile_size / 2 + flat_side_modifier`, thus its default value should be `tile_size / 2`.

clangd / IWYU would report the `so_wrap.h` files as "not used directly" because what's used from them in most cases is structs or enums from the thirdparty headers. Using the `export` pragma, IWYU now considers that the `so_wrap.h` file is providing those symbols directly.

body:
If this needs to only be added to the header and not the implementation, this patch will do:

```diff
diff --git a/generate-wrapper.py b/generate-wrapper.py
index 62b6294..77abc12 100755
--- a/generate-wrapper.py
+++ b/generate-wrapper.py
@@ -146,9 +146,9 @@ def generate_header(sysincludes, functions, initname, implementation_headers):
 
     for include in sysincludes:
         if include.startswith("<"):
-            retval.append(f"#include {include}")
+            retval.append(f"#include {include} // IWYU pragma: export.")
         else:
-            retval.append(f"#include \"{include}\"")
+            retval.append(f"#include \"{include}\" // IWYU pragma: export.")
 
     for function in functions:
         retval.append(f"#undef {function}")
```

Will make a PR upstream.

On my RTX 5090 on Linux + Vulkan, the limits for the texture offset appear to be `-8; 7` and `-32; 31` for texture gather offset. The limit for texture offset is the same in OpenGL.

body:
The idea seems good to me, but I haven't delved into the details and am unsure what the implications might be in edge cases (such as multithreading). We need to ensure that during hot reloading, all script instances are updated before the `old_member_indices` in the script is cleared. We also need to ensure that this works correctly for inherited classes (the correct order parent-child classes) and cyclic dependencies.

But we should probably still do this at the beginning of the 4.8 dev cycle, despite the risk of regressions. Hot reloading is an important feature, but not the most critical one. In the worst case, we may introduce strange behavior, which could confuse users during debugging with hot reloading. But I'd still like to reduce the likelihood of silently masking errors (see my comment about the `is_reloading_members` flag).
author: dalexeev

body: I'm a little concerned about the empty `old_member_indices` playing a dual role here. It might be empty because the class previously had no members, or because we made some mistake and the script is reloading at an unexpected time. Perhaps we should add an `is_reloading_members` flag and check its value at the appropriate points (here, at the beginning, and at the end of the reload)? Especially considering that this flag will now be part of `GDScript`, not `GDScriptInstance`.

I'm not exactly sure what you mean by empty array. This checks for the absence of values but not for a completely empty array. So basically we ignore members that did not exist before the reload and do not copy them over.

I've seen very little use of dynamically linked ANGLE in Godot projects in the wild, so I agree with this change.

Note that this is a "soft dependency", and compilation will continue with ANGLE disabled if the libraries haven't been downloaded. This check is probably too aggressive, as it uses the CPU name and not the GPU name reported by the VM. It will cause initialization to fail when you install llvmpipe in a VM (instead of relying on the VM's own 3D acceleration).

For contex, the general advice to run Godot and other 3D apps in a VM (outside of headless mode) is to turn off the VM's own 3D acceleration and install llvmpipe. VirtualBox's 3D acceleration is pretty outdated in 2026, and while vmWare and Parallels fare better, it's still far from ideal in terms of API compliance.

Either way, I think this check should be added to a separate PR as it warrants its own discussion.

body:
Makes sense to me.

`metadata_properties` was introduced in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/59452. As far as I can tell, it was meant to be an optimization for the `set` and `get` case (not needing a substring).

3 reasons why I I think `metadata_properties` is premature optimization:
1. `starts_with` is not meaningfully slower (probably faster) than hash lookup, in the 'miss' path. Regular property access will not be slower.
2. `set` metadata is likely faster through this change than before (less hash lookups).
3. The fast path to get metadata is `get_meta`. The regular property getter is a convenience method and is overshadowed by the rest of `get` anyway — this won't make a difference.

The only caveat to (1) is that we make an unnecessary `String` copy here, which increments and decrements an atomic. This is unavoidable until https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/118856 is merged. I'd prefer if https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/118856 was merged first to avoid a lookup regression from this.

body:
So, before, the three different methods (`add_constant`, `add_enum_constant`, and `add_variant_constant`) all had different levels of checking for each other; I simply unified them so that they all check for each other. 
They should never (and currently indeed never do) have members with the same. This just hardcodes that check. 

It is technically unnecessary and maybe outside the scope of this PR, but since I was touching that code, I deemed it only fit to bring it up to what I consider a reasonable standard. 

Think of it this way, if those checks aren't hardcoded, a type could have a variant constant and an int constant (or enum) with the same name... Yeah no.
author: StarryWorm

body:
`add_enum_constant` was using the following code:
```
enum_data[p_type].value[p_enum_type_name][p_enumeration_name] = p_enum_value;
enum_data[p_type].value_to_enum[p_enumeration_name] = p_enum_type_name;
```
This means it was not adding it to either `constant_data[p_type]` (it was using the `EnumData` struct, not the `ConstantData` struct). So the number of values in each enum were not counted. `Variant` did not include enum values in integer constants.

This approach should result in the same number as before, namely integer constants + variant constants. 
I could be wrong though, and please do let me know if so.
author: StarryWorm

body:
Same as for `get_constants_count_for_type`, afaik `Variant` was not treating enums as constants. I don't know why, but that's how it was (unless I misunderstood the code).

I actually believe they should be counted, it's just that it would be a change from the existing model, so I didn't do it. This is especially relevant for `has_constant()` which will return false for enum values even though they are exposed all the same... Same logic for me as with the newly added checks for adding new integer/enum/variant constants cross-checking each other.
author: StarryWorm

body: Looking at when the existing checks were added, it looks like they were just added here when bugfixing other things, and weren't as thorough as they should have been https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/99424 https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/38891

body:
Just saw the edit, was typing out my comment whilst that happened, I guess. As far as speed, there's really not much that can be done about it? The fact that `GDType` does not support non-enum integer constants to be directly accessed kind of prevents it from being made faster than through the loop for that part. 

Now, just like the counting thing, this is all because `Variant` does not consider enums as constants (not even talking about enum values, just the enums themselves). Why? I'm not sure. 
* If we depart from this model, which I would be in favor of, then the counting would become as fast as it used to be again. 

This method is only there for GDNative, added by #44733 , with the intent of pre-allocating buffers with the correct size. I don't think that we need to worry too much about performance, as it's a one-off operation.

author: Shadows-of-Fire

body:
The order is meaningful as the patterns will be evaluated in that order, and some of them can match the same files, e.g.:
```
  - Regex: ^<(windows|Jolt/Jolt|platform_gl)\.h>$
    Priority: 6
  - Regex: ^<.*\.(h|hpp)>$
    Priority: 7
  - Regex: ^<.*>$
    Priority: 8
```
All three would match `<windows.h>`, so it needs to be in that order to work as intended.

So at least `<.*>` and `".*"` need to be the last in their respective category (`""` or `<>` includes).

So this should work too:
```
  - Regex: ^"(core|drivers|editor|main|scene|servers|tests)/.*"$
    Priority: 3
  - Regex: ^"(modules|platform)/.*"$
    Priority: 4
  - Regex: ^"thirdparty/.*"$
    Priority: 5
  - Regex: ^<(windows|Jolt/Jolt|platform_gl)\.h>$
    Priority: 6
  - Regex: ^<.*\.(h|hpp)>$
    Priority: 7
  - Regex: ^<.*>$
    Priority: 8
  - Regex: ^".*\.compat\.inc"$
    Priority: 1
  - Regex: ^".*"$
    Priority: 2
```

(Initially I didn't have as specific options for `"(core|drivers|editor|main|scene|servers|tests)/.*"` so the current apparently random grouping comes from necessity, but now it can be reordered a bit indeed.)

As for using large numbers, we could, but I feel that if we were to slot something in between existing groups I'd want to change the other numbers too to stay consistent, and this won't be changed often so I don't think we need to worry about minimizing diffs or conflicts. So I'm neutral on it, we could use 10-based or just keep it sequential.

body:
I like the idea of this a LOT, but from past experience with these options I'd say there's room to formalize matters even further. In particular: we should take advantage of `SortPriority`, to allow for ordering within a group without causing spaces. For example, the following would solve the gap issue for `*.compat.inc`:
```diff
   - Regex: ^".*\.compat\.inc"$
-    Priority: 1
+    Priority: 0
+    SortPriority: 1
```
Trying to adjust this even further gets a bit messy, especially if we try to capture with a wildcard after the fact, but I would like to cover our bases as much as possible before fully formalizing anything

body:
This is not good approach, and it may corrupt the pose.

If you want to retrieve the modified pose, you should call `get_bone_pose` within the `skeleton_updated` signal, rather than adding `get_bone_pose_final` to `Skeleton3D`. When you first select the Skeleton, you can set the dirty flag and call `NOTIFICATION_UPDATE_SKELETON` to trigger `skeleton_updated` at will, allowing you to retrieve the modified pose. You can refer to `Skeleton3DEditor::insert_keys()` for the example.

By doing above, we should be able to follow modified pose in any place. However, we must never allow the handles (blue/yellow circle) to follow modified pose.

Since setting the "modified pose" to the Skeleton "original pose" will cause issues such as time paradoxes and break the behavior of the Modifier. For example, if you move only the arm using IK and adjust the finger pose using handles, there is no issue since the finger is a bone that is not directly affected by the Modifier. However, if you move the arm using IK and adjust the arm’s pose using handles, a paradox occurs and the system breaks down.

So you will likely need to implement an option to force the Modifiers to be disabled when entering BoneEditMode. Or, you need to retrieve the list of bones marked with `Bone.make_bone_modified` and disable only those handles.

`EditorSceneFormatImporterBlend` has an import option prefixed with `gltf/` (not `blender/` like the other options). `ResourceImporterScene` borrows options from all format importers and ends up with two options `gltf/naming_version`. I removed the duplicate when generating the documentation, but it still appears in the editor (because `EditorHelp` generates documentation again after the format importers have been registered).

Is the presence of the `gltf/naming_version` import option in `EditorSceneFormatImporterBlend` a bug? Should it be named `blender/naming_version` or `blender/gltf/naming_version` instead? Or maybe this option shouldn't be declared again?

body:
This does look a bit weird. Given that `classes` has value-keys, calling `classes.erase` is going to delete the `ClassInfo`, but `ClassInfo` only has a default dtor meaning it doesn't really do any cleanup for its various pointer members (nor can I even tell what the expected ownership model is from just looking at it).

The call site is in `GDExtension::_unregister_extension_class`
```c++
#ifdef TOOLS_ENABLED
	ClassDB::unregister_extension_class(class_name, !ext->is_reloading);
#else
	ClassDB::unregister_extension_class(class_name);
#endif
```

So it wants to keep the method binds around during a reload for... undocumented reasons.

It _appears_ to be a way to cross-communicate with `GDExtension::_register_extension_class_method` to avoid recreating the `GDExtensionMethodBind` objects, instead updating the existing ones with the reloaded extension data. It only does this if `TOOLS_ENABLED` though (I suppose reloads are not legal otherwise).

The context from the [original PR](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/80284) is
```
When methods are gone after the reload, it marks the method binds as "invalid" and if you try to call them an error is printed and it won't be called. However, if something is caching method binds, it should probably check if it's still valid, and if not, stop caching it! If GDScript or anything else in the engine is doing this, we should update it. This could be handled in a follow-up PR - what is in this PR is at least safe.
```

So... Maybe a bandaid over poor behavior of things holding onto `MethodBind*` objects when they ought not to be.

The two checks for `type->disabled` will not behave in this PR the same way as they used to due to using `gdtype->get_method_map(p_no_inheritance)` instead of the old looping through every single type. 

Assuming `p_no_inheritance == false`, otherwise it's not relevant
Before: type -> check disabled -> add methods if not -> supertype replaces type -> loop
After: type -> check disabled -> add all methods of self and all supertypes

This means we go from only including methods for type and all non-disabled supertypes to including methods for type and all supertypes if type is not disabled. 

This can be handled:
A. By reintroducing the loops and using `gdtype->get_method_map(true)`
B. By changing the way method maps are handled on `GDType` to take into account disabled types when using `get_method_map(false)`

body:
There is an easy solution here. Merge this PR and see how many users actually miss the setting being right there. We don't need to speculate how many people find it useful. Just default to false for now, if enough people complain after Beta 1 than we default to true in a subsequent Beta 2. 

I am very skeptical about the need for this dropdown in the first place. First, it was added for the benefit of engine developers, not users. Second, we have several experienced developers telling us that it hurts the UX of the editor (especially on Mobile), we should listen to them. 

The only mention of this being needed is from Bastiaan saying he is aware of developers who are targeting PCVR and mobile VR that benefit from rapid switching between the renders while developing (since they want to preview what the mobile version will look like when running on the PCVR headset). This is a niche segment within a niche platform, we shouldn't be taking up valuable editor space to cater to it. 

Finally, if we default to false, we might as well not make the change at all. Users will never wade through the already bloated list of editor settings to find the setting to disable the bad default UX. We should default to behaviour that is good for the _majority_ of users, and then let the users with specific needs enable the specific editor setting for their use-case.

body:
Since the description in #116051 is a bit convoluted, let me reword the issue:

> - `locale/fallback` is set to source language `X` (the language in which hardcoded strings are written)
> - The project only provides translations for language `Y`
> - The current locale is set to `X`
>
> When `X` and `Y` are related (e.g., `fr` and `fr_CA`, `en_GB` and `en_US`, `zh_Hans` and `zh_Hant`), the translation for language `Y` is used directly, rather than the original string.

This process does not actually involve `locale/fallback`, so skipping `locale/fallback` does not solve this problem.

What you need is skipping the whole translation process in this situation I think.

body:
Tested locally, it works as expected.

Some feedback:

- `FWPLUS` in warnings and enums shouldn't be abbreviated. Instead, we should write it in its full form `FORWARD_PLUS`, like we do in the renderer name.

- To disable motion vectors on an object, you need to write a very small but *non-zero* value (e.g. `vec2(0.0000001)`). If you write `vec2(0.0)`, the default motion vectors based on camera motion will apply. This isn't very intuitive, so maybe there should be `render_mode motion_vector_disabled` for this.
  - See also https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/77523.

- Whenever motion vectors are overridden, camera motion no longer influences motion vectors. Is there a way to keep both? This is what we need for scrolling texture UVs, where we want the constant motion of the scrolling texture to affect motion, but preserve automatic motion vectors from camera motion.
  - Setting `MOTION_VECTOR` to a very high value makes the scrolling texture sharp as if TAA was disabled, but it makes anything in front jitter heavily, so it's not a correct solution.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/57bb9f1d-965d-4d05-8f43-1a94a8d25cea

- Motion vectors seem dependent on the viewport aspect ratio (like normalized UV coordinates), unlike the automatic default motion vector. You need to account for this when writing your shader. Is this how it works in other engines? If not, I can see this being a pitfall for supporting multiple aspect ratios.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/982ced9b-ec38-45fc-9a10-fd047f2b5021

> [!NOTE]
>
> The videos above have the editor capped to 30 FPS for consistent TAA display.

Looks good to me, but we should probably add some comments:

1. (`VariantInternal`) That `object_assign_without_ref_unsafe()` should be used with extreme caution.
2. (VM) That destructors for fixed addresses aren't called because `Variant`s are initialized with `object_assign_without_ref_unsafe()`.

Tested locally on the MRP from https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/100846 (rebased on top of `master`), I found some issues.

On my end, the behavior already appeared to work fine on `master` when following these instructions:

- Double-check the particle's emission mode is **Directed Points** and not **Points** (it was set to **Points** when I first opened the MRP).
- When testing the MRP, make sure to set **Spread** to `0.0` and **Direction** to `(0, 0, 0)` in the ParticleProcessMaterial.

We should also document the fact that **Direction** being set to `(0, 0, 0)` is a special case when using directed point emission. Non-zero directions *are* valid to create particles that are emitted along a surface (not going away from it), but are probably not what most users expect.

body:
I feel that what this PR is trying to achieve does not make much sense. Although SkeletonModificationStack2D is experimental, to be honest making it a Resource was a design failure as pointed out in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/117090#issuecomment-4009741726. That is the reason why SkeletonModificationStack3D was removed at the launch of 4.0 and SkeletonModifier3D was added instead.

As a class that uses similar resources, there is AnimationBlendTree, which holds the current state as a parameter dictionary in instances of AnimationTree node. If you want to correctly instantiate SkeletonModification2D as a shared Resource, you would need to have its parent, Skeleton2D node, hold something like a dictionary to store things such as the transform information from the previous frame for IK, for example `skeleton_2d->store_mod_parameter(*self, SNAME("prev_transform"), t2d);`. Otherwise, if a ModificationStack needs to retain prev_rot, a conflict may occur when sharing a reference. For instance, if SkeletonA (prev_rot: 0.5) and SkeletonB (prev_rot: 1.0) share the same ModificationStack and are processed sequentially, SkeletonA's prev_rot will be incorrectly overwritten by 1.0 in the ModificationStack.

However, as also mentioned in https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/10247, I believe that SkeletonModification2D should ultimately be deprecated and migrated to SkeletonModifier2D.

To solve the problem in #117090, the correct path is to proceed with the implementation of SkeletonModifier2D, but that will likely take time. While this PR hides the errors, it should not change the fact that they are not working correctly. I think the only thing we can do here now is to issue a warning that Skeleton2D, which holds a SkeletonModification2D, should be deep-copied and made unique when instantiated.

body:
Tested locally (including runtime loading support), it works as expected. Code and documentation look good to me.

I did a test on the TPS demo where I replaced its soundtrack (112 Kb/s Vorbis, 3 minutes of audio, 2.6 MB total) with Opus-encoded versions (64 Kb/s Opus). This provides a 1.3 MB size reduction, which stays roughly intact in the exported PCK size:

- `master` with Vorbis soundtrack: 582,804 bytes
- This PR with Opus soundtrack: 581,692 bytes (-1,112 KB)

The same goes in an exported ZIP data pack (therefore with compression):

- `master` with Vorbis soundtrack: 252,776 bytes
- This PR with Opus soundtrack: 251,772 bytes (-1,004 KB)

Tip: Use this shell script to mass-convert Vorbis to Opus (run at project root):

```bash
shopt -s globstar nullglob
for audio in **/*.ogg; do
  ffmpeg -hide_banner -i $audio -b:a 64k ${audio//.ogg/.opus} -y
done
```

Remember to assign the .opus files in AudioStreamPlayer nodes, and move the .ogg originals outside the project folder afterwards so that they're not included in the exported PCK.

For best results, you should encode Opus audio from a lossless source (WAV or FLAC), as encoding from a lossy codec to another will make the loss of quality more significant. 64 Kb/s Opus should be equivalent to 128 Kb/s Vorbis when both are encoded from a lossless source, but this may not hold true when re-encoding lossy Vorbis audio.

That said, I can't seem to build Godot with `builtin_opus=no` despite having installed `opus-devel opusfile-devel` from the Fedora 43 repositories:

Nice to see Opus was revived here !

I see this PR was based on #47114, which was from 2021, so this PR missed the modern patterns :
- no overrides such as `tag_used_streams`, `set_parameter`, `get_parameter`, `set_is_sample`, `get_is_sample`, `get_sample_playback`, `set_sample_playback`
- `data` using `void*` instead of the container like `TightLocalVector`
- Still initialize the values in the constructor instead of initializing as default values
- properties like `length` and `loop_offset` are still using `float`. But sibling implementations like Vorbis use `double` (MP3 is using `float` too)

Compared with [my own implementation from almost a year ago (outdated branch, not based on #47114)](https://github.com/gongpha/godot/tree/opus), I am skeptical about `_mix_internal`'s infinite loop handling. But I think I would leave it there if there is no significant issue or crash

body:
Tested locally, it works as expected. Code looks good to me.

Compared to https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/91263, this is not as fast and files produced are larger, but it has almost no binary size overhead (< 1 KB), since we're exposing an existing option in libpng instead of introducing a new library (however small it is). I would still like to get QOI merged as it's still a good deal faster than this PR, making real-time speeds much more likely to be a reality for many projects.

Even if we do merge QOI support later on, I think this PR still has merit on its own as it allows games to opt into faster screenshot taking with a popular image format. This makes sense when you still want a format that can easily be shared on social media. For example, Steam, Discord, etc. don't support QOI file uploads with previewing, but accept PNGs that may be recompressed to smaller lossy formats.

A set of frames in each format for validation, just so you can see the output looks identical: [frame_1250.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26392064/frame_1250.zip)

Some feedback:

- The `editor/movie_writer/png/optimize_speed` project setting should be `true` by default, as most users will want to favor speed over compression efficiency (since PNG frames are often thrown away after encoding a video from them). It's a small behavior change, but one that I consider acceptable as we don't guarantee MovieWriter outputs to be bit-for-bit identical across releases.

## Benchmark

<details open>

<summary>PC specifications</summary>

- **CPU:** AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D
- **GPU:** NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090
- **RAM:** 64 GB (2×32 GB DDR5-6000 CL30)
- **SSD:** Solidigm P44 Pro 2 TB
- **OS:** Linux (Fedora 43)
</details>

Using a release export template build with `production=yes lto=full`. All tests are done with branches rebased on top of `master` https://github.com/godotengine/godot/commit/4a919adccf8e398aceca75399c539078c54fe97f.

Time taken to record 30 seconds of https://github.com/Calinou/godot-movie-maker-demo at the default window size (1152×648), V-Sync disabled:

Format | Encoding time | File size of all frames
-|-|-
PNG (`master`) | 5m37s (8% of real-time) | 1294 MB
PNG with Optimize Speed (this PR) | 56s (53% of real-time) | 1950 MB
[QOI](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/91263) | 19s (157% of real-time) | 1533 MB

I'd like to test [fpng](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/101268) for completeness, but I can't compile it due to https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/101268#issuecomment-2602756658 which still applies on my Fedora 43 system.

Tokage says:Processing only when fitting to a spline causes sudden changes, so I am interpolating the tilt based on the distance from the path using fade-in/fade-out.

body:
Yeah, I considered your approach at one point.  If you run the tests, you'll see this breaks existing unit tests, which is why I didn't go with it:

`test_fuzzy_search.cpp:48`:
```
	// Short query, many matches, few adjacent characters
	{ "///gd", "./menu/hud/hud.gd" },
```

Your version does not score `./menu/hud/hud.gd` highest for the search `///gd` but instead scores `./menu/menu/characters/dead_guy/dead_guy.gd` highest, like this:

`.[/]menu[/]menu[/]characters/dead_[g]uy/[d]ead_guy.gd`

The `[d]` earns a +4 bonus for being a substring of the `///gd` token that matches at the start of a filename!

I was so surprised by this outcome that I decided it would be better to not yet attempt solving this more general case of "user starts to type filename then jumps ahead in filename and is superseded by shorter path that also has both words on word boundaries" :)

As to rewriting the system to address broader concerns, I'd argue that goes against Godot's [Best Practices for Engine Contribution](https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/engine/guidelines/best_practices.html).

Edit to add - the `menu__debug` search case could *possibly* be resolved in the future by giving a score bonus to matches (exact or inexact) at the start of the filename, but only when they are the first substring in the `FuzzyTokenMatch.substrings` vector.  But I'd want a lot more test cases to show that this doesn't have unexpected behavior like the above proposed change.

body: The `is_meta_type` flag is used to indicate the type of expressions whose values ​​are types (first-class types, types of types). For example, the identifier `points` is of type `PackedVector2Array`, and the identifier `PackedVector2Array` is of type `PackedVector2Array (type)`. For built-in properties, this is likely impossible, but I chose to explicitly check the `is_meta_type` flag since we had many bugs related to this flag.

body: This should never be merged. If you apply the `step` directly there, a discrepancy will occur between the actual animation’s current time and the displayed time. To give a simple example, if you set the snap to 1.0s, the current time will always show 0s from 0 to 0.4999 seconds. In other words, you cannot use the direct `step` setting here. A possible solution would be to provide a separate button for the spinner, distinct from the spinner itself. Alternatively, a fundamental modification to the SpinBox is required to allow the `step` value and the displayed value to diverge, see also discussion in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/106352.

body:
Tested locally, it works as expected.

When paired with https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/97646, that PR's **Write Depth** property will make heightmaps cast contact shadows:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/fa139753-3bd9-460d-aef0-45d4764ac336

Some feedback:

- The maximum length a contact shadow can cover depends on viewport resolution (e.g. changing **Scaling 3D > Scale** will affect this length). Higher resolutions reduce the contact shadow's maximum length. This isn't ideal for reasons similar to [#54518](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/54518), but it ensures performance figures don't vary too much across resolutions.

- In terms of API design, I think the property in DirectionalLight3D should be called **Allow Contact Shadows**, as it does not enable contact shadows by itself. Instead, you need to enable contact shadows in the Environment resource.

- Changing **Max Steps** appears to have no effect (visual or performance).

body:
I had already made a PR to do this with a different approach (https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/116134) but I suppose merging macos and wayland makes sense.

One thing to note is that compositor luminance updates are already event-based and handled here https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/137fa73ed4d71d2e7b3a53e2ab6b2690e1f46149/platform/linuxbsd/wayland/display_server_wayland.cpp#L2043-L2050

I felt that since we don't poll for HDR state, we didn't need to check if any values are actually different since this path is executed too infrequently for that to be a performance concern (and I'm not aware of any other concerns about calling these HDR methods or emitting a signal) and just always emitted the event.

If performance is indeed only reason for checking values changed before calling methods/emitting events, I believe the checks can be removed and the event emitted unconditionally (and maybe place a comment explaining that this code path is executed infrequently so this is not a performance concern). Otherwise I'm okay with the changed in `_window_update_hdr_state`.

I also noticed that toggling HDR enabled/disabled emits the event, if this is the case consider also putting event emission here https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/137fa73ed4d71d2e7b3a53e2ab6b2690e1f46149/platform/linuxbsd/wayland/display_server_wayland.cpp#L1866-L1893

I'm not aware of any driver except llvmpipe for which enabling HDR should fail, but if such a driver ever exists emitting the appropriate value when returning to SDR rendering might be appropriate.

body:
There are two systems at play:

1. `_popup_menu`, and it's argument (always a string list). This is used primarily to decide whether to show a menu item or not.
2. The callback, which is fired when the item is clicked. This can send a single variant value I believe. Usually a list of *objects* that were clicked. 

If you read the documentation for other CONTEXT_SLOT_* you will see that each of them handles this differently, by sending the best-possible data given the limitations. It feels like it's always a compromise. 

For our particular case you could for example invent a format like ["objectID:property_name"], or since only a single property can be right-clicked at once, even something as crazy as ["objectID", "property_name"]. I view these as not desirable, since they both require parsing...

IMO, it would be better if the argument passed to `_popup_menu` and the callback would somehow be aligned. It's weird that you can only gain access to the clicked object after it's been clicked. 

I view this as potentially of out-of-scope for this PR though? A proper fix would include deprecating `_popup_menu` and providing a new version with some different signature. Probably a dictionary of some kind.
