body:
> We could consider setting total_gravity = Vector3() as soon as a body is made kinematic and stop updating it (maybe for another day).

The default `CharacterBody3D` script template calls `get_gravity`, so this is not an option currently.

`get_gravity` is however broken in multiple ways (see [here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/84640#issuecomment-1927117203) and [here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/112656#issuecomment-3553204312)) due to relying on `PhysicsDirectBodyState3D`, especially for kinematic bodies.

I guess `get_gravity` could also just calculate the total gravity itself as-needed, by iterating over its overlapping areas, but the bodies themselves don't actually know about their area overlaps on the scene side of things, so that would need to be introduced first.

Either way, that's a battle for another day. I would say point gravity is probably a pretty niche feature, so for most projects you now won't be updating gravity/damping for kinematic bodies at every simulation step (unlike before).

body:
Tested locally, it works as expected. Code looks good to me.

**Testing project:** [test_pr_118226.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29264030/test_pr_118226.zip)
This is a project that downloads Godot export templates in a resumable fashion. Quit and reopen the project to resume.

(If testing with other files, make sure the host supports range requests.)

Some feedback:

- If you get HTTP response code 416 ([Range Not Satisfiable](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/416)), the full file is downloaded again and the original is removed. This means that if you've completed a download and try to start it, the original file is gone. Not sure if we can resolve this without side-effects.
  - This can be addressed at the project level by renaming in-download files (similar to `.part` files in Firefox or `.crdownload` in Chromium), so that fully downloaded files can be distinguished from files that are still being downloaded. This way, you know you don't need to perform another request when the file is done downloading.

For future PRs:

- There should be a code sample in `HTTPRequest.append_to_download_file`'s description that shows how to make use of range requests to resume a file download. The testing project I linked is a good start, but it should be modified to use [`If-Range`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Range_requests#conditional_range_requests) to ensure we don't append to an outdated file.
- Thinking about it, we could perhaps have a full-blown demo project showcasing HTTPRequest usage. There are several features that can be demonstrated:
  - Resuming file downloads.
  - Parallel downloads (multiple range requests on different parts of the file; faster than using a single HTTP connection, makes better use of fiber/5G connections).
  - Server-sent events.

body: Is changing an `EXBIND2RC` not going to change GDExtension ABI? Would this require a compatibility shim?
author: hpvb

body:
Based on my understanding: no. `EXBIND2RC` is just a util that wraps `GDVIRTUAL2RC_REQUIRED` while also creating the necessary virtual function in C++ to call to the gdvirtual function.

Since `EXBIND2RC` is replaced with an equivalent `GDVIRTUAL2RC_REQUIRED` it should look the same to extension. All that changes is that the C++ side virtual function is now implemented explicitly since it needs to ignore an argument that extensions are not aware of.

body:
I appreciate your dedication to compatibility with keeping `height` as the full height so that GDScript code touching this property is unchanged. However, actually, we want to move this over to mid-height. So we would keep it as `sub["height"] = get_height();` here. Above where you have `if (extension != "OMI_collider"`, we would flip around the logic: instead of computing a full height from the mid-height for non-OMI_collider cases, we would compute a mid height from the full height only for OMI_collider cases. And then every place using the height would need to be adjusted, and the docs updated too.

The goal of this class is to represent the data similarly to the glTF file's contents. OMI_collider is deprecated, so we need to focus on the more-modern replacements of OMI_physics_shape, KHR_implicit_shapes, and soon, glTF 2.1's shapes array will replace both of those. All 3 of these define the height of capsules to be the mid-height.

Furthermore, with the OMI_collider stuff as the separate unusual code branch, we can isolate it and wrap it in `#ifndef DISABLE_DEPRECATED`.

As for existing GDScript code expecting full height capsules... it's not really an issue, few users even know the GLTFPhysicsShape class exists, almost nobody is using or manipulating this class in the real world, and potentially actually nobody is specifically manipulating the capsule heights directly from GLTFPhysicsShape. I would just break compatibility and we can move on with the definitions that the glTF ecosystem has chosen. But I would feel better if @lyuma also approved of this approach.

This changes the semantics of `WorkerThreadPool` while this is correct for ResourceLoader, I don't think that this is always correct for all (potential) callers. WorkerThreadPool is bound to scripting and available to GDExtension. 

For instance the pattern that we are changing in ResourceLoader could be a deliberate choice of some extension author. With this change that behavior is impossible to achieve.

Whether these are desirable semantics is a different matter of course :) But I think that that requires more than a passing note in a bug fix.

body:
The current code in `ResourceLoader::_load_complete_inner()` expects `ResourceLoader::_run_load_task()`  to  be synchronous and for `ThreadLoadTask::resource` to be valid.

This opens a new data race, where it is possible for the retried `_run_load_task()` to return to `_load_complete_inner()` before `_load()` has returned. 

At that point this load will return a (partially) constructed resource at the end of `_load_complete_inner()`. 

This is a new race!

body:
The issue isn't with the `max_size` we get from `c->get_combined_maximum_size()` but rather the one given to it at the end of the layout phase here:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/321b8c944fa32ee94eef44a56925105d7091be03/scene/gui/box_container.cpp#L275-L281
The problem we are encountering is that the 22.33 height that the MSDF font needs (in this example case) gets rounded down to 22 (since we use ints everywhere in layouts for some reason), and since the `Label` doesn't have `SIZE_EXPAND`, it will be given 22 as a max size (lines above), which will then make it not render.

If the user gives the `Label` a max size too small for its font, that's a user error, and that not rendering text is a limitation of MSDF fonts. 
Furthermore, the fix you propose would have minimum size take priority over maximum size, which is the opposite of the decision (I) made during the max size PR, which is that it takes priority over minimum size, not the other way around.

body:
Interesting. How could it work before? Consider this hierarchy:
```
A        (filtered_parent - the first visible predecessor of C2)
- B      (p_parent->get_parent() - direct parent of C2, it is not visible)
  - C1   (p_parent->get_prev())
  - C2   (p_parent)
    - D  (ti)
```
`D` would be removed from `C2` and added as a child of `A`  and then it would be moved "after" `C1`, which is not child of `A`.

Do you know why the node needs to be moved at all? Why `filtered_parent->add_child(ti);` is not enough?
author: prvak

body:
In my opinion, this code cannot work correctly before. I guess it presume there is only one level of parent which need hide.

```
A        (filtered_parent - the first visible predecessor of C2)
- B      (p_parent->get_parent() - direct parent of C2, it is not visible)
  - C1   (p_parent->get_prev())
  - C2   (p_parent)
    - D  (ti)
- B1
```

When there are more children of A, e.g. B1 above, `filtered_parent->add_child(ti)` will put `D` after `B1`, if `B1` is visible, there result order is wrong. Our aim is keep the original order of tree, so we want to put `D` before `B1`.

body:
The problem with dynamic strings is that they're effectively leaked, leading to an explosion of RAM use on many calls. At least, this was the case with tracy, which is why we needed to avoid their 'dynamic strings' API.
This has led to the (somewhat complicated) interning implementation found in the `.cpp`.

I strongly recommend testing if perfetto's implementation interns the strings automatically and handles complex loads well. If no, I recommend copying / abstracting the approach we took for tracy. Otherwise, you'll likely be limited to a few seconds of tracing in complex projects (as previous tests showed).
author: Ivorforce

body:
I tested by running Kenney's 3D Platformer for several tens of minutes (left the game running) and memory usage looked normal. I suspect this is due to a couple of reasons:
- From their documentation, perfetto seems to automatically interns the strings as mentioned in https://perfetto.dev/docs/instrumentation/track-events#interning
- perfetto provides an [in-process and system backends](https://perfetto.dev/docs/instrumentation/tracing-sdk#in-process-vs-system-mode) and we use the latter which means that the application only as a producer, connecting to the external traced daemon (system daemon)

body:
I have mixed feelings about this PR.

You've covered the pros quite well, I think, and I agree with your rationale. 
However, by using a template, we run into the typical "ambitious template" problem: It shoehorns descriptions into the chosen schema, whether it fits or not.
Your headings are well chosen, and I think they fit the majority of pull requests well. However, here are my specific concerns:

For one, pull requests that are small and trivial (e.g. quick bug fix) might get an **overly verbose** description, making it harder to understand the change at face value.

Pull requests that are more complicated than the average (e.g. new feature) typically require an **even more verbose** description. We have [guidelines for PR descriptions](https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/pull_requests/pull_request_guidelines.html#explain-your-contributions) in the contributing docs. I'm missing the following from your template:

- Summary of changes (useful to understand the contribution without reading the whole description)
- Technical overview (useful to describe the changes in prose, filling in what the code can't cover)
- Testing (useful because PRs should be tested, and we have guidelines for some types of PRs)
- Discussion (half covered by the 'uncertain' heading)
- Additional work (useful if the PR needs work / follow-up PRs are planned)

Next, PRs might be **inadequately described** by the headings. Like I said above, the headings are generally good, but I personally tend to switch out my PR description format depending on what the PR does. With a template, we effectively take away the freedom of bespoke descriptions (since it discourages / disallows custom headings). 

Finally, PR templates might alienate some users. I've come across some in other repos that come across as condescending. I personally think yours is acceptable, but some people might draw the line elsewhere.

---

I realize the above sounds a bit negative, but like I said, that's just because you've covered the pros well already 😄

author: AThousandShips

body:
This code finds the first selected item in the selection list, then gets the next item after it.
If the selected item happens to be the last one in the list, the modulo operation % will wrap the index back to 0 automatically, so it cycles to the first item.
author: RainCmd

body: Yes, I know, I'm asking what is the reason behind that? What is the purpose of that?
author: AThousandShips

body: The idea is that clicking the same item repeatedly cycles through the selection forward one by one. Since UI elements in the scene often overlap each other, this makes it much easier to select items that are hidden or blocked by others. When reaching the last element in the list, it just loops back to the first one and repeats the cycle.

body:
Actually, I noticed a potential issue. This can still happen with the initial code you submitted.

Imagine the following scenario:
- The MSAA framebuffer gets created. The intermediate texture gets attached to it in the Android path.
- At some point in the next frame, "use_internal_buffer" becomes false.
- The intermediate texture gets freed. The MSAA framebuffer is now attached to stale, freed textures, because it thinks there is no need to reconfigure it.

This scenario cannot happen in upstream because the MSAA framebuffer gets recreated, or is configured to be ignored, each time the function is called.

Thanks for the review!

Here's my "thinking out loud" thoughts on this:

The spirit of this PR is to both subtly and explicitly encourage PR authors to think more about details that they should include in their PR descriptions. With this in mind, I chose the numbered list to encourage PR authors to think about other problems that are solved by their PR, including ones that may not have github issues. In practice, I believe that it is not uncommon for PRs to solve multiple problems. Instead, it is uncommon for a PR to close multiple issues.

So I also agree that most PRs won't close multiple issues at once. We could alternatively omit the "closes" suggestion entirely:

```suggestion
1.
```

I think this is a bad idea because there are some benefits to encouraging users to link existing issues in this way that I shared in the "Discussion" section of this PR.

In practice, I've found it convenient to have a numbered list that I can reference in my description, just like I did in this PR. But this is only relevant when there is more than one problem solved by a PR.

So I settled on simply having the numbered list because I don't see any real problem to have most PRs use a numbered, other than maybe... this accidentally encourages people to try and make PRs that solve multiple problems at once? If it does encourage PR authors to try and solve multiple problems at once, that's a bad thing because that's against the [Godot contributing guidelines](https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/engine/guidelines/best_practices.html#to-each-problem-its-own-solution)...

---

All that to say, I think I'm convinced that putting a numbered list is a problem because it may encourage PR authors to try and solve multiple problems at once, which goes against contributing guidelines. The unordered list does not strongly encourage this problematic behaviour, but still allows PR authors the ability to quickly list some other problems that are solved if they know of any.

So I think your suggestion to change it to an unordered list is the right middle ground that has the most benefits with the least problems.

I believe a short description of the PR is already covered by the commit text that’s included as first lines of the PR and the PR’s title. This is part of why I left this section as intentionally “Additional information” instead of “Description”.

Also, to me, “Description” is a misleading heading that does not well describe the intent of this section: Problem numbers 2, 4, and 5 are much better solved with an “Additional information” heading than with a “Description” heading; although I could make it work, it would not be intuitive for me to put the information required to solve problems 2, 4, and 5 under a “Description” heading.

I think it’s best to avoid accidentally encouraging PR authors to simply describe the changes of the PR because this is duplicate information; the “files changed” section of a PR already perfectly and accurately describes the changes of the PR. Additionally, I believe new contributors are sometimes inclined to simply describe the changes they made without providing reason because they don’t realize that their description text is simply duplicate of the “files changed” section of the PR. It’s similar to those problematic code comments that say nothing but describe what the code does — it’s better to not include those and let the code speak for itself.

So all that to say, I interpret a “Description” to be far too specific of a heading that leads the author in the wrong direction of describing the changes they made rather than explaining why they made the changes or providing other information in a free-form style that is most appropriate for their PR.

body:
Indeed, I think it's possible to reduce the frequency of `_clear_cache`, but as I mentioned in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/115550#issuecomment-3825635801, I think it would be better to make TrackCache retention an optional property, such as `keep_cache`.

Keeping cache after stopping causes memory to be occupied even when the player is stopped.

But, the main problem for keeping cache is that TrackCache continues to hold references. For example, if you delete a scene object after stopping the AnimationPlayer, the remaining reference in the cache could unintentionally create an orphan object.

While both issues can be addressed by explicitly calling `clear_cache()`, the former is simply a performance issue, whereas the latter has the potential to cause errors.

Conversely, if there were an implementation that avoided cases where orphan objects are created (such as having the AnimationMixer detect changes to the scene or resources), there would be no need for it to be an optional property.

In any case, we must carefully consider any changes to the behavior of _clear_cache. Besides that, as I mentioned in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/115550#issuecomment-3825635801, I think it would be better to have a separate method for creating a cache even while the player is stopped.

body:
Hey guys! I just thougth to add what I think here (premise: I have been in software development for 18+ years). Also, please do not take my comment as specifically defending OP or offending (quite the opposite!) maintainers, NOR directly relates to this PR; I just happened to open this PR and read its comments.

Also, I am not expert with the internals of Godot, but I hope to open a sane discussion about this. Mind, I **won't** use any AI to generate **any part** of this answer just to prove my point.

@AThousandShips as a human developer, by looking at the cpp API, I really see how either an agent OR a human could get confused by `is_null` vs `is_valid`, plus I'm trying to understand your comment saying `_sock.is_null()` is the same as `!_sock.is_valid()`:

```
_FORCE_INLINE_ bool is_valid() const { return is_inet() || is_unix(); }
```

this is not just checking if it's null, so saying that `is_null` and `!is_valid` are the same isn't completely true, is it?

Forget for a second AIs exist. If I, as a human (before agents became quite smart in the recent months/years) had seen that API, I probably for the sake of being 100% sure, would have done both of those checks.

Plus, OP seemed to have thrown two different errors on those checks, which sounds reasonable to me: if it's null, throw UNAVAILABLE, otherwise, throw UNCONFIGURED (e.g. that sock is not null but it's unconfigured). As a developer, to me those two errors/exceptions quite make sense to be separate (again, I don't know the internals, but the check seemed sound).

What I'm trying to say is: if the API isn't clear (having two different methods `is_null` and `!is_valid` that, by reading your review, "do the same") then why being defensive if a contributor or their AI agent checks both, unless it actually affects performance (and if it does, it should be added in the c code as a method documentation)? From a **human coder** point of view, `is_valid` and `is_null` have two very different meanings, and probably I also would have checked both.

Two issues here I'm seeing around on GitHub in these days: over-defensiveness (sometimes justified, sometimes totally prejudiced) against AI-aided contributions, hurting both human coders AND the code their agents produce with genuine mistakes even a human would have done, and "you are mistaken because you use AI" vs "actually, this API is not perfect and I see how that issue could have happened to a new human contributor".

In my experience across multiple fields, if an AI can mistake around a public API, it's usually API's fault (e.g. unclear or unexisting documentation, wrong naming, obsolete methods that haven't been made deprecated etc), and asking developers to read the whole documentation available somewhere else aside from in code about every little is a bit unreasonable in any professional or non-professional setting!

Please, take this comment as my own contribution to start a constructive conversation, we are all smart people and if we feel this comment has offended in any way, just ignore it instead of transforming it in a battle ground. Thanks 🙏🏻

body:
A very useful addition. Makes it much easier to drive joints to a desired rotation for e.g. driving ragdolls to a pose. Technically speaking you can achieve this using the old 'equilibrium point' API as well, but it is super easy to get lost in the math as you have to do:

* Calculate body1 to constraint space (technically doable by getting the 'global_basis` of the joint and body1 in the rest pose and calculating the relative transform)
* Calculate body2 to constraint space (same)
* Convert the desired target orientation to constraint space: constraint_to_body1.Inversed() * target_orientation * constraint_to_body2
* Converting the resulting matrix/quaternion to Euler angles and setting it as 'equilibrium point'

With this change you just calculate the desired relative transform between the two bodies and pass it to `set_angular_target_rotation`.

Note that I think it would be possible to implement this change as sitting on top of the 'equilibrium point' API, where a call to `set_angular_target_rotation` would do the calculations above and set the equilibrium point (so no changes to the physics server needed), but this solution is more efficient as it does not need to go back and forth between quaternions and Euler angles.

body:
The old approach using `CONNECT_ONE_SHOT | CONNECT_REFERENCE_COUNTED` is buggy. It fails to invoke distinct `p_callable` instances separately. Instead, only the very first `p_callable` gets executed, because all `p_callable`s are bound to the same Callable `Control::call_on_all_layout_pending_finished`.
This might be an inherent issue with `CONNECT_REFERENCE_COUNTED`. Refer to: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/112682#issuecomment-4366372526
That’s why I adopted a new Callable type for this case. I’d be glad to see any better alternative solution if you have one.

body: Tested locally on Windows 11 24H2, it works as expected. **Testing project:** [test_desktop_notifications.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/27731488/test_desktop_notifications.zip) Some feedback: - `send_toast_notification()`'s `image` and `callback` parameters should be optional and default to `null` and `Callable()` respectively. - `hide_toast_notification()` should print an error when passed an invalid value (namely, a negative number, as I believe toast IDs are always positive). body:
I don't think the current `clamp_to_embedder` is correct. Currently you can have an embedded window where you can drag it outside of its embedding window, but resizing the parent window moves it back into view, which is a strange behavior. It was intended that "windows that are clamped to their embedder are now automatically shifted/resized on popup, and when the parent is resized." (https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/75141#issuecomment-1483656600), but in `Viewport::_set_size` it never checked if the child had `clamp_to_embedder`. 

So I don't think `clamp_to_embedder` is intended to have a different purpose, and the properties should be merged into one.

- Also see https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/99946
author: kitbdev

body:
If `fit_to_parent` is true, then the window can pop up outside of the bounds of the parent, so I don't think it makes sense to restrict its position or size at all.
Only if `clamp_to_embedder` is also true does it make sense to restrict the position and size, and it can be done not just in the editor.

body:
## Pull request overview Adds a new `preserve_alpha` flag to `Viewport` and the rendering backend interfaces, intended to control whether the viewport’s alpha channel is preserved when the viewport output is used in shaders (via render target/backbuffer handling). **Changes:** - Added `preserve_alpha` property + bindings on `scene/main/Viewport`, with new RenderingServer/RendererViewport plumbing. - Extended `RendererTextureStorage` with `render_target_set/get_preserve_alpha()` and implemented it for RD, GLES3, and dummy backends. - Updated RD render-target backbuffer copy to optionally avoid forcing alpha to 1.0 based on the new flag. ### Reviewed changes Copilot reviewed 14 out of 14 changed files in this pull request and generated 1 comment.
Show a summary per file | File | Description | | ---- | ----------- | | `servers/rendering/storage/texture_storage.h` | Extends texture storage interface with preserve-alpha setters/getters for render targets. | | `servers/rendering/rendering_server.h` | Adds `viewport_set/get_preserve_alpha()` to the RenderingServer interface. | | `servers/rendering/rendering_server.cpp` | Binds the new viewport setter to scripting (getter not bound). | | `servers/rendering/rendering_server_default.h` | Adds default-server forwarding stubs for the new viewport APIs. | | `servers/rendering/renderer_viewport.h` | Stores `preserve_alpha` in renderer viewport state and declares new accessors. | | `servers/rendering/renderer_viewport.cpp` | Implements viewport preserve-alpha setter/getter and forwards to texture storage. | | `servers/rendering/renderer_rd/storage_rd/texture_storage.h` | Adds render-target `preserve_alpha` state and method declarations for RD. | | `servers/rendering/renderer_rd/storage_rd/texture_storage.cpp` | Implements RD preserve-alpha state + uses it when copying to backbuffer (alpha-to-one toggle). | | `servers/rendering/dummy/storage/texture_storage.h` | Adds no-op dummy implementations for the new interface methods. | | `scene/main/viewport.h` | Adds `preserve_alpha` member + public setter/getter declarations. | | `scene/main/viewport.cpp` | Implements/binds the new property and forwards to RenderingServer. | | `drivers/gles3/storage/texture_storage.h` | Adds `preserve_alpha` to GLES3 render target + method declarations. | | `drivers/gles3/storage/texture_storage.cpp` | Adds GLES3 setter/getter, but currently doesn’t apply the flag to any rendering path. | | `doc/classes/Viewport.xml` | Documents the new `preserve_alpha` property. |
Comments suppressed due to low confidence (2) **drivers/gles3/storage/texture_storage.cpp:2984** * In the GLES3 backend, the new `preserve_alpha` flag is stored on `RenderTarget` and can be toggled via `render_target_set_preserve_alpha()`, but it doesn't appear to affect any rendering path: `_update_render_target_color()` and `render_target_copy_to_back_buffer()` don't branch on `rt->preserve_alpha`. As a result, enabling/disabling `Viewport.preserve_alpha` is effectively a no-op under GLES3. Consider wiring this flag into the backbuffer copy (e.g., force alpha to 1 when `preserve_alpha` is false to preserve legacy behavior, and keep alpha when true), or document that it’s only supported on RD. ``` void TextureStorage::render_target_set_override(RID p_render_target, RID p_color_texture, RID p_depth_texture, RID p_velocity_texture, RID p_velocity_depth_texture) { RenderTarget *rt = render_target_owner.get_or_null(p_render_target); ERR_FAIL_NULL(rt); ERR_FAIL_COND(rt->direct_to_screen); // Remember what our current color output is. RID was_color_texture = render_target_get_texture(p_render_target); bool create_new_color_fbo = true; bool create_new_velocity_fbo = true; if (rt->overridden.color == p_color_texture && rt->overridden.depth == p_depth_texture && rt->overridden.velocity == p_velocity_texture && rt->overridden.velocity_depth == p_velocity_depth_texture) { ``` **servers/rendering/rendering_server.cpp:2931** * `RenderingServer` gained `viewport_get_preserve_alpha()` in the public interface, but `_bind_methods()` only binds `viewport_set_preserve_alpha()`. If this API is meant to be script-accessible like other `viewport_get_*` methods in this section, it should also be bound; otherwise consider not binding the setter either to avoid exposing an asymmetric API to scripts. ``` BIND_ENUM_CONSTANT(RSE::VIEWPORT_UPDATE_WHEN_PARENT_VISIBLE); BIND_ENUM_CONSTANT(RSE::VIEWPORT_UPDATE_ALWAYS); ```

body:
Part 1, just getting several things out of the way so we can discuss sooner.

There's a lot of improvements here and it's overall very welcome. The audio-related class reference has been smelling old and lacking in details.

As I understand, the PR isn't meant to standardize this side of the class reference, but given that it affects so much at once, it should be expected.
Yet, there are a lot of minor inconsistencies across multiple affected descriptions which add up. To be clear, what bothers me personally is that the affected descriptions add **more** inconsistency, instead of at least keeping the current state of things.

There's also a lot of cases where "_this audio stream_" was changed to "_the stream_" and I am frankly not sure why, other than preference.

> Maybe closes: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/115825

Just a tip. GitHub detects specific keywords (like "_closes_") behind issue links in the PR's description, and automatically closes them when the PR is merged. If you're very in doubt, do not use those keywords, otherwise we may need to manually reopen it.

body:
The [spec](https://docs.vulkan.org/refpages/latest/refpages/source/vkGetPhysicalDeviceSurfaceFormatsKHR.html) states:

> If pSurfaceFormats is NULL, then the number of format pairs supported for the given surface is returned in pSurfaceFormatCount. Otherwise, pSurfaceFormatCount must point to a variable set by the application to the number of elements in the pSurfaceFormats array, and on return the variable is overwritten with the number of structures actually written to pSurfaceFormats. If the value of pSurfaceFormatCount is less than the number of format pairs supported, at most pSurfaceFormatCount structures will be written, and [VK_INCOMPLETE](https://docs.vulkan.org/refpages/latest/refpages/source/VkResult.html) will be returned instead of [VK_SUCCESS](https://docs.vulkan.org/refpages/latest/refpages/source/VkResult.html), to indicate that not all the available format pairs were returned.

This seems to indicate that we should accept both `VK_SUCCESS` and `VK_INCOMPLETE`, but still return an error if any other status is returned.

I'm concerned this condition as written might hide legitimate errors, while still reporting `VK_INCOMPLETE` as an error, unless I'm reading the logic wrong here.

Alternatively, would there be any value in re-querying the surface format count if we get `VK_INCOMPLETE` until we actually get all of the surface formats?
author: DarkKilauea

body:
> I'm concerned this condition as written might hide legitimate errors, while still reporting VK_INCOMPLETE as an error, unless I'm reading the logic wrong here.

You're correct in that assumption, actually. I'm assuming that it'll only write a lower number whenever it returns `VK_INCOMPLETE`, but I suppose that it could keep the number the same if any other error would return. The initial idea here was that `VK_INCOMPLETE` is only an error if there's less formats than we expected, but that also isn't as serious so long as there's a non-zero number of formats.

> Alternatively, would there be any value in re-querying the surface format count if we get VK_INCOMPLETE until we actually get all of the surface formats?

I didn't want to add much more code here given I'm not that experienced with Vulkan, but it's certainly worth a try. I'll update the code to do that instead.

body:
Thinking about this now, I'm not sure it's the right final shape, and the reason for it is unfortunately hiding in what the code already does (outside your PR / the GDType work).

The code as now expresses constants in the following way:

- There are integer constants.
- There are variant constants.
- Some integer constants belong to an enum. Other int constants are "non-enum constants".

I think the right shape is:

- There are variant constants.
- There are enums. Enums have int cases.

This "downgrades", on a semantic level, enum cases from being an 'integer constant' and separates them into their own concept.
To keep the behavior of GDScript (where enum cases are accessible directly on the class) we need to make this a GDScript concern, forwarding them the same way constants are.

However, I think this is preferable to the somewhat messy current representation.

Practically, the way forward, I think, is to keep the current code as-is (agnostic is good) and wait for an impetus / opportunity to move forward with `Variant` constants. When that happens, we refactor (which includes a change to `GDType` where the underlying representation is exchanged to serve the new shape).

body: Just to clarify the usage pattern of  `vertex_formats`, `vertex_format_create` is a thread safe method, at the end it inserts a new vertex format into `vertex_formats`. After that `vertex_formats` is only accessed to obtain a const reference to the vertex format that is created. I.e., once created, vertex formats are immutable. So we just need to ensure that we aren't reading from `vertex_formats` during `vertex_format_create`. We don't need to worry about the underlying vertex format being deleted or mutated
author: clayjohn

body: Same, here we have a `const` access to an immutable resource. We just need to ensure that we aren't reading from the hashmap while it is being modified
author: clayjohn

body:
Okay, I went through the code and checked the other uses of `vertex_formats` and `framebuffer_formats` and I can confirm that this code is safe. 

The case we are guarding against is inserting a new element into the HashMap while we read from the Hashmap on another thread. While it is totally safe for us to use the pointer we get from the lookup from any thread, we need to avoid indexing into the HashMap while we are doing an insertion. 

As you pointed out in the other thread, a more granular lock would be better since this will lock on a bunch of other unrelated methods. But this code is the safest, least intrusive fix for now

I don't think we should be unilaterally suppressing a warning when only a single scenario is triggering it. I'd sooner recommend suppressing the warning within the macro itself:
```diff
diff --git a/core/typedefs.h b/core/typedefs.h
index 91f5fda2ec5..1195379fb33 100644
--- a/core/typedefs.h
+++ b/core/typedefs.h
@@ -339,8 +339,10 @@ constexpr bool is_fully_defined_v = is_fully_defined<T>::value;
 /// This can be used to reduce include coupling and keep compile times low.
 /// The check must be made at the top of the corresponding .cpp file of a header.
 #define STATIC_ASSERT_INCOMPLETE_TYPE(m_keyword, m_type) \
+	GODOT_GCC_WARNING_PUSH_AND_IGNORE("-Wsfinae-incomplete") \
 	m_keyword m_type; \
-	static_assert(!is_fully_defined_v<m_type>, #m_type " was unexpectedly fully defined. Please check the include hierarchy of '" __FILE__ "' and remove includes that resolve the " #m_keyword ".");
+	static_assert(!is_fully_defined_v<m_type>, #m_type " was unexpectedly fully defined. Please check the include hierarchy of '" __FILE__ "' and remove includes that resolve the " #m_keyword "."); \
+	GODOT_GCC_WARNING_POP
 #else
 #define STATIC_ASSERT_INCOMPLETE_TYPE(m_keyword, m_type)
 #endif
```
(This is assuming that the warning is suppressable during SFINAE. If not, disregard)

Before returning an error, `active` has to be set to `false`, since I'm stopping the stream.
In MP3 and OggVorbis, this is not a problem. When `start()` is called (which is the same as `play()`), it sets `active` to `true`, then calls `seek()` with the time. I can set `active` to `false` in it (or call `stop()`, as I'm doing in this PR) when time is invalid, and all is well ([function](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/ef02314f2bd0305035ecbe907883401a393da7a7/modules/mp3/audio_stream_mp3.cpp#L110)). However, in WAV, within the `start()` function, `seek()` is called first, then `active` is set to `true`. So even if I set `active` to `false` within `seek()`, it'd be set right back to `true` when the `seek()` call is over, continuing/starting the stream.
My initial idea was to have the same conditional in `seek()`, inside `start()` too, but that seemed unnecessary. Instead, I just changed the order of operations to be the same as MP3 and Ogg Vorbis: set `active` first, then `seek()`.

author: Akosmo

body:
I'm realizing it's surprisingly hard to explain :D
Basically, state is any value that persists, e.g. a field to the object.
That means when you call a function, the output/behavior depends not only on the function arguments but also the state of the object.
If you have no state, a function is perfectly deterministic: whatever goes in dictates what comes out. That makes it easy to understand and reason about.
When you have state, that also influences behavior, making it more complex. For example, there is the risk that your `beat_loop` boolean desynchronizes from the value it "should be", for example because of execution order, and you suddenly have a bug.
Audio stream players already have state of course, but more state means more complexity, which means more risk of bugs.

body:
Thank you for your contribution!

I really appreciate the effort, but unfortunately I can't agree with most of the changes here. Converting the IME position sounds fine, but the rest of the logic brings some issues back.

Inheriting toplevel scale is somewhat fine, although there are really no guarantees that the window scale will actually be the same as the parent. Because of this, is there's any issue, I'd really like to see a deep-rooted solution. Popups seem to have stronger guarantees, as they're supposed to be extension to the toplevel itself. At least this is my understanding of it.

Removing "scale compensation" opens a few edge cases. Notably, changing the output scale *while* a window is open will lead to the same auto-restore issue. I could replicate it with this PR applied on top of commit 16bb065ac31b79c0ed24b3b944d3b5275123e854.

To replicate the bug you need to:

 1. Open a window (scale 1)
 2. Change scale (scale 2)
 3. Close the window (scale 2)
 4. Change scale (scale 1)
 5. Open the same window again (scale 1)

It will be restored to the wrong size.

What other issues have you been seeing? Are there issue reports open? Please note that there are also still a few engine limitations here and there, so not everything is fixable by simply working on the Wayland backend, although we can definitely improve it further.

body:
Thanks very much for picking this up @KoBeWi 

I argued in the earlier PR that I'm not convinced an auto-fix like this is a good idea:

* It has to pick an arbitrary place to break the cycle or make the user pick one
* Since godot users often don't use git or other revision control (lack of native non-plugin IDE integration) this may modify user files that aren't under revision control in a way that may not be obvious to the user or easy to find
* Since godot projects don't often have an extensive test suite, users may inadvertently save the now-nil resource and not notice what it broke until much later.

For those reasons I suggest the UI should tell the user how to fix it, but not fix it for them.

It's also worth noting that this improvement fixes the loading-side of the problem. But users will still get confusing exceptions about nil values where they are visibly not nil if they have just created a reference cycle; godot returns nil instead of the resource to be loaded, rather than throwing a more informative exception. That doesn't need to be solved in the same PR of course, but is worth knowing about.

It mostly boils down to introducing information that is either unnecessary, or too specific. Sometimes saying less is good.

As a side note, you can see that the [static checks are failing](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/actions/runs/26018124573/job/76480012837?pr=119536) because there are trailing spaces at the end of some sentences. Beware of this. If you're using an IDE, most of them have a "Trim trailing spaces" shortcut.

And, as a tip, there's many [documentation issues](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues?q=is%3Aissue%20state%3Aopen%20label%3Adocumentation) open which you can look up via the `documentation` label. Similar case in the [Godot-docs repository](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-docs/issues?q=is%3Aissue%20state%3Aopen%20label%3A%22area%3Aclass%20reference%22).
The solution to them may involve writing something extra, or fixing existing inaccuracies. Although it's not always that easy, they should give you a general clue on what is missing. [The problem comes before the solution](https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/engine/guidelines/best_practices.html#to-solve-the-problem-it-has-to-exist-in-the-first-place).

body:
Is this really the best place to fix the issue?
While making `Callable` / `Signal` comparisons predictable across sessions is very defensible, the 'real' issue in my mind is that `.tscn` files depend on the intrinsic comparison order of these objects in the first place. 
As a file type, I'm wondering whether they shouldn't be defining their own comparison order, one that's focused on readability and well-defined stability rather than speed. The change presented here makes comparisons _very slightly_ slower, establishing a precedent of sacrificing core comparison speed for the sake of predictability, which I'm not quite sure is the way to go long-term.

Edit: Will discuss in the core meeting.

body:
> I noticed that in the first video, when typing before the unknown variable this_does_not_exist, the newly typed text doesn't get underlined until it re-parses (expected behavior); however, typing after the variable results in the newly typed text instantly being underlined. I suppose this still ends up being valid? But if I can figure out how to resolve that later, that might be nice for consistency's sake.

This was controlled by the `bool p_include_selection_begin = true, bool p_include_selection_end = true` parameters. Having both as true makes sure that removing text changes the selection appropriately, but it causes inserting text at the end to expand the range. For example `insert_text` has `bool p_before_selection_begin = true, bool p_before_selection_end = false`, which are in effect the same parameters but renamed for inserting, and the different defaults are better for inserting text.

`p_include_selection_begin` doubles as an option to insert before or after the caret when there is no selection, but that's not really applicable to underlines. Sometimes when the selection starts or ends at the beginning of a line different insert functions have different behavior when inserting new lines to expand the selection or not.
But I don't think we care about that for underlines, we probably don't ever want an underline to grow when text is added at the edges.

So we could either add a parameter or detect when text is inserted vs removed to determine whether to include the underline end, which should just be `bool include_end = edit_height == 0 ? edit_size < 0 : edit_height < 0;`

body: Sometimes the underline will go past the last char: It would be better if it clamped to the point, even if it is not at the top or bottom position. Here is some pseudocode to get the vertical position of the last point. The y portion should be the same as the x portion since it is linear. ```cpp float last_point_portion = (end_position - points[points.size() - 1].x) / distance; float last_point_y = squiggle_top_y + combined_rect.size.y * (current_squiggle_side == squiggle_top_y ? last_point_portion : 1.0 - last_point_portion) ``` And there may need to be a check to make sure it is not too close to the last position, especially if the end point does already match the end of the character perfectly.

body:
Neat, thanks for looking into VS Code's implementation!

I was thinking of using a similar approach to what I'm doing currently (drawing a polyline with calculated points) but following a similar shape to VS Code:
- First point at (0, 0)
- Second point at (0.25, 1)
- Third point at (0.75, -1)
- Fourth point at (1, 0) - maybe omit this if it's not the last underline to be drawn, so we're not putting down duplicate vertices for the end point of underline i and the start point of underline i + 1

Then, the coordinates would be scaled to match the space underneath each character:
- x = 0 is left edge of character, x = 1 is right edge
- y = 0 is a distance underneath the character, y = 1 is underneath the character but closer to the bottom edge, y = -1 is farther from the bottom edge

Do you foresee issues with an approach like this, in contrast to keeping the current zigzag-drawing behavior but offsetting it?
author: Meorge

body: I don't think it should be scaled to each character individually, I imagine it would look weird to change frequency with each character that is a different size, especially on tabs. Note VSCode doesn't scale it per character, it repeats the pattern until it fills the entire width, and then somehow cuts it off. Sorry, I meant when the svg was sampled at the resolution appropriate for the font size that it looks rounder than it actually is, not that it is actually scaled for each character width. Using a fixed value (the current `distance_between_points`) as the 0.5 distance between points 2 and 3 as they repeat would be better. Here is some non-uniform text if you want it ```gdscript func _test_lang(): var variable := "test string" var عامل := "سلسلة الاختبار" var מִשְׁתַנֶה := "מחרוזת בדיקה" var 变量 := "测试 字符串" var 変数 := "テスト 文字列" # テスト　文学 var 변수 := "테스트 문자열" var emoji := "👏👏👏👏👏" ```

Code and design look good to me. ### 100% editor scale Default | Light -|- | ### 150% editor scale Default | Light -|- | ### 200% editor scale Default | Light -|- | **Edit:** Seeing the above screenshots scaled down to 100% makes me realize that line spacing currently depends on editor scale somewhat. Fixing this can be done in a separate PR as there are many other locations in other Control nodes where it occurs, but it's fairly involved: - The editor uses the `disabled` stretch mode, and increases the font size according to the editor scale. At higher font sizes, the underline thickness automatically increases. - Intuitively, I'd say projects with the `canvas_items` stretch mode don't automatically increase their font size. Instead, oversampling does the job. Therefore, underline thickness doesn't automatically increase. In fact, `theme_cache.base_scale` is not automatically increased either; it's a project setting that can be set only at startup, not at runtime. Therefore, no scaling actually occurs if you use the `canvas_items` stretch mode and just rely on Godot's automatic scaling. - However, testing with LinkButton (which relies on font underline thickness) in a project contradicts this. The underline does scale there. Since this isn't exposed to scripting, I think you could remove the `* theme_cache.base_scale` multiplier (with a comment to explain why). body:
So earlier in the function we use `get_shallow_script` when there is no script, but here we recognize that the shallow scripts don't work for the purposes of this function.

I'd argue we should not call `get_shallow_script` in the function then. A better approach IMHO would be to go by `kind`.
- `kind == CLASS` -> `class_type` is always valid
- `kind == SCRIPT` -> `script_type` is always valid
(We really need to clean this datatype representation up. A tagged union would make sense. I'd argue accessing `script_type` on a `CLASS` is just asking for bugs since initialization is very inconsistent.)

Also this proposed fix will still not be able to correctly handle a case were one type is `CLASS` and the other one is `SCRIPT`.

body:
So about the last sentence. Let's take https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/95847 as example. If not set, the id of item is dynamically chosen based on it's index. So the id of an item can be 0 if it's index is 0. However since the initialization is dynamic the default value used for serialization purposes is the default (implicit) integer value `0` (it's horrible UX to use dynamic init for something in the inspector like this, but that's not the point.) The implicit default and the dynamic initialization can be identical.

So let's take the following chain of actions:
- add item A: -> index = 0 -> id = 0
- add item B: -> index = 1 -> id = 1
- move item A after item B -> index = 1, id stays 0
- save the scene -> id of A does not get saved since it overlaps with the implicit default, even though the dynamic initialization would initialize to a different value
- load the scene -> the id of A has changed to 1, since after rerunning the dynamic init in the new context it resulted in a different value.

So in this case we set the flag to always serialize the property value. Regardless of the implicit integer default.

If you can pack that in a good sentence that's understandable feel free to do so! I did the best I could :sweat_smile:

body: ## Pull request overview > [!NOTE] > Copilot was unable to run its full agentic suite in this review. Adds coverage and adjusts `Curve::set_point_count()` behavior when expanding, aiming to keep existing indexed point properties stable. **Changes:** - Add a new regression test for expanding point count while preserving existing point indices/properties. - Change `Curve::set_point_count()` expansion path to append default-initialized points and update tangents, then mark dirty. ### Reviewed changes Copilot reviewed 2 out of 2 changed files in this pull request and generated 3 comments. | File | Description | | ---- | ----------- | | tests/scene/test_curve.cpp | Adds a new test intended to validate indexed point property preservation when expanding. | | scene/resources/curve.cpp | Changes how new points are created during `set_point_count()` expansion (defaults + tangent updates + dirty marking). | --- 💡 Add Copilot custom instructions for smarter, more guided reviews. Learn how to get started.
author: copilot-pull-request-reviewer

body: This test mutates the curve after `set_point_count(3)` by re-setting `point_0/position` and `point_1/position` from cached values, which makes it incapable of catching regressions where expanding the point array changes/remaps existing indexed properties. To actually verify preservation, remove the `set(...)` calls and assert that `curve->get(\"point_0/position\")`/`curve->get_point_position(0)` (and index 1) are unchanged immediately after `set_point_count(3)`.
author: copilot-pull-request-reviewer

body: Replacing `_add_point(Vector2())` with a raw `_points.push_back(Point(...))` risks bypassing any invariants `_add_point` enforces (e.g., tangent/handle modes, per-point metadata, sorting/normalization, or ensuring neighboring points’ tangents are updated). This can lead to behavioral differences vs the prior code path beyond just the default position. Prefer calling `_add_point(Vector2(default_offset, default_value))` (or introducing/using a helper that adds a point with a specific position) so point initialization and tangent updates stay consistent.
author: copilot-pull-request-reviewer

body: The `old_size > 0` branch uses `_max_domain` without clamping, while the `old_size == 0` branch clamps a literal `0.0`. To keep the behavior uniform and robust against future domain changes, clamp `_max_domain` as well (or compute the default from the last point’s offset/value if the intent is to append ‘at the end’ of the current curve). This makes the default-point placement logic easier to reason about and reduces surprises.
author: copilot-pull-request-reviewer

@TokageItLab I was somewhat invested in this PR due to my issue #115382 requiring a similar solution, an "At End" exit out of a inner Root statemachine without hitting the T-pose.

I want to ask: what is the purpose of ever encountering a T pose apart from the outermost State Machine? To put it another way: why ever treat any inner End state as a T pose rather than an anticipated transition out of the StateMachine? I have many complex cases in my game that keep seeing the T pose get mixed into transition frames, where a freeze at the last animation before end would be far preferable. As a result, I end up having to avoid inner StateMachines most of the time, and design more complicated trees.

Is this really not a bug? What behaviour would not having a RESET there break? If this is indeed intended, then surely the amount of times it is erroneously encountered (even though a transition has been adequately provided) has to be a bug, at least?

Would appreciate your thoughts, here or in my issue. The gameplay demo in that issue shows the real-world problem it causes, and there are many more instances that I've had to work around.
author: vaner-org

body:
I haven't been intentionally playing the End state as a T-pose. Essentially, the internal blend amount of the StateMachine is 0 on the Start/End state, which means the Rest/RESET animation is simply being applied as a fallback.

And I don't think there is any issue with Start and End being treated as a RESET animation due to this fallback. In a deterministic AnimationTree, there is likely no other way to handle cases where the system remains at Start or End without prev/next transitions. Especially for Root/Nested are not designed to allow child StateMachines to view the state of their parent StateMachine.

Also, there is an option called reset_ends for intentionally playing the End state as a RESET animation. When this is set to false and if there is xfade, the xfade time is considered for the transition to the End state, but blending with the RESET animation does not occur. (However, if it transitions to End immediately after the xfade finishes and remains there, it will result in a RESET animation = T-pose).

Upon re-examining the Final MRP above (in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/119748#discussion_r3352802282), I found that the xfade time of the internal StateMachine's transition to the End was 0. Matching it with the xfade time of the parent StateMachine was all that was actually needed to solve the problem.

[Final-fixed-by-xfade.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29137233/Final-fixed-by-xfade.zip)

If the T-pose is still being played after matching the xfade times between the parent and the internal state machine, it implies that a bug is occurring somewhere that is processing unintended frames after ending xfade or unintended interrupt the crossfade. In other words, the main cause of the T-pose appearing should be a discrepancy somewhere regarding the intended timing of the End state.

While not transitioning to the End state and instead holding the last frame of the previous state is one possible workaround, it only corrects the "pose drawn during an unintended frame" and is not the correct path to prevent the "drawing of an unintended frame" itself.

body:
Thank you for the explanation.

> Also, there is an option called reset_ends for intentionally playing the End state as a RESET animation. When this is set to false and if there is xfade, the xfade time is considered for the transition to the End state, but blending with the RESET animation does not occur. (However, if it transitions to End immediately after the xfade finishes and remains there, it will result in a RESET animation = T-pose).
> 
> Upon re-examining the Final MRP above (in [#119748 (comment)](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/119748#discussion_r3352802282)), I found that the xfade time of the internal StateMachine's transition to the End was 0. Matching it with the xfade time of the parent StateMachine was all that was actually needed to solve the problem.

Regarding the above, in the demonstration case I described in my issue,

> ..I've forced it to occur by having a sync transition from one shorter "static impact" animation leading to end, mixed with another "moving impact" animation that has a different length, that I trigger by moving my character mid-animation. This leaves the animation momentarily stranded inside the inner statemachine, resulting in a T pose on exit.

Any `Root` inner StateMachine of moderate complexity may have variable xfade paths both to the end and out from the StateMachine - which is entirely resonable and is needed to make games. It is not feasible to account for the xfade from every state to end and out from the StateMachine to other states to be the exact same, so encountering the undesirable T pose becomes inevitable.

As for why `Nested` isn't suitable to use, apart from the reset to Start that's needed, it cannot reliable escape when `At End` is expected on the outside, [as I explain here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/115382#issuecomment-3800792328).

Regardless of what the the logic is,
1. I cannot foresee any instance where a developer would intentionally desire the T pose's appearance (for a frame or two) on the way out of a StateMachine, I can't see why making this change should be viewed as altering intended behaviour rather than making a long-needed change.
2. The fact that the developer themselves might not encounter this but the player might in-game, through no fault of either of them, just makes the engine appear more error-prone.
3. Similar to how solving #95688 was needed to complete root motion implementation, I truly believe this is needed as a step to complete the StateMachine implementation. It simply isn't reliable as anything other than the root of the AnimationTree otherwise.

For the points above, I request that the animation team reconsiders this, and can approve a PR that can guard against this quirk of StateMachine proactively, either with this PR if it can also solve #115382, or [@spinalcord's](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/115382#issuecomment-4400490037), whichever would be a more suitable solution.

Alternatively, would it be appropriate to the case implemented here as an added part when `reset_ends` is false, since it already implies avoiding the RESET pose?
author: vaner-org

body:
As I have said many times, if you want to keep it stopped at a specific frame, you can use Nested mode. Also, ending at an arbitrary timing is possible with a transition to the End with xfade when reset_ends = false. If an unintended End state execution occurs there, the problem lies outside the End state behavior. I believe this judgment remains unchanged.

The most issue where the animation of the previous state is retained when transitioning from Root/Nested to End, as seen in this PR and the commit you mentioned, is that it becomes completely unclear what the actual state is when the `current_state` the user has retrieved is "End".

And not only that, but Nested mode will not go to Start when reset unless it is an End state, instead restarting the animation of the current state from the beginning. This raises questions about how to handle this "fake end" scenario, requiring us to rethink the definition of "End" in multiple places, which could reduce maintainability.

> Similar to how solving https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/95688 was needed to complete root motion implementation, I truly believe this is needed as a step to complete the StateMachine implementation. It simply isn't reliable as anything other than the root of the AnimationTree otherwise.

It’s completely off the mark to say this is the same case. That was a mathematical problem, but this issue is likely a usability problem with the StateMachine settings.

As mentioned above, I assume we can consider adding a Custom mode for Root/Nested, but nothing more than that will happen for them.

Regarding the case you mentioned where you want to have multiple xfade values for End in an inner StateMachine, I think the correct approach is to improve Grouped mode to have multiple Ends and expose multiple ports (although we might be able to apply multipe port/ends to Root/Nested mode as well). That means, if you absolutely want to disallow fallbacks at Start/End, improving the usability of Grouped mode, which interprets Start/End conceptually rather than as actual States, should be the most logical approach.

body:
No. I’ve said this many times before, but what this PR is attempting to implement which holds the previous state without transitioning to "End" should not be implemented, even in Custom mode. As I sent in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/119748#discussion_r3442552794, the only thing missing in your case was the correct setting for xfade in the transition to the End in your MRP.

As explained above, Custom mode simply exposes the branching logic that depends on the two existing Root/Nested options: "detect_dead_end: whether to treat dead ends as the end of the StateMachine" and "keep_state_on_reset: whether to transition to Start when reset (internal seek to 0) occurs while in a state other than the End state".

In other words, since only 2 of the 4 possible combinations are currently available, like:

- `Root`: detect_dead_end = false, keep_state_on_reset = false
- `Nested`: detect_dead_end = true, keep_state_on_reset = true

`Custom` mode will expose two boolean variables to allow selection from those 4 combinations, then `Root/Nested` are become the template for those boolean options.

Anything beyond that should be handled through additional implementation, such as implementing multiple ends/ports, as also explained above.

Another possibility to consider might be implementing a helper function (on the Editor) that statically copies the parent's xfade and propagates it to the inner StateMachine to handle cases where the xfade on the transition to the End in the inner state machine is not configured as intended, like https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/119748#discussion_r3442552794 case.

None of the three recommendations I listed (Custom mode / multiple Ends / xfade helper) are tightly coupled or conflict with one another, but introducing cases where the flow does not transition to "End" as in this PR will cause issues to spread throughout the StateMachine code and will undoubtedly lead to a combination explosion, then loss of maintainability.

body:
I have a few concerns here: 

1. Users can extend the build directory with custom code and files, such as notification icons, modifying gradle dependencies, and other changes. If we auto delete the build directory when exporting from a newer version, users could accidentally lose those modifications. So instead, I think we should only install the build template when it is not already present. If there is a version mismatch, we should show a dialog with two actions: Open the existing build directory, so users can review or copy their modifications if needed. And delete and reinstall the gradle template.

2. We should also keep the `Install Android Build Template` menu option. When the Android export template is not present or downloaded, it currently provides an option to Install from a file.
Removing this dialog would remove the ability to manually install a build template.

body:
In video, each second is measured in frames. 24 FPS (Frames Per Second) is the PAL standard for movies (25 FPS for TV), and 30 FPS is the NTSC standard. In fact, it's not exactly 24 FPS or 30 FPS; it's 23.976 or 29.97 FPS.

Internally, Godot uses "frame_duration" to obtain the on-screen time of 1 frame (which is equivalent to 1s/ fps) and to perform all calculations.

FPS = 1 second / frame_duration
FPS = 1 / 0.04166666666667 = 24 fps

body:
Self-review: I realized after some thought that the previous version ([`fd064b5b`](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/compare/fd064b5b6308ef8354203eccbca40decf61b762b..8bb39ce41ef2a316cce79737ca7891f1ead385c1)) was creating quadratic behaviour if you set a bbcode with lots of tags while `visible_characters` was not -1. (It would call `add_text` for every piece of text inside the bbcode, which would then call `get_total_character_count`, which is linear in the number of items, hence O(N^2)).

To fix that, there are now two different paths to recalculating:

- If bbcode is disabled, it calls `_recalculate_visible_ratio` here in `add_text`.
- If bbcode is enabled, it does not call it here. Instead, it calls it at the end of `append_text`.

Added a test making sure it still works if bbcode is enabled.

@TokageItLab 
(Sorry for the late reply)

I actually came up with a different solution.

The root issue is that `AnimationBlendTree` was created before animation sections were implemented, and so had its own logic for processing and looping its own timeline section. To keep this looping logic working as-is, the right thing to do would be to have `AnimationMixer` pretend that the animation is being played with no sections. (Thus using 0 for `pi.start` and `anim_size` for `pi.end`)

Alternatively uniting the timeline section processing with the one in `AnimationMixer` can also be more desirable, but I suspect this would be tricky to implement. I'll leave the decision up to you.

(Note: The fix I have here works for https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/119769 and does not break https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/118101 either)

body:
`cur_time` is taken from `p_playback_info.time`, and `cur_playback_time = cur_time + playback_start`, so the range of `cur_playback_time` would be `[playback_start, playback_start + playback_end]`. Therefore taking modulo of `anim_size` would result in values before `playback_start` once `cur_time` is in the range of `[anim_size, max(anim_size, playback_start + playback_end)]`.

I suspect that a looping custom timeline with non-zero `start_offset` would behave incorrectly because of this, but it's also possible that `AnimationMixer` is clamping the playback time back within `playback_start` and `playback_end` automatically, so it looks like it's working. (Though in this case I think a bit of the delta time would get lost to the clamping every time it loops)

body:
The backward playback logic has been changed. In its current state, this breaks backward compatibility, so it cannot be merged.

Previously, the timeline was reversed first, followed by trimming:
```
0s ABCDE 1s -backward-> 0s EDCBA 1s -custom length-> 0s EDC 0.5s
```
In this PR, that order has been changed:
```
0s ABCDE 1s -custom length-> 0s ABC 0.5s -backward-> 0s CBA 0.5s
```

While this order was not explicitly documented, compatibility must be maintained. Discrete is broken and should be fixed in this PR, but the behavior of Continuous keys should definitely not be changed before or after this PR.

This is my personal opinion, but considering the user’s input order, I believe it’s easier to calculate the duration if we reverse the playback first and then trim it. For example, if you want to play only the first 0.5 seconds of a reversed animation, you should simply enter 0.5 instead of subtracting the animation_length and end point with remembering animation_length on the user side.

Also, with that in mind, I noticed discrepancies in the feature that creates custom timelines from markers. I’m not sure if the marker list needs to be reversed, but this needs to be taken into account for reverse playback.

I think youre right that `has_bones` is only true on the `needs_clear` path so the ternary was redundant so I've move the call into the branches.

I think there is an issue with setting it only in the `else` block though `mesh_clear()` resets `mesh->aabb` but not `custom_aabb` (`mesh_storage.cpp#L884`). So if the fast path sets a custom AABB and a later draw hits `needs_clear` with different bounds, for example because the vertex count changes, `mesh_add_surface()` updates `mesh->aabb` correctly but the stale `custom_aabb` still shadows it in `mesh_get_aabb()`. The polygon then gets culled against the old bounds.

I reproduced it by 

* drawing a square
* moving it off-screen with the same vertex count so the fast path sets `custom_aabb`
* replacing it with a 5-vertex polygon at the center so it takes the `needs_clear` path

so I set the custom AABB on the fast path and clear it on needs_clear which falls back to the surface AABB.

Ah, you're right, I've overlooked this.

body:
This is the right solution for 4.7. Its not ideal since just adding a single area light to the scene will bring back this performance loss when it is in view. 

Overall this leaves us with some open questions:
1. Is this really a big deal? It seems most modern hardware has a much more acceptable performance tradeoff that is more in line with expectations (10% or so). For most users, this solution might be totally fine.
2. Should we prioritize a deferred renderer now? With deferred rendering we can have a dedicated shader pass for area lights, so they will be waaaay faster and won't impact the performance of other light types
3. Should we kick area lights into a hybrid pass? We could calculate area lights in a hybrid pass before the opaque pass. But then they would be more limited (no custom shader support as now, and would support fewer shader features)

For 4.7, this PR is the right approach. We just also need to update the docs (fine to do in a separate PR) to warn that area lights are very expensive and are intended for cinematics.

body: Note that according to the documentation, Jolt's priority works opposite to Godot's priority. Godot: Vs Jolt: > /// Priority of the constraint when solving. Higher numbers are more likely to be solved correctly. Looking at the code for GodotPhysics I think the tooltip doesn't describe what actually happens: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/417cd33bf636a0ede02e5e940e963306ea6fc21c/modules/godot_physics_3d/godot_step_3d.cpp#L136-L158 If I read this code then it will first call `solve()` `iterations` times on each constraint in the current island. Then it will loop and remove all constraints with priority 1. After that it will call `solve()` `iterations` times on the remaining constraints. Then it will loop and remove all constraints with priority 2. etc. This happens until there are no constraints left. So if you set the constraint priority to 1000, then that constraint will actually be solved `1000 * iterations` times, which will be insanely slow. Note that the UI limits the max value to 8, but I think you can set it to any value if you script it. Waht this boils down to is that joints with higher priorities will be solved more accurately. Jolt on the other hand uses the priority only to sort the constraints, so all constraints will be solved `iterations` times, but the highest priority joints are solved last which means that they will be solved more accurately (the first constraints can be violated when solving the last constraints). I think the tool tip needs to be adjusted to: * Reflect that higher values have a higher priority. * Remove the note that Jolt doesn't support it. As you can pass an int to the `set_solver_priority` function and it is cast to an unsigned integer, I think the value set should be `max(0, value)`.

It means the nearest keyframe _before_ the current time.

In this case, the nearest keyframe before t = 1.0 is at t = 0.0.

author: TokageItLab

body:
In the case of nearest interpolation, only the keyframe before the current time matters, regardless if the playback is forward or backward.

Which is to say,
* t = 1.0 -> Nearest is t = 0.0
* t = 3.0 -> Nearest is t = 0.0
* t = 5.0 -> Nearest is t = 4.0
* t = 7.0 -> Nearest is t = 4.0
* t = 9.0 -> Nearest is t = 8.0

> t = M (Between the keys { t = L, v = X.f } and { t = N, v = Y.f })

Writing it like this may mislead the reader into thinking that it's "nearest keyframe in terms of distance" and thinking that the answers should be something like this instead:
* t = 1.0 -> Nearest is t = 0.0
* t = 3.0 -> Nearest is t = 4.0
* t = 5.0 -> Nearest is t = 4.0
* t = 7.0 -> Nearest is t = 8.0
* t = 9.0 -> Nearest is t = 8.0

body: I support this feature, and the code looks good to me. I did not test it. It makes a lot of sense to import data that is semantically "here is my custom data" rather than shoe-horning custom data into further "TEXCOORD_\*" attributes. It's good to keep supporting "TEXCOORD_\*" forever so that Godot doesn't lose data from arbitrary glTF files where that data exists, but "_CUSTOM\*" as a more direct option should take priority when it exists. The name "_CUSTOM\*" is arbitrary and not in the glTF spec, but anything else would be equally arbitrary, and I think "_CUSTOM\*" is a generic enough name (not Godot-centric) that it's not at all unreasonable to see other places or assets adopt this style for arbitrary user-choice custom vertex attribute data. It's not about texture resolution, but whether the texture is meant to be pixel art (precise color palette).

Sometimes, you want to use VRAM compression on small textures because you have a lot of them, or because they cover a tiny surface in 3D space. I've incorporated the latter part of the suggestion still.

body:
The Tab indent regression https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/120103 definitely needs to be fixed, but this PR causes inconsistencies in the calculation of vertical height during line breaks by making it dependent on the presence of characters on the line.

---

Before (RC1):

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8355a913-0757-44f0-91e3-fe538c9cb33f

The height of all line breaks is calculated, consistent.

e.g.

```


```
^ height is x3

```
a

```
^ height is x2

```
a


```
^ height is x3

---

After (this PR):

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c0da60a9-9033-4d40-9b5f-945935257b50

When everything is just line breaks, the height is calculated; however, if there are characters, in cases with two or more line breaks, the height is calculated for only one, inconsistent.

e.g.

```


```
^ height is x2

```
a

```
^ height is x1

```
a


```
^ height is x2

---

[mlttest.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28772301/mlttest.zip)

When there are no characters and only a line break, the vertical height is calculated. If we take this as the base, the current behavior of the RC is more consistent.

If we take this PR as the base, I think you need to make the vertical height for a string with only a line break like:

```


```

should become x0 or x1.

However, personally, I consider the current state of the RC to be more desirable. This is because there are many cases where it looks better to calculate the vertical height of the dialog first before displaying the first character of the line. Ideally, we should make this as options like `ignore_line_break_on_end_of_text` and `merge_consecutive_empty_lines` allow users to choose between "always calculate" / "never calculate" the height of lines containing only line breaks in end of the text, but adding that option should probably be done in version 4.8.

|text|ignore_line_break_on_end_of_text|merge_consecutive_empty_lines|result height|
|--|--|--|--|
|\n\n\n|false|false|x4|
|\n\n\n|false|true|x1|
|\n\n\n|true|false|x3|
|\n\n\n|true|true|x0|
|A\n\n|false|false|x3|
|A\n\n|false|true|x2|
|A\n\n|true|false|x2|
|A\n\n|true|true|x1|
|A\n\nA|false|false|x4|
|A\n\nA|false|true|x3|
|A\n\nA|true|false|x4|
|A\n\nA|true|true|x3|

In any case, I think we should ensure consistency in one of these behaviors here and fix the regression related to tab indent. And I think the right approach is to set that as the default value for the two options mentioned above in version 4.8.

Given the current state of this PR, I assume the default behavior for maintaining the current state is to set `ignore_line_break_on_end_of_text` to `true` and `merge_consecutive_empty_lines` to `false`. However, in that case, the behavior of ignoring the final line break in text consisting solely of line break is missing, so this PR should fix that behavior.

So eventually,

```


```

should become x1, not x2.

body:
I came across this once and while this is an obvious performance hole, I think it's one not fixed so easily.

The key insight is that `memnew_placement(&VariantInternalAccessor<T>::get(v), T);` isn't actually guaranteed to initialize the pointee. It is skipped for primitives such as `double`.

Here you can see it demonstrated clearly: https://godbolt.org/z/1W3aTr7ah

In practice, it still happens to be correct most times because `clear()` happens to reset the payload to `0` for most types, and most types happen to default to `0`. However, I wouldn't put my hand in the fire for this. Even if happens to be true for all types today (I haven't checked), it would be relying on UB.

I think to properly fix the double initialization, more parts of the initialization logic have to be refactored. High time, but will require a good amount of sleuthing work.
author: Ivorforce

body:
Thinking about this again, I think the new version is the right trade-off for the moment.

What we lose: primitive types are sometimes initialized twice (but probably 'optimized away').
What we gain: Allocation types are not initialized twice needlessly.

So it should be overall a safe and needed performance improvement. But nuances are hard so this should be merged early in the cycle.

The unit tests are a little verbose for my taste, but they're acceptable. I wouldn't say a 'templated' version would be strictly better so we can leave them as is.

As a note to the future: This essentially increases the guarantee of `VariantInitializer` to produce the type's default value.
