body:
This is expected behavior. It maintains the behavior[^1] from before https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/119871 caused the regression. The workflow originally envisioned was as follows:

1. Suppose you have a 3.5s walking animation and a 0.7s running animation
2. To blend these smoothly, you unify them to 1s (or any duration) by `custom_timeline` with `stretch_timescale`
3. You adjust the offset so that the same foot is put forward at the 0-second mark for the both animations

Some people might want to swap the step 2 and 3, but in that case, it would require implementing some kind of option or a helper function that allows specifying the start of the cycle with markers when stretch is enabled; For example, one could conceive of an interface where a `use_stretch_timescale` option is added to the AnimationNodeAnimation's marker dialog, allowing the user to specify only a start marker without setting an end.

However, in any case, the addition of such functionality should be done in 4.8 or later, and in 4.7, we must focus only on fixing the regression.

[^1]: Strictly speaking, there is a bug fix. A bug similar to #119980, where `stretch_time_scale` was being read even when `use_custom_timeline` was `false` and `stretch_time_scale` was invisible, existed since before #119871, so I have fixed it by changing the nesting with `use_custom_timeline`. However, since the calculation formula remains the same as it was before #119871, the only change from the behavior before #119871 is the fix for that bug.

body:
There are parts of this that I agree with and think are a good improvement. Thanks!

>I removed the unnecessary explaining of why master needs to be targeted. That info could be (should be) found under the linked page; the rule is simple, and the explanation doesn't need to be there.

I agree with this and think the implementation is good. I agree there is benefit to shrinking lines 2 through 4 to this new single line.

> I changed the wording so that PR's aren't just about fixing problems, but also about addressing proposals.

The intent behind `master`'s "problem(s)" wording is twofold:
1. It frames the PR in a "problem-first" or "problem oriented" paradigm, which encourages both authors and reviewers to think about this PR in terms of the problem(s) that it solves. This is about getting all folks who are involved in PR authoring and review into the [Godot mindset](https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/engine/guidelines/best_practices.html). Review meetings have demonstrated that even seasoned Godot maintainers sometimes need a reminder to use this framing/perspective when reviewing PRs.
2. Creating GitHub issues or proposals for PRs is not strictly required by the Godot project; there are a fairly large number of very good and valid small bugfix PRs that do not have associated GitHub issues or proposals. `master`'s heading is better suited for free-form text that describes small problems that don't need a related GitHub issue.
   - Examples: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/120030
   - https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/120088
   - https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/120259 (this PR)

To make this heading fit better with the two other headings in this PR, we could change it to be `## Problem(s) solved by this PR` instead of the current question-like wording. The question-like wording is a bit of a holdover from a time where each heading would ask a question of the author; with the other two headings not being questions, it prompts revisiting this wording. But this is a super minor style thing. I don't care much about this nitpick on `master`'s wording.

> I removed the second link because nobody is going to check a link for examples, and if they want to, then perhaps that info should be part of the first link?

My perspective is that we should have well-meaning new contributors who are putting effort and thought into their PRs as our primary target audience. Including this link helps these contributors to submit their best work. I believe those who don't bother visiting the relevant links that they are directed to are a secondary audience that should be targeted in ways that do not hinder the primary target audience.

I believe that removing this link that specifically describes how to write a good "Additional Info" section could hinder our primary target audience from doing their best work, even though it may make things slightly better for the secondary audience that doesn't bother looking at linked documentation.

I've included one other comment in this review. Thanks for putting this together!
author: allenwp

body:
Additional info is redundant of the title, whereas the original word of "explanation" is, in my opinion, the most important word of this comment that describes what should be in this section.

```suggestion
Provide an explanation, mention code you are uncertain of, or highlight details that require special attention from reviewers.
```

Otherwise, I like this wording. Another option that is even shorter is to use the original phrasing, but without the redundant "additional info" words:

```suggestion
Provide an explanation of your PR, including areas that you are uncertain of or require special attention from reviewers.
```

(See my main review comment for thoughts about removing the URL from this text)

body: At a quick glance, I would say this is the wrong fix to a real issue. The issue appears to be that `VBoxContainer` in your scene is not putting the `ColorRect` in the right location, not that the `TextEdit` is reporting the wrong size. You can see your `VBox` has a size of `200,240`, with that height being computed from 20+200+20. However, for some reason, the bottom `ColorRect` is being drawn outside of the `VBox`. Image has the `Vbox` selected. From the way the system was designed for maximum sizing, `get_minimum_size()` **should not include it**. That's what `Control::get_bound_minimum_size()` is for. The fact that changing it fixes it in this scenario indicates to me that I messed something up in `BoxContainer`'s children positioning code. I'll have to look into it but I suspect it's due to this line https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/c92ef757cb0fbf3cd4495fcf4bd11299e743ed49/scene/gui/box_container.cpp#L70 not using bound minimum size instead of default minimum size... Frankly ridiculous oversight on my end if so.

Calling `range(0, 10, 0)` already prints an error, but only at runtime:

```gdscript
# [Runtime error] Error calling GDScript
# utility function "range()": Step argument is zero!
print(range(0, 10, 0))

# But:

# [No error]
for x in range(0, 10, 0):
    print(x)
```


The fix (and tests) should be more comprehensive:

1. The analyzer (`step` is a constant expression equal to 0) vs runtime (`step` is a non-constant expression).
2. `range()` inside a `for` loop (a separate opcode) vs regular `range()` (a utility function call).

body:
The thing is that before the fix, when `src_rect.zw` was negative, a flip was applied in the vertex shader - for regular rects this worked correctly since UV is also computed there. 
But NinePatch computes UV in the fragment shader, and there is another flip at line 600. 
These two flips cancelled each other out so NinePatch had no visual flip. 
The fix removes the vertex shader flip for NinePatch, since line 600 in the fragment shader already handles it.

What files exactly do you say that issue has to do with?

body:
Looking at the `p_prologue` parameter, I see that it's added underneath the title of the currently-hovered symbol. As such, I think it makes sense that it would be more dedicated to the symbol being described in the title, and not necessarily the warning the user is hovering (which may include the hovered symbol but also other symbols nearby).

If I'm following correctly, I think the second approach you described with the `VBoxContainer` is essentially what I'm doing now. Here is the current (simplified) result of `EditorHelpBitTooltip`'s `print_tree_pretty()`:
```
 ┖╴@EditorHelpBitTooltip
    ┠╴@Panel
    ┠╴@VBoxContainer
    ┃  ┠╴@RichTextLabel (Errors and warnings)
    ┃  ┖╴@EditorHelpBit
    ┃     ┠╴@RichTextLabel (Title of hovered symbol)
    ┃     ┖╴@RichTextLabel (Description of hovered symbol)
    ┖╴@Timer
```
A single `RichTextLabel` is used for all of the errors and warnings, rather than inserting a `RichTextLabel` for each individual one. Currently, the concatenated warnings and errors are passed as different strings to `make_tooltip()` so that the text coloring can be applied in the method; I could change this to accept a single string that is displayed above `EditorHelpBit`, and then format the text with BBCode before passing it to `make_tooltip()`. That would simplify both the parameter list (one parameter for diagnostics instead of two) and method body of `make_tooltip()` (more of the diagnostic string logic is moved outside of the method).

This (and other functions fixed to be accessors rather than copy-returning functions) fixes downstream bugs, where callers used to call like the following:

```
uint8_t *ptr = image->get_data().ptr();
```

This is a violation of the contract because it's only valid if the returned data is a CoW copy of the owned data - which _happens to be true_ in our codebase, but is not guaranteed by the interface.

So either we could fix callers by forcing them to hold on to the data themselves, or expose a const ref instead. The latter is less work and totally defensible for internal use.

body:
Just to double check before approval (as this change to accessors is the most controversial in the PR), is there any possibility that the previous version might have provided some kind of COW like protection of the internal `Vector<uint8_t>` being changed while the client still had their own `Vector`?

i.e. Is it always a good idea for us to return const reference instead of e.g. `const Vector<uint8_t>`?
author: lawnjelly

body:
Since it's returned as `const`, it's immune to tinkering (unless illegally `const_cast`). 

> i.e. Is it always a good idea for us to return const reference instead of e.g. const Vector<uint8_t>?

I would say so. Returning a copy unnecessarily bumps the refcount too.
Two situations that speak against it:

- If you don't want to expose what data format you store (keep the door open for synthesizing it). In most cases this is a bad idea because requiring conversion on access could be a performance footgun.
- If the data is likely to internally mutate, so your const ref might not be stable. Though in practice you can just make a copy, and this is a risk present all throughout c++, so returning a copy just for that is premature optimization.

So yea, in practice, I would always return a const ref instead of a copy.

body:
I haven’t looked into this much at all, so I am not aware of whether `params.color` and `color_multiplier` use nonlinear sRGB encoding or linear encoding. This implications of this are as follows:

1. If there is a mismatch between the two variables (maybe with the HDR 2D setting or 3D vs 2D rendering), you will get unexpected results.
2. If both use nonlinear sRGB encoding, then the contrast (and hue and saturation) of the colour will be affected by this math. For example, multiplying a nonlinear sRGB colour by 0.1 will reduce the contrast of an image and reduce the saturation of the colour because of the colour channels converging near zero from the nonlinear encoding.
3. If both use linear encoding, then simple brightness adjustments will be somewhat less intuitive to the user because multiplying by 0.5 will not produce 50% brightness, but the contrast of the image and hue and saturation of the colours will be preserved, as the multiplication will be a linear operation.

Other things to consider is whether behaviour changes between the HDR 2D setting or between other rendering configurations (some use linear other use nonlinear sRGB).

Anyway, this stuff is more complicated than it might seem on the surface due to how Godot uses colour maths on both of these encodings, so I wanted to point out the implications so that the right decision can be made on this PR.
